en: Preface to the Selected Carvings from the *Jiaohu ji*:
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of bhikṣus numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, without waiting for the assembly to request it, spoke of his own accord.
In the *Amitābha Sūtra*, from the beginning up to the phrase "single-mindedness without distraction," the essential core of the entire scripture lies in these four characters.
This is just as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, "According to the purity of one's mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-land"—this serves as a commentary on the present point.
It culminates in the final instance of holding up the flower, when [the Buddha] further said, "In my forty-nine years, I have never uttered a single word. At that time, there were a million people...
The heavens are unfathomable. Only the Golden-Colored Dhūta stood by his side, breaking into a smile. The World-Honored One then said:
"I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa to guide future generations."

As schools and sects were established, those who followed the Zen school derided the Pure Land as being attached to forms, while those who practiced Pure Land mocked the Zen school for its nihilistic emptiness.
Thereupon, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, pitying the various factions who had not yet attained the Perfect Teaching, composed the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
By analyzing the three subtleties and six coarsenesses, he demonstrated that the ultimate goal lies in the Pure Land of Mind-Only. From the flow of the Dharma...
In China, at Donglin, there was Master Huiyuan. He revered the sutras and śāstras and attained a profound, intuitive realization of the Mahayana.

He gathered eighteen eminent worthies to practice the *nien-fo* samādhi together; all the friends within that society attained rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, Master Huiyuan was the pioneer of the Pure Land dharma-gate in the southeast.
Furthermore, when the First Patriarch came from the West, he said: "I do not establish written words; I point directly to the human mind."

When it was said that "the mind sees its nature and one attains Buddhahood in this very place," none among the śramaṇas who were scholars of the doctrinal teachings could help but turn their eyes away and look askance;
only Master Ke, alone, was able to accept this under the master’s words and thus first clarified the intent of the "special transmission outside the teachings.

From the six patriarchs down to Dajian Huineng, the Southern and Northern schools diverged into the sudden and gradual approaches, while the Xianshou, Tiantai, and Ci'en schools each established their own lineages in succession. Regarding these...
This was Chan Master Yongming Jue, who succeeded the ocean-like vows of Amitābha and opened the gateway to the practices of Samantabhadra.

He synthesized the three schools of Buddhism into a single, unified thread and exerted every effort to advocate for the Pure Land of the Mind-only. Thus, there is the analogy of the tiger among horned beasts.
The world ranks Yongming as the foremost master in the Eastern Land; who would dare to fathom even a single word or deed of his?

Ah! From the lineage of Emperor Yan down to the present era, there have been such masters as Tianyi Huai, Zhenxie Le, Yang Woei, Tianru Ze, Chushih Qi, Zibo, Hanshan, Xueguan, and Tianjie—each of whom was a towering luminary of the Chan school.
How could they ever have made a distinction between Chan and Pure Land? For this reason, Master Jinen observed these later [developments].

Having studied with faith yet remaining undecided due to lingering doubts, he consequently gathered the essential sayings of eminent masters from successive dynasties whose ultimate intent was directed toward the Pure Land.
He compiled these into a book titled *The Tiger’s Horn* (*Jiaohu*), so that those who follow the Zen school would not dare to treat the Pure Land lightly.
For those who cultivate purity, this work does not disparage the Chan school; it transmits rather than invents, and its benefit is profoundly deep.

Since obtaining this secret treasure twenty years ago, I have never let it leave my hand; it truly serves as an aid to the Eightfold Path. Now, if words are not sublime, they cannot be called ultimate words;
if principles are not perfect, they cannot be termed ultimate principles. This compilation contains words that are true and principles that are direct—is this not indeed so?
"A torch of wisdom for the dark path; is this not the guide for Chan and Pure Land? When my nephew Fa saw this book, he regretted that his reading of it had been so late.
He immediately donated his robes and alms bowl to carve the woodblocks for its circulation, benefiting beings most universally.

However, the original version of this collection was incomplete and lacked full texts. Observing that many of today’s Chan practitioners prefer brevity and weary of verbosity, [he thus undertook this work].

Not presuming upon my own ignorance, I have pruned away the redundant branches and retained only the essential nodes, so that beneath a single word the nature-ground may be illuminated, and within half a scroll the sky of meaning may shine brightly.
Thus one may suddenly perceive the Buddha of one’s own mind without waiting for flowers to bloom, and realize that the light of constant quiescence is not some other land.
How could this be a mere minor supplement? It is truly a great affinity. I hope that you will see it thus.
Upon hearing this, all shall believe and accept it, exhorting one another to read it and transmitting it from one to another to repay the Buddha’s kindness and to support ordinary beings.
May this serve not to辜负 (waste) the original intention behind its composition nor the noble purpose of its publication.
Thus says the eighty-year-old Xindan, who respectfully inscribed these words with washed hands in the Chonglai Jieji Xuan (Hall for Reassembling the Collection) at Haitang.
Table of Contents for the *Jiaohu ji* (Collection of the Tiger’s Horns),

Chan Master Sixin Xin (Linji School) and Chan Master Yihai.
Chan Master Chu-shih Qi; Layman Zhang Wu-jin of Shangzhou;
Layman Ji-chuan Feng; Chan Master Tian-chieh Xin;
Chan Master Tian-ru Ze; and Chan Master Kong-gu Long.
Chan Master Tian Qi, Chan Master Gu Yin Qin,
Chan Master Tiantong Wu, Chan Master Jingshan Xin,
Chan Master Dengwei Zang, and Chan Master Yunding Neng.
Chan Master Zhenxie Le (Caodong School), Chan Master Hongzhi Jue,
Chan Master Wansong Xiu, Chan Master Wan’an En,
Chan Master Dafang Qian, and Chan Master Dafang Tong.
Chan Master Daguan Ke, Chan Master Hanshan Qing,
Chan Master Shouchang Jing, Chan Master Yongjue Xian,
and Chan Master Zhanran Cheng.
Volume II:
Chan Master Boshan Lai, Chan Master Xueguan Yin,
Chan Master Juelang Sheng, and Chan Master Shiyu Fang.
Chanshi Qiju Benjue (Yunmen School):
Chanshi Tianyi Huai, Chanshi Yuanzhao Ben,
Chanshi Mingjiao Song, and Chanshi Fayun Xiu.
Chan Master Fayun Tong, Chan Master Cishou Shen,
Layman Yang Jie (Wuweishi), Lord Wang Mang Zhongyan,
Chan Master Yongming Shou (hereafter the Fayan and Guiyang schools), and Chan Master Wuxu Wuzhuo.
Bai Juyi of Xiangshan, Wen Yanbo of Lugu, Wang Gu,
Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Wang Ruhui of Longshu,
Chen Guan, Attendant Censor, and Qian Xiangzu, Chancellor.
Jiang Gongwang, Palace Attendant for Censorship; Master Huisi, the Distant Ancestor of Mount Lu;
Master Zhiyi, the Patriarch of Great Wisdom;
and Master Yuzhan, the Lord of Compassionate Illumination. (The following are ancient and modern venerable masters. Master Fuyuan.
Chan Master Shanqi Chufeng, the Patriarch of Yudun;
Chan Master Duanyun Che; Master Yunqi;
the Lotus Leaf Man; and Master Xiangguang.
*Jiaohuji*, Volume One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jien of Yixue at Mount Yunzheng.
Proofread by Shangyu, Disciple of Xi Yin at Baiyun Peak.
Chan Master Wuxin (Wu Xin), known as Sishi (Dead Heart), of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture of the Linji School (he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zuxin of Huanglong).
He was the son of the Wang family of Shaocun. At birth, he had a purple flesh-mat covering his left shoulder, which, when bared on the right, resembled a *saṃghāṭī* robe. In his maturity...
He left home [to become a monk] at the age of twenty. Upon arriving at Huanglong, he visited Huaitang. Tang held up his fist and asked, "If you call it a 'fist,' you contradict the truth;
if you do not call it a 'fist,' you turn your back on the truth. What do you call it? The Master was at a loss. It took two years before he finally attained realization;
yet, he still remained fond of verbal debate. One day, Tang suddenly said, "Stop! Stop! Talking about food will never satisfy one's hunger. The Master...
In his distress, he said, "I have come here with my bow broken and my arrows exhausted. I pray that the Master will show me compassion and point out a place of peace and happiness.
The Hall Master said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens; a single mustard seed falls and covers the earth.

As for a place of peace and happiness, I simply detest such a multitude of 'treasures' (conceptual baggage) as you possess, Venerable One. You must die the death of the thieving mind that has persisted since immeasurable kalpas; only then will it be possible. The Master hurried forward.
He departed. Later, while he heard the administrative official beating a practitioner, a sudden clap of thunder struck him, and he attained great enlightenment.
He hurried to see Huìtáng, forgetting to put on his sandals, and immediately proclaimed, "All the people under heaven have merely studied Chan; I am one who has realized it.

Huìtáng laughed and said, "To have won the first rank in the examination for selecting Buddhas—how could you possibly be contained by such a title? Consequently, he was given the sobriquet "Old Man Sīxīn" (Dead Heart).
To one who requested the final word, he showed this verse: "The final word— One must simply cut off the path of the mind.
When the gates of the six sense-faculties are empty, The myriad dharmas are without arising or ceasing. If you penetrate the source here, There is no need to seek liberation.

Throughout my life I have loved reviling others, Only because it brings me long-lasting joy. The Master frequently spoke words of exhortation regarding the cultivation of the Pure Land, saying: "Maitreya..."

The name of Amitābha is very easy to recite, and the Pure Land is very easy to be born into. Those who practice Chan meditation should especially focus on Buddha-recitation. Should their faculties be dull, they may fear that they will not attain great enlightenment in this life;
thus, they should temporarily rely on the power of Amitābha’s vows to be welcomed and led to rebirth there. He further said:
"If you recite the Buddha's name and yet are not born in the Pure Land, I, this old monk, shall fall into the Hell of the Severed Tongue."
Chan Master Huihai Yi of Tokyo (who succeeded Chan Master Fayun Gaofeng) ascended the hall and said:
"The formless Tathāgata manifests his body; he destroys the hosts of Māra and cuts off even a speck of dust.
Where the seven stars cast their slanted reflections and the wind arises, the four seas return to their original master. O worthy ones! At Vulture Peak, Mahākāśyapa..."
At the assembly, he saw the Buddha hold up a flower; seizing upon the opportunity, he smiled. Subhūti, hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, deeply understood its meaning and significance;
he wept with tears of sorrow. Now tell me: who is it that smiles? Who is it that weeps? Have you not heard it said: "Ten thousand streams flow crosswise, yet all head toward the East;
transcendent on all eight sides, naturally brilliant and clear. On the battlefield, the courage of ten thousand men is shattered—a single arrow, two birds."
A hawk fell from the azure sky. A student asked, "I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land; I wonder if such a Pure Land truly exists. The Master said, "The Sūtra says:
'If you wish to attain a pure land, you must purify your own mind. As your mind becomes pure, so too will the Buddha-land become pure.'"
If the mind is pure, wherever one dwells, it is all a pure land. For example, one born into a royal family is certain to inherit the royal heritage;
likewise, one who resolves their mind toward the Buddha-way is born into a pure Buddha-land.
If the mind is not pure, then wherever one is born, it is all a defiled land. Purity and defilement reside in the mind, not in the land.
Chan Master Fanchi Chu-shih of T'ien-ning Monastery in Hai-yen Prefecture (who succeeded Chan Master Yüan-sou Tuan of Ching-shan).

He was a native of Ssu-ming. His secular surname was Chu, and his family had resided for generations in Hsiang-shan. His mother, Lady Chang, conceived him in a dream in which the sun fell into her bosom.
While the Master was still in his swaddling clothes, a divine monk stroked him and said, "This child is the Sun of the Buddha. Consequently, he was given this childhood name.
Tanyao, at the age of nine, followed his clan ancestor Jinweng Xun at Chong’en Monastery in Hushu to receive the tonsure.

At sixteen, he received full ordination. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization. He went to visit Yuansou at Mount Jing, asking, "What is meant by 'speech issues forth but is not sound;
form stands before one but is not an object'? Yuansou immediately replied, "'Speech issues forth but is not sound; form stands before one but is not an object. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!"
The Master was about to offer a word when the old man let out a thunderous shout; the Master, taken aback, withdrew.

Later, having been selected for the project of transcribing the Great Canon, he reached Chongtian Gate in the capital. One night, hearing the sound of the drum atop the watchtower, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
He composed a verse, saying: "Outside Chongtian Gate, the drums roll on and on; In a flash, empty space collapses to the ground. Picking it up..."
"A single sheet of snow upon a red furnace; yet it is the ice of the Yellow River in the sixth month. Later, he went to the Bao Guo and other monasteries in Haiyan, and then moved to Tianning in Jun.
There, he ascended the hall and gave this discourse: He cited a monk who asked Qianfeng, "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions all share one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.
I wonder, where does the beginning of that path lie? Qianfeng drew a line with his staff and said, "It is here."
At this point, the Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. The monk cited the previous conversation and asked Yunmen about it.

Yunmen said, "The fan leaps and bounds up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nostrils of Śakra. A sea bass from the Eastern Ocean receives a blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin.
The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Suppose someone were to come forth and ask: 'Why does Tianning issue such a verdict?'"
[The Master] judged: "Does this still satisfy the intent of the two great elders? To them he said: 'Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Heh-heh-he! La-la-li!
In every land and every dust mote, how many are there? At the crossroads stands the Stone Daring One; suddenly he sucks dry the waters of the vast ocean.
You fellows, you eggplants and gourds—how could you possibly know this? [He] struck the meditation seat and rose. The Master himself—

From his youth, he knew of the teachings of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Pure Land. Every morning at dawn, he recited the ten recitations (*daśanāman*) seeking rebirth in that land, never for a single day being remiss.

Upon residing at Tianning Monastery, he built a chamber in the western wing and dedicated himself exclusively to the practice of pure karma (*viśuddhakarma*). Consequently, he named it "The Western Studio" (*Xizhai*). Within the room, he placed a small bed;
there, he sat daily in the lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), meditating in silence until a great lotus flower appeared. From the stem of that flower...

Leaves filled the entire Dharma-realm. There was a Tathāgata, majestic and dignified in his marks and signs, seated upon them. From the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, he emitted a brilliant light.
Wherever that light shone—upon the towers, pavilions, ponds, groves of trees, and railings—it revealed them as being interspersed with various precious jewels.
The water birds and celestial music all proclaim the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

One beholds Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta at his left and right, surrounded before and behind by the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude, all of whom have attained the stage of non-retrogression.

Rising from meditative concentration, one turns back to observe the observer; both the observed and the observer are empty and unattainable, for even "unattainability" is itself unattainable. (Hongwu)
On the third day of the first month, he was summoned to preach the Dharma, and the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased.

Not long after, he manifested his passing at Tianjie Temple. Having bathed and changed his robes, he wrote a verse, which said: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death. The wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west.
Having finished writing, he said to his attendant, Master Mengtang E: "Brother, I am going. The master replied, "You are going?"
"Where are you going? he asked. "To the West," the Master replied. The official said, "The Buddha is in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?

The Master let out a single, piercing shout and passed away peacefully. Throughout his life, the Master composed the *Hua Jingtu Baiyun Shi* (A Hundred Verses on Rebirth in the Pure Land) in the seven-character regulated verse form, along with various other miscellaneous poems, all of which have circulated in the world.
The true body of our Buddha is immeasurable; Great beings attend him, radiating brilliant light.
At mealtime, there are celestial delicacies; Wherever he walks is a sacred site of enlightenment.
Beneath the courtyard, the azure stream softly murmurs its melody; Before the hall, the jade-like herbs gently waft their fragrance.
The lands of the ten directions are equally adorned; In the end, it is said that the West stands apart from other regions.
The sacred realm of golden cords lies afar; Every pavilion and terrace leans against the clouds and sky.
The warbling of yellow orioles remains beautiful throughout spring; The branches of the jade trees flourish without withering through the years.
Flowing waters have sound as they turn along the banks; Countless beautiful flowers drift with the wind.
On the day the rustic returns of his own accord, Why wait for the worthy ones to summon him with a brief note?
Not yet having returned to Sukhāvatī, he still lingers in Jambudvīpa; Wandering through the dust and wind, how many more autumns will pass?
Fragrant dreams are frequently startled by the rain on banana leaves; My native land lies but a lotus-island away.
In the space of stretching or contracting an arm, the distance is not great; I occupy the very pinnacle above the throngs of men.
The two Great Beings take pity on my old age and illness; Why should they not join hands with me and enter the jade tower?
Pointing afar toward the setting sun at my hometown, A single path home stretches straight as a bowstring.
In the air, music plays every kind of joy; Upon the water, lotus flowers bloom in clusters.
The branches and stalks of various trees become a hundred jewels; Dwelling together and partaking of these, we surpass the gods.
My Master has made a vow to grant us his compassionate reception; May our fifty years of diligent devotion not be in vain.
As we attend the Dharma assembly to pay homage to the Golden Immortal, We gradually follow the fragrant breeze out from the precious lotus.
The light from the red flesh-ushnisha flows on without end; The golden-lotus body shines forth boundlessly.
Layer upon layer, nets of trees hang over the level earth; Each and every flower pedestal reaches the distant heavens.
This rare event within the realms of all Buddhas Is as clear as a bright mirror appearing before me.
The single phrase of my original nature, Amitābha, Is understood by the golden crow and the jade hare.
In an instant he enters the sea and flies back up; In a moment he ascends to heaven and falls again to the west.
Apart from the brightness of day and the darkness of night, There is neither sage-enlightenment nor ordinary delusion.
I urge you to return home; if you do not return, The spring mountains will grieve with the cries of the Sichuan birds.
Speaking of impermanence, one treats all affairs as light; Eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, one is weary of worldly toil.
With a single mind, never retreating, one contemplates the Pure Land; Cultivating myriad virtues together, one remembers Yongming.
Thoroughly cleansing the prayer beads and replacing the string, One firmly upholds the Buddha’s name without ceasing the sound.

Delusive conditions are exhausted, pursued like flowers falling into the void; Leisurely walking before the wind and beneath the moon, one first must study suffering and emptiness when training in the Buddha-way.
When the mind’s expectations are exhausted, hindrances melt away;
One dwells directly beyond the twelve links of dependent origination, Transversely cutting through the three thousandfold world-system.
Profound azure, traceless, opens like a mirror’s surface; Pure blue, spotless, emerges from the lotus grove.
Only when a man reaches this state is he truly extraordinary; In joy and ease, self and object are one.
A pavilion of gold and a terrace of jade, Upon a ground of lapis lazuli, utterly free of even the finest dust.
The Pure Land is but the mind; it has no high or low. The Amitābha of one's own nature neither departs nor arrives.
The red sun was never set behind the horizon; The white lotus is planted only within the root of the mind.
Sentient beings with heavy obstructions must maintain visualization; When visualization reaches its limit, emotion ceases and the eyes open wide.
Do not compare the womb-prison to a flower pond; Hasten toward that pond to claim a branch for yourself.
Once seated upon the Great Flower as a Buddha-child, What need is there for a compassionate mother to bathe an infant?
With the mouth one partakes of the true delicacies of Dharma-joy, And with the mind one attains the wondrous *dhāraṇī* of the Gate of Radiance.
On the day he returned from meditative absorption before the Prajñā Terrace, people were made to long remember the Master of Yanmen.
Though many speak of seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss to the west, in truth it is never apart from the pure mind.
Empty reflections entering the pond are all of jade; sunlight piercing through the trees is entirely of gold.
Phenomena are like dreams and illusions, though not real; yet when the principle is reached, it is perfectly eternal and profoundly deep.
With the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of physical excellence, I entreat you to sit upright and strike upon the spiritual breast.
Do not harm silkworms for clothing, nor till the soil for food; by the waterside and beneath the trees, practice the Way well.
Body and mind are blissful, free from all suffering; the primary and secondary adornments are perfected in a single lifetime.
In every thought-moment, the Buddha’s light radiates from his mouth, and at all times, celestial music resounds throughout the void.
Yet one might still resent shoes and socks stained with mud, when a thousand-petaled lotus is held up beneath one's feet.
A Compassionate Boat floats upon the bitter sea of Sahā;

To cross from this shore to the other, one need not point directly to the source of delusion—simply recite the Buddha’s name. Crossing the turbulent waves directly, one avoids being swept away by the current;
For thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, there shall be constant peace and security, And the five destinies and three paths of suffering shall all cease.
Even if one’s own station is the lowest of the low, it is superior to the nobility and wealth of kings;
how much time is there in this weary life on Jambudvīpa? Health lasts but a brief moment before illness invades;
constantly fearing that passing clouds will obscure the setting sun, one must prepare a pure dwelling and study after the manner of the Eastern Grove.
Pitiable are the ignorant folk of this world, Who do not equal the wise birds among the flowers.
Even the precious trees can discourse on the wondrous Dharma; What prevents one from sitting and listening, putting an end to wandering searches?
My home lies in the western White Jade Capital; In my old age, it is hard to dispel the longing for my native land.
Whenever I gaze upon the crescent moon at the edge of the clouds, It first casts its light upon the foremost blossoms.
The shadows of the *qí* trees are dense yet sparse, And the cries of waterfowl come and go.
The red pavilions and purple halls are ever beautiful in spring; Even with the finest brush and ink, they could not be captured in painting.
Chan Master Duan’an’s eulogy says:
Sitting silently in the western chamber, he contemplates the realm of the Buddha; The Master has realized it through actual experience, his face free of shame.
Sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are always in samādhi— How many practitioners of Chan merely know how to talk about it?
The Eulogy for Master Zong of Qu’an states:
“The Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is that which is proclaimed in the multitude of sutras, praised by all Buddhas, and practiced together by all great Bodhisattvas;
it is truly that upon which the former sages of the Chan school focused their attention. Such is the case with Yongming’s *Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds* and Cijue’s...”
The *Weijiang ji* (Collected Works from the Reed River) all point to the practice of Pure Land as the most essential means for entering the Way; how could one not believe this?
When those who study Buddhism in this world hear the doctrine of "sudden emptiness" (*jia kong*), they fail to investigate it thoroughly and instead become mired in a single track.

Consequently, they regard practitioners of Pure Land as shallow and vulgar, and proceed to slander and reject them. This is to reject the myriad sutras of the Buddhas and the teachings of the patriarchs.
Their ignorance is indeed profound. Reverend Xizhai was a supreme master of the Chan school;
observing him from childhood until his old age, he was diligent in making the Pure Land practice his primary task, refining it with precision and intensity, never ceasing day or night.

He composed several thousand songs and poems, all of which flowed forth from within the state of samādhi. His mastery of both doctrine and practice was thorough, and his integration of teaching and meditation was seamless.
Whether in sweeping away delusions or establishing the truth, his manifestations were myriad and diverse; he cannot be viewed through a single lens.
Indeed, with the profound and vast talent and insight of one from the Western Chamber, scholars find it difficult to fathom his depths. He devoted his heart to the Pure [Land]...
Such was the case with Master Tu. Given this, how could one possibly neglect the Nien-fo Samādhi?
Furthermore, the Elder Yunqi praised him, saying:
"Among the foremost masters of our dynasty, none surpasses Chushi. He constructed a stone chamber and inscribed its nameplate as "Xizhai" (Western Studio).
There exists a three-fascicle collection titled *Xizhai Jingtu Shi* (Pure Land Poems from the Western Chamber). I now record only some ten or so verses therein to illustrate its general purport.
Those who style themselves as Chan practitioners yet hold a superficial view of the Pure Land should reflect upon this with deep and long-lasting consideration.

The lay practitioner Zhang Shangying, Chancellor of State (who succeeded Chan Master Doushuai Yue), whose courtesy name was Tianjue and style name Wujin, first visited Donglin Zong. Zong questioned him regarding his realization, and it accorded perfectly with his own.

He received formal certification (yin-ke). Later, he went to visit Master Yue of Tuṣita Monastery. He conversed with Yue until late at night, and their discussion turned to matters of the Chan school.
Yue said, "Since you have already received certification from Donglin, do you have even the slightest doubt regarding the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?"
The Master said, "I have one. Yuanze asked, "What kind of words do you doubt? The Master said, "I doubt the 'One-legged Verse' of Xiangyan and the story of Deshan carrying his almsbowl.
Yuanze said, "If you have doubts about these, how could you possibly be without them regarding the rest?
As for what Yantou spoke of as the 'Final Word'—does it exist, or does it not? The Master said, "It exists. Yuanze laughed loudly and immediately returned to his quarters, closing the door.
At the Gate of Retreat, the Master slept uneasily one night. At the fifth watch, he descended from his bed and accidentally overturned his urinal.

At that moment, he attained great enlightenment and suddenly realized the meaning of the previous dialogue. He then composed a verse: "The drum falls silent and the bell is hushed as he returns with his alms bowl;
Yantou’s single thrust was like thunder. Indeed, he will live for only three more years— Could it be that he has received the prediction? He then went to knock on the abbot’s quarters.
The Gatekeeper said, "I have already captured the thief and brought him here. Yue asked, "Where is the thief? The official was speechless.
Yue said, "Director of Administration, you may go now; we shall meet tomorrow. The next day, the official recited the previous verse.
Yue then said to him, "In the practice of Zen, one merely fails to sever the life-root and gives rise to intellectual understanding based on words. You have already deeply realized this."
Reaching the point of ultimate subtlety, he caused people to neither perceive nor know it, yet they fell into the realm of conditioned existence.

He then composed a verse to testify to this. The Master once wrote a *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) in which he lamented: "My body occupies the rank of a high minister, yet my mind delights in the Gate of Emptiness.

I contemplate this world: its five turbidities disturb the mind; its multitude of evils confuses one's nature. There is no power of right contemplation, nor any power of the cause of realization; the fundamental nature is ever more [obscured]."
"Oṃ. Regarding the Land of Purity as being solely Mind, I am unable to attain realization through that path; therefore, I respectfully follow the golden-mouthed teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha.
I single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, seeking the great vows and mighty power of that World-Honored One to bestow his grace and protection.
When my karmic retribution is exhausted, I shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, as effortless and natural as a boat riding upon a following current."
...arrived by means of his power.
The Giver of Service, Feng Jie, the Layman Jichuan (who succeeded Chan Master Fuyan Yuan of Longmen), had traveled extensively to visit various teachers since his youth.
Later, he relied upon Fuyan. One day, while walking together with Fuyan in the Dharma Hall, they happened to encounter a boy...
The Master hurried into the courtyard and recited: "Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. He then patted the Master’s back and said, "How wonderful!

At that, the Master attained realization. Later, when he met Chan Master Dahui, who was presiding over the opening of the hall at Mingqing, Dahui raised the story of how Yaoshan attained enlightenment through his study under Shitou and Mazu.
After Dahui finished citing the case, the Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said, "Just now, the Master..."
Regarding the causes and conditions that were raised, the Master understood them. Huì asked, "How do you understand it?
The Official said: "It is not so; *sulu svāhā*. It is also not not-so; *xili svāhā*. It is neither so nor not-so; *suluxili svāhā*. Huì then sealed this with a verse:
So, not so, Neither so nor not so— The three gates of liberation are all open. If one can enter here, One will never again be subject to birth and death.
The Sanskrit and the Chinese are unified as one. Alas for worldly people! To attain this samādhi—afterward, he served as the Prefect of Yangzhou, remaining serene and unflagging wherever he went.
He composed a verse of his own saying: "Beyond my public duties, I delight in sitting in meditation; Rarely have I rested my side upon a bed.
Though I manifest the appearance of a civil official, My name as an Elder is renowned throughout the four seas. From this time forth...
He was styled the Layman Fudong (Immovable). From his youth, the gentleman enjoyed a reputation for brilliance; he ranked first among the scholars at the Imperial Academy.

In composing his examination essays, he frequently employed terminology from the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), demonstrating a profound realization of the nature and principles of reality that commanded the admiration and submission of the scholarly community. Furthermore, he traveled extensively to visit various Zen monasteries.

He profoundly mastered the five schools of Buddhist doctrine. In his later years, he placed firm faith in the teachings of Amitābha, remaining sleepless day and night as he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practices of the Pure Land.

He composed three fascicles of the *Western Paradise Liturgy* (*Xifang li*) and one collection of the *Amitābha Repentance Rite* (*Mituo chan*). He established a Pure Land assembly in his native district.
He was moved by the appearance of śarīra relics within his incense burner, which manifested a ray of light extending across the heavens.

He once used his official stipend to commission copies of the Great Canon and the Four Great Agamas, each in forty-eight sets, distributing them among various mountains to manifest the Buddha’s original vow. One day, he was moved by a profound reflection.
In the style of Huiyuan’s “Return of the Wild Geese” (Guiqulai), discussing the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, the verse says:
“Return, return! The Lotus Society has already opened; why not return?

Reflecting that my years are daily approaching decline, and considering how worldly conditions are truly lamentable, I contemplate the traces left at Donglin and find there the sages of old whom I may follow. Seizing upon the remainder of my life...”
I still remain here, repenting for my errors prior to the age of sixty, like one who dusts his cap after a fresh wash, or shakes his robes after bathing;

cleansing away the dust and grime to hasten toward purity, I seek the subtle and profound mysteries of the wondrous Way. Looking back upon the path ahead, my heart turns toward it with the urgency of a galloping horse.
Entering the chamber of compassion, ascending the gate of liberation, the myriad objects of perception are simultaneously stilled, and the single reality alone remains. Incense fills the burner;
pure water overflows the vessel. Gazing toward the West to cultivate contemplation, one prays to swiftly behold the compassionate countenance.

Entering the samādhi of Buddha-recollection, one experiences the lightness and ease of body and mind. Transcending the highest grade of the nine lotus realms, one closes the dark gates of the six destinies.
Concentrate the spirit in right absorption; shut out the superficial observations of the ears and eyes. Wait until this retribution is exhausted, then point directly toward Sukhāvatī and return.
Walk in meditation along the jeweled trees, linger amidst the flowery gardens, and then go back—return! Go back! Come! Come! (Nirvṛta).
One can only roam within the Pure Land. Reflecting upon the turbidity and evil of Jambudvīpa, what else could one seek but to abandon this land?
Rejoicing in the immeasurable span of life, why should one ever suffer or give way to grief? One meets with those of supreme goodness and takes the Bodhisattva of the Next Stage as a companion.
The ponds are composed of the seven treasures, with boats made of gold; the ground is spread evenly with lapis lazuli, free from any unevenness of high or low.
At the mounds and hills, music arises from the wind-swept trees; from the flowing waters, the voice of the Buddha resounds.
Those who hear it all bring to mind the Triple Gem and rejoice that the conditions of worldly dust have naturally ceased. Alas! Human life is like a dream—how much time can one truly possess?
Why linger here, entangled in fame and profit? When this single retribution is exhausted, where will one go? This floating world is entirely an illusory realm; [only] the Land of Bliss...

A truly auspicious occasion! I have sown lotus seeds within the pond and nurtured them with constant mindfulness of the Buddha. I hope that at the time of my death, the Buddha will come to welcome me.
As I prepare for our parting, I leave behind this poem. From this point forward, may you advance step by step; you shall certainly realize Bodhi—why harbor any doubt?

"Householder, with the dual adornments of compassion and wisdom, you never grew weary of the gift of Dharma. Were it not for one who had manifested through the power of past vows, how could such a thing have been possible?
Later, while serving as a Chamberlain (Jishizhong), he led both monastics and laypeople to hold a 'Concentration on the Buddha' assembly when the army was dispatched to Lunnan.

Upon taking office as the Prefect of Qiangzhou, he ordered a high seat to be set up in the rear hall; facing the imperial palace, he performed a solemn prostration, donned monastic robes to ascend the seat, and expressed his gratitude to the officials."
He passed away while leaning his staff against his knee.
The Chan Master Zhonghuai (who succeeded the Dharma of Chan Master Tiantong Tan) was the son of the Jang family of Fenghua in Ming.
He went to Mount Wutai to receive the tonsure and studied under Chan Master Zhuxi Tan. Xi—
Knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, Xixi assumed a stern countenance toward him and would not exchange a single word with him. The Master’s doubts grew ever more intense.

One day, as Xixi ascended the hall, he brought up the story of Xinghua striking Kebin and questioned the Master about it. The Master replied, "How magnificent! A lion cub indeed. Xixi nodded his head in approval.

Later, while serving as an attendant at Tiantong, Xixi bestowed upon him the robe and whisk, whereupon the Master took the seat of the abbot. When Xixi subsequently moved to reside at Putuo Tianzhu, [the Master followed him].
Regarding the Zhuyongzu and other temples: at the end of the Yuan dynasty, he resided at Dulongxiang Monastery. When the army of Emperor Taizu of Ming descended upon Jinling, the monks dispersed;
the Master alone sat in meditation. Soldiers with weapons filled the space before him, yet they cast down their staves and prostrated themselves.

The Emperor once visited his monastery, and as the Master preached the essentials of the Dharma, the Emperor marveled at the purity and excellence of his conduct and speech. He specially renamed Longxiang "Dadianjie" (Great Celestial Realm). The Master...
Throughout his life, he had practiced the Pure Land teachings in secret. During the Mid-Autumn Festival, he encountered a practitioner of the Pure Land who requested instruction from him.

The Master spoke two verses, saying: "The purple and emerald hues gradually fade as leaves fall; The moon shines bright, making this Mid-Autumn all the more dear. Seek well to return to your Father’s home;
The wild geese cry across the vast sky, stirring the traveler’s sorrow. "Never forget, throughout the day, the one hundred and eight [recitations]. *Mi...* (The text ends here.)
Dhāraṇī remembered that fluency comes from the mouth; she remembered that what is in the mind is what is in the mouth. Spontaneously, birth and death were uprooted from their very source.
One day, after bathing and changing her robes, she sat in the lotus position and wrote this verse: "A lifetime spent in human affairs and worldly entanglements;
Seventy-eight years of leaking and divulging. This morning, I loosen my hands and journey west; Ten thousand miles of clear sky, a single flake of snow. Having finished writing, she passed away.
Chan Master Linru Weize of Shishilin, Suzhou (who succeeded National Teacher Zhongfeng): "Those who have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray.
Those who have no Chan but the Pure Land—of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go [to rebirth]. (Note: This passage includes a citation from Yongming Yanshou Chan Master.)
Observing such statements as these, he advocates for the Pure Land without the slightest concession;
is this not to belittle his own Chan practice while over-praising the Pure Land? This doubt is no small matter; Master, please resolve it for me.
The Master said: "How great is this question! You should know that Yongming’s praise was not excessive; he was one who rendered profound service to both the teachings and the school.
I have once perused various texts on the Pure Land and gained a slight understanding of its general outline.

Fundamentally, it is a method easy to practice and easy to enter, yet it is also a dharma difficult to explain and difficult to believe. This is why, even when the Compassionate Father Śākyamuni was present in the world..."

For the sake of his disciples, he preached the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Foreknowing that sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age would rarely be able to believe and turn toward it, he invoked the Buddhas of the six directions to extend their broad and long tongues and speak words of truth, thereby giving rise to faith and destroying doubt.

And at the end of the sutra, because he was praised by all the Buddhas, he further said of himself: "You should know that in this world of five turbidities and evil, I have performed this difficult task;
for the sake of all the worlds, I have preached this dharma so difficult to believe—this is truly most difficult."
All of these are bitter words of earnest exhortation intended to encourage people to have faith and turn toward the Dharma.

Furthermore, when the Great Compassionate World-Honored One descended to save the beings of the final age, every verse and every phrase proclaimed from his golden mouth was faithfully accepted and practiced by humans and non-humans alike.
Regarding the teaching of the Pure Land alone, why is it that there are those who harbor doubts?
This is truly because the gateway of the Pure Land teachings is most vast and great, and the methods for practicing the Pure Land are most simple and easy.

Because they are so vast and yet so simple, those who hear them cannot help but feel doubt. What is meant by "vast" is that they encompass and include all capacities and faculties without exception. Above...
From Bodhisattvas in their final birth before attaining equal enlightenment who are reborn in the Pure Land, down to the most ignorant of men and women—
even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds— if, at the moment of death, they are able to recite the Buddha’s name, repent,
and direct their hearts toward the Pure Land, they shall all attain rebirth there. What is called "simplicity" means that from the outset there is no hardship or toil.
Furthermore, there are no conditions for confusion or error; one need only uphold the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha.
By this means, one shall leave the Sahā world, attain birth in Sukhāvatī, and reach the stage of non-retrogression, continuing until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Since its vastness is such as described and its simplicity is likewise so great, one may know the praise of Yongming.
There is indeed deep meaning in this, and it is not an error.

A questioner asks: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings. Once the Great Matter is clarified, one ought to practice the Buddha-dharma by manifesting transformation bodies according to the various types of beings.
Yet, those who have attained awakening now seek rebirth in the Pure Land; thus, they loathe suffering and pursue pleasure, showing no concern for others."
"This is not what I desire.
The Master said, "To seek the night-watch upon seeing the dawn—how premature is your calculation! Do you suppose that after a single awakening,"

If habitual outflows are forever eliminated, does one then immediately attain non-retrogression? Is there no further need for the universal study of the Buddha-dharma, the practice of cultivation, or the realization of the fruits [of the path]?
Can one then immediately equal the Buddhas, entering birth and death without being disturbed by obstructive conditions?
If this were truly so, then the great Bodhisattvas who cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices would have spent as many eons as the sands of the Ganges River in vain.
As for "kalpas," one would feel ashamed before you. The ancients said: "Even Śrāvakas possess the confusion of emerging from the womb;

even Bodhisattvas possess the darkness of being separated from their mother's womb. How much more so for those of recent times with meager understanding and shallow realization, who cannot even save themselves?

Even if one has attained a profound realization, possesses lofty insight, and has brought their practice and understanding into accord, with the resolve to deliver others—what can be done if they have not yet reached the stage of non-retrogression and their spiritual power is insufficient?
To dwell in this defiled and evil world and attempt to transform those who are stubborn and fierce is something that even the former sages did not permit;
it would be like attempting to ferry many people across a treacherous sea in a boat that is incomplete and unstable. From oneself...

Both are submerged together; this principle is necessarily so. Therefore, the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on the Rebirth [in the Pure Land]) states: "Those who wish to sport at the gates of hell must be born in that land.
Once they have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the realm of birth and death to rescue suffering sentient beings. For these reasons.
One should seek birth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, as former sages have said: "Until one attains the stage of non-retrogression, one must not mingle with the secular world to save sentient beings;
until one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one must never be separated from the Buddha.

This is like an infant who never leaves its mother, or like a fledgling with weak wings that can only cling to a branch. Now, within this land, the four evil realms of suffering are driven by the laws of cause and effect.
Ensnared by external paths and demonic influences, agitated by disputes over right and wrong, deluded by the appearances of beautiful forms and licentious sounds,
and invaded by the defiling contact of evil conditions, those who have recently awakened and attained realization rarely escape falling back or being defeated.
This is why the World-Honored One earnestly pointed toward the return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This is indeed for a good reason. For in that land, Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma, and the environment and conditions of that Land of Bliss are of every kind of purity.
If one relies upon that Buddha, the power of patience is easily perfected, and one may attain the high stage of Buddhahood and personally receive a prophecy of enlightenment.

Only thereafter does one emerge to transform sentient beings, coming and going without hindrance. For this reason, even those of the highest faculties and sharpest capacities still aspire to be reborn there.
How much more so for those of middle or inferior capacity who have only recently attained initial illumination?

Have you not seen in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* how Mañjuśrī himself recounted his past causes, stating that he had attained the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and would be reborn in the Pure Land?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One recorded of him, saying: "You shall be reborn in the world of Ultimate Bliss. And have you not also seen in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* [the account of] Samantabhadra...
He exhorted the youth Sudhana and the great assembly gathered like an ocean, leading them back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss by means of the ten great kings of vows.
Furthermore, it is not seen that in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, there is a verse of prophecy concerning Nāgārjuna which says:

"In the land of South India, there shall be a monk of great fame and virtue; his name shall be Nāgārjuna. He will be able to shatter the tenets of existence and non-existence, and manifest my unsurpassed [teaching] within the world."
Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma: one attains the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and is reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

Furthermore, it is not seen that in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa harbored a vow to seek birth [there], nor that in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa*, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu possessed the aspiration to go [thither].
Moreover, it is not seen in the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* that King Śuddhodana and the seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were granted permission [to be reborn there].

They were reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). In the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, it is indicated that Lady Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants all went together to behold Amitābha.
Furthermore, Śuddhodana, Vaidehī, and others had all already attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In Western India, those of this caliber are beyond counting. In the Eastern Land [China], there was Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who led his entire community...

As for the eminent sages—the venerable masters of the Tiantai, Xianshou, and other schools—whether monastics or laypeople, who practiced for their own benefit and for the sake of others, how could those reborn in the Pure Land possibly be counted?
Furthermore, King Śuddhodana was the Buddha’s father, and the seventy thousand Śākyas were his kinsmen;
if birth in the Pure Land were of no benefit, would the Buddha have tolerated such a waste of himself?

Regarding his father and kinsmen: as for those previously mentioned who had attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it was permissible for them to mingle with the mundane world to save sentient beings.

Now, since his father, the King, and his kinsmen have likewise attained this patience, yet they still remember their rebirth [in the Pure Land], how profound and far-reaching must be the Tathāgata’s intention to protect and nurture them!
I have often observed that contemporary Chan practitioners do not investigate the Tathāgata’s...
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Not understanding the profound mechanism of the Dharma, they remain empty-minded and arrogant, habitually practicing such狂妄 (frivolous delusion).
Upon seeing those who practice the Pure Land, they mock them, saying: "That is the conduct of foolish men and women;
how vulgar it is! I have often argued that this is incorrect; for while they despise foolish men and women, they actually despise Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, and others.
Not only do they delude themselves regarding the Right Path, lose their own roots of goodness, forfeit their body of wisdom, and extinguish the seeds of the Buddha;
furthermore, they commit the karma of slandering the Dharma and incur the calamity of despising the Sages. Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs regard them as objects of pity.
Thereupon, Master Yongming, out of deep compassion and poignant sorrow, laid bare his very heart and liver to advocate for the Pure Land. Since—
Because they cultivated themselves and transformed the world, when their end approached, they knew in advance that the time had come;
consequently, various extraordinary signs appeared, and their physical remains were encrusted with *śarīra* relics. How could this be limited to Yongming alone?
It was likewise so for Chan Master Xinxin, Chan Master Zhenxie Li, Chan Master Tianyi Huai, Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben, and Chan Master Cishou Shen.
The Masters: Chan Master Sengcan of Nan Yue; Chan Master Fazhao; Chan Master Jing’ai; Chan Master Datong of Jingci; Chan Master Huaiyu of Tiantai;
Chan Master Daozhen of Liang; Chan Master Daocuo of Tang; Chan Master Fazhen of Pilu;
Chan Master Shounu of Gusu; Chan Master Jian of Beijian; and Chan Master Fali of Tianmu—these great masters...

Lao et al. were all masters of the Chan school. When examining their secret cultivation and manifest transformations, they were in complete agreement in promoting the essential principles of the Pure Land.
This was not merely the case for these great elders; I once heard an old master say:
Combining the lineages of the five houses and including all Zen monks throughout the world—whether they have attained awakening or not—not a single person fails to return to the Pure Land.
When asked the reason for this, he replied: "Take, for example, Chan Master Baizhang Dazhihai;
he was the dharma-heir who received the transmission from Mazu of Jiangxi. The monasteries throughout the world were established based upon him. From antiquity until now..."
Nowadays, not a single person dares to debate its flaws; the world’s pure regulations are practiced according to this tradition.
From beginning to end, there is not a single matter that dares to contravene its laws. Observe the rules for reciting for sick monks, which state:
"The assembly gathers and chants in unison, 'Namu Amida Butsu,' either a hundred times or a thousand times. The dedication of merit (hōkō) and prayer of aspiration is as follows:"

While the conditions for remaining were not yet exhausted, he attained lightness and ease prematurely; his great life-span could not be escaped, and he returned directly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Furthermore, when escorting a deceased monk, the assembly recites mantras and performs the dedication of merit, with the following prayer: "May his spirit transcend to the pure realm and his karma cease from worldly toil;
may the lotus of the highest grade bloom, and may the Buddha grant him the prediction of one more birth. As for the occasion of cremation, there is nothing else to be done.
Simply have the *vinaya-dhara* lead by chanting "Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss" in a loud voice ten times;
as the assembly chants along with him ten times, this is collectively termed the "Ten Recitations."
Having finished the recitation, he again performed the dedication, saying: "The ten recitations of praise above were intended to assist in rebirth in the Pure Land;
is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land teachings? Since the time of Baizhang, all rites for escorting deceased monks have been conducted according to this method."

If this is so, then it must be true that when one unites the lineages of the five houses and encompasses all the Chan monks in the world, there is not a single person who does not return to the Pure Land—is this not so?
One must understand that the intent behind the founding patriarch Baizhang’s establishment of the rules could not have been such without some basis.
Since you do not comprehend the patriarch’s intent, yet you yourself fail to give rise to introspection.

Regarding the mind of awakening, you falsely claim that those who have attained enlightenment do not aspire for rebirth there; in this regard, no one among the world’s Chan practitioners holds a more stubborn adherence than you.
You ask: "There are many categories of pure lands where beings dwell together; why then do you single out the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and exclusively praise it?"
The objects are superior and the conditions are superior.
Why is this? The Master said: The sutra states, "The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings; they experience only various joys. Therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)."
Now, let us compare this by contrasting it with the Sahā world. Here, one possesses a physical body of flesh and blood; for all who are born, there is suffering.
There, however, one is born through transformation from a lotus flower; thus, there is no suffering of birth. Here, the seasons shift and change, and decay gradually encroaches;
there, cold and heat do not alter, and thus there is no suffering of aging. Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize, and illnesses frequently arise; there, however...
Their transformed bodies are fragrant and pure, free from the suffering of illness; whereas here, those over seventy are rare, and impermanence is swift.
There, their lifespan is immeasurable, free from the suffering of death. Here, there is affectionate attachment to kin, and where there is love, there must be separation;

there, they have no parents, wives, or children, and thus no suffering of being separated from loved ones. Here, there are enemies and vengeful foes, and where there is enmity, there must be a meeting.

That [state] is a supreme gathering of the virtuous, free from the suffering of association with the hated and disliked. This [state], however, is one of hardship, hunger, and cold, where greed and seeking are never satisfied.
There, clothing, food, and precious treasures for enjoyment are spontaneously present; here, the physical form may be ugly and foul, with many impaired faculties.
There, the appearance is upright and majestic, and the body possesses radiance; here, one revolves through birth and death. That [state], however...
They have eternally realized non-arising. Here there are the sufferings of the four realms of existence; there, even the names of the three evil destinies do not exist.
Here there are hills, mounds, pits, and chasms; forests of thorns; mountains of earth and stone; and it is filled with foul impurities. There, however, the ground is made of pure gold.

Jewel trees reach toward the heavens; towers soar with the seven treasures; flowers bloom in four colors. Here, the Buddha of the Twin Śāla Trees has already passed into extinction, and the Buddha of the Dragon Flower has not yet appeared.
There, the Honored One of Immeasurable Life currently preaches the Dharma. Here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are merely objects of veneration for their empty names;
there, he is personally accompanied by those two superior beings as his most excellent friends. Here, the various māras and heterodox teachers cause turmoil and distraction.
In the land of True Cultivation, the Buddha’s transformation is unified, and the traces of Māras and heretics are severed. Here, however, seductive colors and lascivious charms delude practitioners.
In that land, the primary retribution is pure, and there are truly no women; here, evil beasts and malevolent spirits stir up perverse sounds.
In that land, water birds and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. When these two lands are compared, their environments and conditions are vastly different.
The excellences of the Land of Bliss are infinite in number; I have not yet had the leisure to enumerate them all.
Its environmental excellence can satisfy the sentient beings' aspiration for purity, and its causal excellence can augment the practitioners' power of cultivation.

Although there are many types of pure lands where one may dwell together [with the Buddhas], it is specifically the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss that is indicated here, for its conditions for practice are fully complete.

Question: If one creates evil throughout a lifetime but recites the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, one can still be reborn there while carrying one's karmic burdens, and furthermore, there is no falling back from that state.
This power of Amitābha’s vows is truly inconceivable. Nevertheless, while alive, I shall first attend to my worldly affairs.
"Regarding one's practice: is it acceptable to wait until the very moment of death before practicing nianfo?
The Master said, "Alas, alas! What kind of foolish and erroneous words are these? Arsenic and poisoned wine are the most lethal of poisons;
yet your current words are more toxic than arsenic and poisoned wine. Not only do they deceive and mislead yourself,"
Furthermore, this is precisely what deceives and misleads the monastics and laypeople, both men and women, throughout the world.

As for those so-called "evil ordinary beings" who recite the Buddha's name at the moment of death, it is because they possess roots of goodness and the karmic conditions of merit from past lives that they encounter a spiritual teacher and are thus able to practice nianfo.
Such fortunate occurrences are rare; among ten thousand people, there is not even one or half a person who experiences them.
Do you truly believe that everyone has such good fortune at the moment of death? Have you not seen what the *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) says?

There are ten kinds of people in the world who are unable to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*) at the time of their end: first, because they may not encounter virtuous friends, there is no one to exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name;
second, because the suffering of karma envelops their bodies, they have no leisure to practice Buddha-remembrance; third, perhaps due to pervasive wind...
1. Loss of speech, such that one cannot invoke the Buddha’s name. 2. Madness and loss of mind, whereby focused contemplation cannot be achieved.
3. Encountering water or fire, leaving no leisure for sincere devotion. 4. Meeting with jackals or wolves, resulting in the absence of virtuous friends.
5. Having evil friends at the time of death, who destroy one's faith. 6. Overeating to excess, leading to a stupor that persists until death. 7. Being in the midst of a military array.
In battle, they perish in an instant. Tenth, they suddenly fall from high cliffs, their lives destroyed.
These ten kinds of events are all matters commonly heard of and seen with the eyes; whether monk or layperson, male or female, everyone encounters them.
They may be summoned by past karma or induced by present karma, yet they suddenly appear before one's eyes, impossible to avoid. Furthermore, you...
These are not sages with supernormal powers who possess the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and can thus know whether one has karma at the time of death;

nor are they those with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which can discern whether a death will be auspicious or miserable due to the ten kinds of evil conditions mentioned above.
Suddenly encountering it, one kind [of karma] simply brings it to an end; then there is no room for further maneuvering.

Even if you are surrounded by learned masters or living Buddhas, they cannot save you. You must then undergo retribution according to your karma, suffering pain and punishment within the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties.
By that time, you will wish to hear the name of the Buddha, but you will not hear it. It is straightaway...
Even if you were not subject to such evil conditions and died merely of a natural illness, you would still not escape the wind-swords that dismember the body and the separation of the four elements,
like a live turtle shedding its shell or a crab falling into boiling water— overwhelmed by agony, terrified, and trembling with fear.
One cannot practice the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo).

Furthermore, even if you die without illness, or if your worldly affairs are not yet concluded and your attachments to this world have not ceased—such that you are agitated in your heart by craving for life and fearing death—even if you are a layperson, with domestic matters unresolved and funeral arrangements unfinished, amidst the wailing of your wife and children and a hundred kinds of anxieties and torments, you will still be unable to practice the Buddha-remembrance. Moreover...
Even before you die, when you are afflicted by even a slight illness, you will endure pain and suffering, wailing and groaning;
you will seek out medicine and doctors, offer prayers and perform repentance, and your distracted thoughts will fly about like birds, such that you will be unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even before you fell ill, it was simply because your years had grown old and the signs of decay had appeared;

you were exhausted and frail, filled with sighs, lamentations, and anxieties, and amidst this aging body, you could not manage to settle yourself in mindfulness of the Buddha on either the left or the right.
Furthermore, even before you grew old—during the days of your youth and vigor—it was precisely then that you should have been well-suited for mindfulness of the Buddha.

At such times, should your deranged mind not yet have subsided and you remain entangled in worldly affairs—clinging here and there, lost in chaotic thoughts, with your karmic consciousness wandering aimlessly—you will be unable to achieve success in reciting the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even if you possess leisure and freedom and are determined to practice cultivation, [you will still fail].
Within the phenomena of the world, one cannot yet illuminate them through insight, let go of them, maintain them firmly, or remain seated amidst them without interruption.
Suddenly, when even a slight境 (object-condition) manifests before one, the single master follows along in delusion; thus, one is unable to recite the Buddha's name.
Look at him when he is old and sick, compared to the days of his youth and leisure.
If even a single matter hangs upon his mind, he is already unable to recite the Buddha's name; how much more so when facing the time of death?
And yet you say, "Just carry on with worldly affairs"—you are truly a fool to speak such foolish words. I can guarantee that you have misapplied your body and mind. For now—
The world and worldly affairs are like dreams and illusions, like shadows and echoes; which of them has any real efficacy?

Which of them can substitute for [escaping] birth and death? Even if you extensively construct monasteries, increase the permanent endowments, strive for fame and status, and form alliances with officials and the powerful—though you may think you are performing many good deeds, you do not realize that you have offended the Tathāgata and failed to embody the Way.
Fundamentally, this concerns the precepts regarding the extensive construction of monasteries and the like. Have you not heard it said that conditioned achievements harbor many faults?
Before the heavenly realms are realized, the hells are already formed; before the nature of birth and death is clarified, all things become the root of suffering.

When the light of the eyes falls to the ground and one undergoes suffering, only then will one realize that everything done throughout one's life was merely adding shackles to shackles and adding chains to chains—within the cauldrons of hell.
In the boiling cauldron below, firewood and charcoal are added; atop the Sword-Tree, blades and spears are supplied. Beneath the *kāṣāya*, one loses their human form;
for ten thousand kalpas it will be difficult to recover. Even an iron-hearted man would shed tears upon hearing this.

When the Patriarchs thus spoke with such bitter urgency to exhort people, did they ever permit you to merely attend to worldly affairs, waiting until the moment of death to recite the Buddha’s name? You should reflect: while a person exists in this world, can there truly be...

If one can secure even a single day’s light to recite the Buddha’s name for that day, or a single period of effort to cultivate pure karma for that period, then as for the time of death—whether it be a good death or a bad death—it will serve as my provision.

Chan Master Hanyue Fazang of Dengwu Mountain (who succeeded Chan Master Wuzu Fayan of Tiantong):

If one’s cultivation of the mind is genuine, one must first purify the mouth. If one recites the Buddha's name without eating vegetarian food, karma will remain and the Buddha will find it difficult to deliver one. The Buddha is purity itself.

O King, how can one be stained by defilements? By failing to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and perform wholesome deeds. A lotus grows upon a stony bank, yet it is moved by water endowed with the eight virtues;

never fail to provide it with nourishing irrigation. Therefore, the Buddha exhorted those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: "Firmly practice the ten wholesome paths and truly uphold the five precepts."

Practice the six perfections alongside the act of giving; with every step upon golden sand, remain unstained by dust. Greed, anger, and delusion—delusion is the root. Alcohol can bewilder even the most enlightened person.
If you are truly enlightened, cut off alcohol first; not a single drop touching your lips makes you a master.
The thirty-six faults have been heard of since ancient times; strive with all your might to firmly maintain your resolve. I speak of this again and again; it is far too much to spare.

If one thinks of Amitābha today and Amitābha tomorrow while intermingling impure thoughts, merely wasting time and years, one will fail to achieve accomplishment. On ordinary days as well, do not speak of being self-complacent or self-assured.
When the time of death arrives, one fails to gain mastery over oneself, leading to the regret of "biting one's own navel.

Consequently, one comes to doubt that the Buddha-dharma possesses efficacy, slanders the Great Dharma Wheel, and falls into the most wretched realms. This occurs solely because, during one's life, one never personally encountered someone who pointed out the essential meaning;
thus, one is misled by a mistaken understanding of the four characters "single-mindedness without distraction" (*yixin buluan*). Now, as for "single-mindedness without distraction":
Simply by single-mindedly reciting the name of the Buddha with all one's might— more fervently than fervent— if emotional consciousness is severed once and for all,

then past events will no longer come to the mind through deliberation, future matters will not be grasped through conjecture, and the objects of the present will not be seized by the mental consciousness.

The three minds are severed; this is called severing the prior and posterior limits. Because of this, when one hears or sees, encounters or meets with conditions, the path of the mind is immediately cut off.
One directly attains the state where empty space is pulverized and the great earth sinks level;
self and others alike vanish, and not a single dharma stands before the eyes. It is like the myriad phenomena manifested within a great round mirror—clearly perceived.
There is not a single thing that can be pointed to or conceptualized; all discrimination has vanished. Body and mind come and go like clouds.
This luminous state is called "single-mindedness without distraction," for at this point there is no mind that can be distracted.
Once this state is realized, even if the five aggregates and the three poisons manifest during one's practice, they are merely floating clouds and bubbles upon water. Thus it is said: "The five..."

The aggregates are like floating clouds, coming and going in the void; the three poisons are like bubbles, vainly appearing and disappearing. This is precisely the perfect realm within the essence of the six perfections and myriad practices.
If one does not reach this realm, although there may be temporary purity, it is merely a place of brief rest.
When pure, it exists; when disturbed, it is lost. If it is lost even during times of disturbance, how much more so at the moment of death?
This is the ultimate moment of extreme pain and suffering. When one is in such agony, even that [state] cannot be attained; how much less so when one is in a state of total collapse?
Thus, the minor states of tranquility experienced throughout one's life are merely matters pertaining to the periphery of the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*).

Upon reaching the point of collapse, the presiding intelligence of the intellect and consciousness is of no further use. Lately, there has been a generation of people who are skilled at lecturing on the Western Paradise and diligent in their practice.
As for those who practice, there are many who have never reached the stage of "fainting" (mental exhaustion) in their cultivation;
when death arrives, they immediately lose their composure and fall into a state of frantic confusion. We must not remain ignorant of this failing.
To escape this failing, one must be a person of great courage and vigor. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there be good sons or good daughters..."

whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days— with single-mindedness and without distraction—

Śāriputra, because I see this benefit, I speak these words: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should resolve to be born in that land.
It can be seen that the ultimate practice personally pointed out by the Buddha does not exceed the single act of upholding the four-character name of the Buddha.
A single phrase atop another phrase; one sound chasing the next. It is like a fierce general brandishing a blade in pursuit of a thief:

exert yourself and press straight forward without even a moment’s rest. Such practice is not something achieved through years or months of leisurely effort, nor is it something that only reaches completion when one reaches old age and death.
