When the shadow of form falls upon the gates of the six sense organs and penetrates deeply into the fields of the eight consciousnesses, it constantly arises within the processes of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
It gives rise to emotion and attachment that cannot be relinquished;
it engenders various delusions, produces various clingings, creates various karmas, and causes one to undergo various sufferings—all of which have this shadow as their cause. This shadow is...

It is the seed; it is also, moreover, habitual tendency (*vāsanā*). Because the Buddha knew that habitual tendencies are difficult to eliminate, he taught people to grasp and hold a single phrase of Amitābha, focusing their minds on reciting it.
As habitual tendencies gradually dissolve, the light of the mind gradually reveals itself, and one’s fundamental nature is gradually realized.
If one continues this moment after moment without ceasing, the habitual tendencies will inevitably be completely eliminated and the seeds of the sense-faculties will naturally be severed.
One will then naturally walk hand-in-hand with all Buddhas, breathing through the same nostrils; is this not what is meant by "a single phrase, clearly transcending ten billion worlds"?
As it is with the desire for form, so it may be understood by analogy for sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If a person wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind so that it is like empty space, remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and the various realms of existence, such that wherever they turn, there is no obstruction.
This realm of the Buddha is inherently present within every person.
Each and every thing is already manifest; it is only because of the obscuration of worldly passions that they are transformed into an ocean of karma.

Now, if you wish to overturn this ocean of karma and turn it into the realm of the Buddha, you must first purify your mind. Once the mind is purified, you will spend your days constantly within the realm of the Buddha.

The reason the mind fails to attain purity is entirely due to its defilement by deluded thoughts and the various realms of existence. Those who wish to distance themselves from these should apply themselves with rigorous self-exhortation.
With single-minded focus and without distraction, hold fast to the name of the Buddha. Do not concern yourself with right or wrong, nor with success or failure;
simply trust in the Buddha’s words. Let pure mindfulness succeed one another, making each phrase distinct. If you maintain this practice for a long time, it will surely come to pass.

To transform deluded thoughts into non-existence and to transform the various realms of existence into liberation—this Dharma-gate of the Pure Land appears easy when observed, yet is truly difficult to uphold. This is because those who study it are few, while those who harbor doubts are many;
thus, few are able to place their faith in this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate. For this reason, the *Amitābha Sūtra* describes it as difficult.
Regarding the Dharma of faith: the profound purport of the Buddha is to cause people to borrow Amitābha of the Western Land to realize the Amitābha of their own original allotment;

to borrow the Pure Land of the West to realize the Pure Land of their own original allotment. Once one realizes the Pure Land and Amitābha of one's own original allotment, then the Western Land is likewise the Buddha-land of one's own original allotment.
It is not only the Western Land that is the Buddha-land of one's own original allotment.
Thus, the defiled lands of the eastern direction and all sentient beings therein are also one's own original pure land and one's own original Amitābha.
Extending even to the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single speck of dust that is not my own original Buddha-land.
Such wondrous function is entirely contained within the single phrase "Amitābha. To develop its root and open its source—this is what is meant by "one being pure and one being [the land]."
All is pure. One realization is the realization of all. This single dharma-gate is profound in its essence and far-reaching in its meaning;
none but those of extensive learning and long-standing cultivation can penetrate it thoroughly.

The western direction is named the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). This is indeed the bliss that accords with the true nature of reality. Clothing and food are spontaneously provided; pavilions and terraces are fully equipped;
jewel ponds appear at will; and celestial music fills the sky. There is no oppression of scorching heat, nor does anyone suffer the freezing cold that cracks the body.
When a gentle breeze blows, afflictions are cast away and extinguished. Flower rain swirls about, and celestial fragrances are richly perfumed. There are birds there—
Because the Dharma is preached, those who are deluded are awakened. Because they have the supreme good as their companions, those who are heterodox are rectified.
Day and night, the light dispels all obscure confusion; pure seeing and hearing cause wisdom to increase. River-sands of samādhis are realized without seeking;
how could inexhaustible wondrous functions require long cultivation? Furthermore, there is no fear of falling back, and there is instead the spirit of diligence.
How joyful! For this reason, the Buddhas of the ten directions offer their praise; it is truly the gateway to the inconceivable Mahāyāna.
It ultimately enables one to transcend the three realms horizontally and ascend directly to the eighth stage—how could this be compared to the provisional vehicles of the two lesser vehicles?

If one focuses the will single-mindedly on the Western Land, within seven days, should one attain the state of "one mind undisturbed," one will immediately reach the ground of non-retrogression and pass away with hands cast loose.
Like the solitary moon shining brightly in the midst of the sky, undefiled by even a speck of dust; like a lotus emerging from a foul land, he reaches his final conclusion.
Standing or sitting, he passes away, roaming at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, no different from Amitābha Buddha himself.
After awakening, one is further able to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name to be born in the Western Land, thereby attaining the ultimate excellence of the various limits [of wisdom].
Being born once in this realm, there is nothing one does not know or understand; one is able to exhaustively fathom the source of all dharmas.
This is called attaining the limits of all wisdom together with the Buddha. First, by drawing near to Amitābha, upon the ground of the ordinary mind...
All afflictions—both their active manifestations and their seeds—are completely severed and exhausted; this is called being equal to the Buddha in reaching the limit where all afflictions are empty.
Even a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* still universally studies all mundane dharmas.
This is for the purpose of transformation and guidance. Those born in the Western Land are as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand;

their various delusions that obstruct transformation and guidance have been severed completely without remainder. This is called being equal to the Buddha in shattering the limits of all dust-mote-like afflictions.

As for the ignorance that is most difficult to sever—this is what the Elder Śākyamuni cultivated throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, and now he has attained birth in the Pure Land.
Such a person immediately attains the sudden severance of ignorance and swiftly ascends to Equal Enlightenment; this is called reaching the same limit as the Buddha in severing all ignorance.
Those who are born in the Western Land walk upon the earth as if on water and walk upon water as if on earth, manifesting various kinds of transformations.
There is nothing they cannot do; this is called attaining the limit of possessing all supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) like the Buddha.

Upon hearing the wondrous sound of the Dharma once, they penetrate to the very depths of the principles of nature, understanding them clearly and without obstruction, experiencing joy in accordance with their true nature;

this is called attaining the limit of perceiving the essence of all natures like the Buddha. Having once received the Buddha’s spiritual power, they possess the power of liberation, being able to perform what is difficult to perform.

That which is difficult to transform, they can transform; that which is difficult to subdue, they can subdue. Regarding the practices and vows for enlightenment, there is nothing they cannot cultivate and nothing they cannot fulfill.
Furthermore, they possess immeasurable wondrous functions and immeasurable wondrous adornments; this is called attaining the ultimate limit of all sublime practices together with the Buddha.
Reaching this stage is termed "being born into the family of the Tathāgata" and sharing the same enjoyment as the Buddha. If one clarifies the mind...
If, after seeing one's nature, one immediately desists and lacks the aspiration for the Western Pure Land, this is to dwell in the illusory city of the śrāvakas;
one will ultimately fail to enter the precious abode of the Tathāgata.
Ordinary people, failing to awaken for even a single thought-moment, become deluded regarding this great matter and lose the adamantine nostrils;
they thus transform into defiled and delusory thoughts. As soon as these thoughts sprout within, whatever manifests at the gates of the six sense organs is nothing but defiled affairs.
Consequently, all that is externally perceived becomes a defiled and impure land. Once a world-system is...
Defilement. The worlds of the ten directions likewise become defiled lands. Immeasurable subtle meanings and hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all transform into thorns.
Whatever is seen by the eyes and heard by the ears—every phenomenon, every dharma—becomes entirely a realm of affliction.
Thus, sentient beings are bound and fettered by these, undergoing immeasurable suffering and failing to attain liberation. The Buddha opened the subtle...
This is a wondrous shortcut that enables one to walk with confident steps; it can sever this suffering and transform this mind.

You must simply cast aside all worldly affairs and single-mindedly hold up the name of Amitābha, never ceasing whether in leisure or in haste. Practice this for years and months, and it will naturally become pure and free from admixture.
When it is pure and yet more pure, you will attain a state of single-minded sincerity; this is precisely what is meant by a single thought of purity.
Purity. Because of the purity of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are also purified.

Once the internal body and mind have attained purity, the external perceived world of the Western Land is likewise purified. Expanding this further, the worlds of the ten directions are all equally pure.
This state is refreshingly free from the four propositions and a hundred negations; it is entirely an extraordinary, wondrous function, and everywhere pure.
It is pure. Indeed, it is so. Thus, as a father, being pure, one can exercise compassion;
as a son, being pure, one can fulfill filial piety; as a ruler, being pure, one can employ wisdom; as a minister, being pure, one can manifest loyalty;
as a monk, being pure, one can accomplish the Way; and as a layperson, being pure, one can maintain simplicity.
In their state, they are pure amidst favorable conditions and pure amidst adverse conditions as well. Even the lustful conduct of the courtesan Puṣpamitra is pure;
the anger of King Anala is pure; and the indulgence in ignorance by the Brahmin Jālandhariputra is pure.
All afflictions and ignorance are transformed into purity. [This applies even to] brothels and wine...
The four quarters are likewise pure. Only upon reaching this realm can one truly enter the demon palaces and tiger dens;

whether in heaven or among men, one may clap hands and stride across with ease, singing sorrowful songs and performing dances as a man of sovereign freedom. Thus, it is through the recitation of the Buddha's name that one can be born in the Western Land.

Shattering birth and death, one emerges from the triple world; transcending entanglements and fetters, one escapes the fiery pit. Revealing one’s original nature and baring one’s claws and fangs—how great indeed is this power!

To possess such a swift path and yet be unable to follow it, even going so far as to reject and disparage it oneself—such are truly inverted ordinary beings, seeds of delusion and confusion; how most pitiable they are!
The single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*) is the method for penetrating deeply and grasping the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible treasury.

This is indeed inherent in every person; yet, because it is obscured by the conditions of worldly dust, one is unable to see it for oneself. One must practice mindfulness of the Buddha to reveal and manifest it.
It is like a destitute person who, knowing the location of a hidden treasure, must focus their mind and apply themselves with single-minded devotion, exerting the utmost effort with a spade.
One weeds it; once the floating mud is exhausted, the treasure store appears of itself. It is by this that one is called a great, wealthy elder.

Know, therefore, that the single phrase "Amitābha" should not be parted from, whether walking or sitting. Without interruption between suffering and joy, let the mind continue in succession with the mouth and ears clearly distinct, advancing ever forward without ceasing.
When the mindfulness is thus earnest, the veils of dust are suddenly opened; having entered the hall and the inner chamber, one is then fit to receive [the teaching].

This is the inexhaustible treasury. Although in this age of the Dharma’s decline there are many who enter the path of Chan meditation, it is difficult to find those who do not remain stuck within their current state.

If one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha while maintaining a superior conduct, then one’s observance will be ever more concise and one's merit ever more profound—just as was the case with Sixin Xin, Tianru Ze, Yuanzhao Ben, and Cishou Shen.
Zhenxie Li, Yongming Shou, and other great masters of the past were the pillars and beams of the Five Houses; they all entered through this single gate to realize the Tathāgatagarbha.

Therefore, by penetrating deeply into this, dregs naturally dissolve away, ignorance naturally becomes utterly purified, the six sense faculties naturally become clear and pure, the ocean of karma naturally dries up, and birth-and-death naturally reach quiescent extinction.

Samādhi will naturally manifest before them; the six supernormal powers will naturally become complete; they will naturally transcend to the other shore; and their merits will naturally be accomplished.
Penetrating both cause and effect, benefiting both self and others, they shall be reborn together in the Western Land and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
An ancient worthy said: "If one fully restrains the six sense faculties and maintains pure mindfulness in succession, within seven weeks one will attain samādhi.
Once samādhi is attained, all are liberated; it is taken from inexhaustibly and used without depletion.
Yunqi said: "To equalize with all sages in a single word, and to transcend three great kalpas in a single thought—this can only be the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name."

Is it not so? Such directness and clarity, without falling into fragmentation, allows for an immediate transcendence of the causes of outflows and the eternal realization of the fruit of the unconditioned.
Regarding this extraordinary Dharma-gate, I vow that all sentient beings throughout the great earth shall enter herein. Someone may ask:
as for the Western Pure Land, what is its underlying meaning?
The Master replied: "Pure Land is precisely the point at which one’s spiritual cultivation reaches its ultimate refinement;

when all dross has been exhausted and not a single speck of defilement remains, such that both sagehood and ordinariness are transcended and both truth and falsehood are forgotten—only then is it the true Pure Land."
This is the very place where we humans find security for our bodies and establish our lives. Regarding the term "the West," it possesses eight meanings.
Discussing it in terms of the five colors, the west is white; it is free from all defilement, which is the symbol of purity.
Those who cultivate the Pure Land take a single phrase of Amitābha to cleanse the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; this is the purification of the cause.

When the cause is purified, the fruit is likewise purified. Therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are born in the Western Paradise at the time of death; this is precisely the correspondence between cause and effect.
In terms of the four seasons, the East is the land of growth and development; it is the image of spring. The West is the land where life ripens;
it is the image of autumn. This is just as an ordinary person awakens the aspiration for enlightenment in the East and attains rebirth through the practice of nien-fo (Buddha-recitation).
Thus, one brings the fruit of the Path to maturity in the West.

To discuss this by way of the Five Elements: the East belongs to Wood, and the West belongs to Metal. When wood encounters the axe, it is carved and shaped, transforming from a piece of crude timber into a ridgepole or beam.
Ordinary beings are like that crude wood; if they are willing to single-mindedly fix their mindfulness upon the name of the Buddha in the West, [they will likewise be transformed].
Respectfully receiving the carving and shaping of the axe, one is naturally able to transform the mundane into the sacred, thereby perfecting one’s virtue and conduct.
Discussing this through the lens of the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*): the East is *Zhen*. *Zhen* is the image of movement. Movement gives rise to all manner of suffering;
therefore, the Sahā world is called the "Sea of Suffering. The West is *Dui*. *Dui* is the image of joyful anticipation. Therefore, the West...
It is thus named the World of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and is also called the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Ji-le).
In terms of the two luminaries: the sun is yang, a celestial phenomenon; the moon is yin, a terrestrial phenomenon. These two—
All ascend in the east and set in the west; therefore, people should take this as their model. Diligently cultivate pure karma and seek rebirth in the Western Land.
This is precisely the Way in which the Three Powers of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity are unified as one.
The people of the East are like wood: when spring arrives, they sprout buds and send forth trunks; when autumn comes, their leaves fall and branches wither.

This cycle of flourishing and decay, of growth and decline, is like that of sentient beings within the ocean of suffering in this Sahā world, who endure the burdens of birth and death, success and failure, gain and loss.
If one were from the West, one would be like gold; for gold remains unchanged throughout ten thousand kalpas.

It is indestructible; it remains unchanged amidst filth and impurity, and it does not shift when entering water or fire. For this reason, those born in the Western Land are called "Utmost Bliss" (Sukhāvatī);
they transcend birth and death and are liberated from the three realms.
The Eastern Land is a land of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*). Whether it be clothing, food, dwellings, or utensils, all must be prepared through human effort before they can be accomplished.
Furthermore, it is a region of desire and pleasure; all who reside here crave the pleasures of the five senses and lose sight of their original, pure countenance.
The Western Land, by contrast, is a land of unconditioned existence (*asaṃskṛta*).
When one thinks of clothing, clothing arrives; when one thinks of food, food comes. There are all manner of natural enjoyments, requiring no laborious effort.

Furthermore, it is a land where the nature [of beings] finds delight. Those born in the Pure Land experience joy that accords with their true nature, clearly perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty.
Question: It has been said by the ancients that if one can let go of everything with total sincerity, one may immediately awaken to the "Master within the sleep.

Why, then, do you not employ this direct method of practice, but instead instruct people to undergo the arduous toil of reciting the Buddha's name, seeking [enlightenment] amidst such fragmented and complex efforts?
Answer: To relinquish everything with one’s whole heart is extremely easy; it is only that worldly people are neither able to relinquish nor know how to relinquish.
If they intend to let go, their affairs become more numerous; if they intend to abandon, their burdens become heavier.

This is simply because ordinary beings make their livelihood within the realm of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). They wish to employ this mind, intellect, and consciousness to relinquish all things.
As for conditions: it is like a firefly trying to burn Mount Sumeru; it can never set it ablaze. Only those who have attained great penetration and great awakening can utilize them skillfully;
all others cannot. Therefore, nothing is better than entering deeply into the single gate of *nien-fo*.
Do not concern yourself with whether they are released or not, or whether they are relinquished or not; simply recite aloud until you reach the hundred-foot pole.
With head hanging over a precipice, one lets go of the hand; emotional attachments are severed though not yet severed, and temperament is transformed though not yet transformed.
Thus, one may lie down across the body at ease, coming and going with freedom. Even in the present, one is in the pure and peaceful homeland.
Question: May that which lies beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, prior to the birth of one’s parents, also be called the Pure Land?
May it also be called the Amitābha of Self-Nature?
Answer: That which lies beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, prior to the birth of one’s parents, is indeed the True Pure Land and the True Amitābha of Self-Nature.
One must simply not cling to these worldly names. If one clings even once to these worldly names, it becomes a defiled land rather than a pure land;
it becomes an ordinary being rather than Amitābha. The sentient beings of the Sahā world, precisely because of these names, cannot depart from them and cannot forget them;
therefore, they transform the originally pure Dharma-realm Amitābha Buddha into—
Ordinary people in this world of the five turbidities are like such antiquities within their chests. If one can rid oneself of these relics, then naturally, when at an impasse, one will transform;
through transformation, one will attain penetration. In this state of penetration, one beholds the self-nature Amitābha; this is precisely the moment of realizing the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
Question: "Master, you have attained the Great [Awakening]. You should simply spend your days within the Constant Radiance of Quiescence (dharmadhātu).
Why must you seek birth in the Western Pure Land before you can say it is beneficial?"

Answer: A Chan master who truly possesses great power has already attained a small portion of the enjoyment within the eternally quiescent light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa*) even upon relinquishing body and life.
Nevertheless, because their residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) remain heavy, progress remains difficult;

thus, even one with wisdom equal to that of Vairocana Buddha must refine the mind for a hundred eons. As for those whose wisdom is not equal to this, there are none who are not struck down and lost by adverse conditions.
Therefore, in seeking birth in Amitābha’s land of recompense and drawing near to Amitābha’s body of recompense, one must first ensure that there is no regression and further increase one's diligence;
in this way, one may hope to enter directly upon the stage of Buddhahood.
Question: This land also possesses ponds, groves, flowers, and trees that are delightful; those in the Western Land are no different from these.
How can you then claim that the West is a manifestation of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)?
Answer: Ordinary beings possess two extremes of attachment that are difficult to transform; thus, they all fall into the cycle of birth and death.
All realms within this land manifest through duality; there is formation and destruction, which are termed the realm of arising and ceasing.
Once one is born in that land, one is free from the dualities of the triple world and transcends birth and death to exit saṃsāra.
Thus, what is sincere within manifests outwardly; through the practice of our own conduct, we reach the state where both truth and falsehood are forgotten.

Consequently, the various external manifestations—pools, flowers, and trees—do not fall into the categories of true or false, but rather allow one to perceive the true realm that accords with the nature of reality.
The bliss that accords with the nature of reality is utterly devoid of such phenomena as flourishing and decline, or filling and emptying;
it is not established through duality, nor does it fall into the realm of arising and ceasing. It is certainly impossible to fathom with an ordinary mind or seek through discursive thought.
How could this land ever be compared to it?
Question: I have heard that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha also attain entry into the pure land of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). What is called the "pure land of the Dharma-realm"?
By what further cultivation does one attain entry? If it is primordially pure, what need is there for mindfulness of the Buddha?
If it is primordially defiled and evil, by what cause does the mere practice of mindfulness of the Buddha result in its becoming pure?
Answer: The Dharma-realm is originally pure. Because the minds of sentient beings are turbid and manifold beyond measure, the Dharma follows the fluctuations of the mind and becomes a defiled realm.

Now, if one can bring forth a single phrase of the Buddha’s name and let go of all myriad conditions—like a mute girl holding a broom and sweeping throughout the two-and-six periods of the day until it is perfectly clean and pure—then because the recitation reaches its ultimate limit, the mind becomes empty. The mind...
If emptiness is empty, then defilement is also empty. Since defilement is empty, it is once again the originally pure *dharmadhātu*.
This is truly the clarification of turbidity and the transformation of the foul into purity. Upon reaching this stage, birth and death are the Pure Land;
heaven and hell are also the Pure Land; high mountains and lowlands are also the Pure Land. Honor and disgrace, rising and sinking, right and wrong—[all are the Pure Land].
Gain and loss are both the Pure Land; throughout the entirety of the ten directions, all worlds are the Pure Land. Therefore, it is called the Dharma-realm Pure Land.
Since entry into this is attained entirely through the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, is this not the direct path?

Question: For one who enters the pure land of the *dharmadhātu*, has the eighth consciousness already attained emptiness? If it has not attained emptiness, why is it called the pure land of the *dharmadhātu*?
Answer: This is merely a partial purification; how could it empty the eighth consciousness? If one desires complete purification, one must proceed until [enlightenment] is achieved.
The Buddha [said]: "The eighth consciousness first becomes empty; therefore, it is said that the retributive consciousness (vipāka-vijñāna) is empty after the Vajra Path.
Question: To which of the four lands does the pure land of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) belong?

Answer: Based on the fact that the severing of afflictions is not yet complete, this is the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder; it is also a partial manifestation of the Constant, Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*).

If one enters this land, one becomes increasingly refined and increasingly pure through further cultivation until the attainment of Buddhahood, at which point one is said to fully dwell in the Constant, Quiescent Light Land.
Question: Since there exists the pure land of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) into which one may be born, why must people be taught to seek rebirth specifically in the Western Pure Land?
Answer: Although the worlds of the ten directions are indeed the pure land of the Dharma-realm, sentient beings possess shallow and meager spiritual power;

how then could they realize and enter it? For this reason, the Buddha opened the gate of skillful means (upāya-mukha) to show people that they may enter by way of the West for the time being. As for the West...
This is the *vipākabhūmi* (recompense land) of Amitābha. His body is sixty million billion *nayuta* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *yojana*s in height;
this is the *vipākakāya* (recompense body) of Amitābha. A *vipākakāya* necessarily dwells in a *vipākabhūmi*.
Those who study the Way and aspire to attain the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit must personally approach his *vipākakāya* and deeply hear his wondrous Dharma before they can realize it.
The Dharma-realm is the ultimate of pure lands. Therefore, once one enters it in a single direction, one can enter all worlds of the ten directions;
when one direction is purified, all worlds of the ten directions are likewise purified; and when one direction becomes the World of Ultimate Bliss, so it is for all.
The worlds of the ten directions shall likewise become the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: Having heard your instructions, I understand that you do not permit silent recitation of the Buddha’s name. However, for those of meager capacity, it is truly impossible to recite aloud day and night.
I would like to follow the ancients who said that the sound should reside between the lips and tongue, remaining continuous...
"Let us set aside these lingering thoughts. How is this method?
He replied, "One who recites silently has weak power and a dull breath; it is easy to fall into indolence, and moreover, one cannot inspire others."
Furthermore, if distracted by various sounds and discursive thoughts, they will take advantage of such moments to intrude; how then could one achieve pure karma?

However, if one truly possesses meager faculties and is unable to recite with a loud voice, this method is permitted. Nevertheless, one must constantly reflect inwardly, resolve upon the Western Pure Land, and ensure that one’s practice renews itself day by day.
Question: For those who recite the Buddha’s name aloud, is it permissible not to keep count?
Answer: For beginners, it is necessary to keep count every day to monitor their progress; only then will they avoid becoming indolent.

If there is no fixed number, sometimes one will be mindful and sometimes unmindful; joy and weariness will alternate, and busyness and leisure will intermingle, making it easy to become negligent and difficult to accomplish pure karma.
Only for those who have practiced for a long time is it well to count the recitations, or it is equally well not to count them.
One should simply grasp the single phrase of Amitābha as if holding the Great Black Sword (Ta'a-jian); with ten thousand [obstacles],...
Now, as for "inappropriate valor": it is to break through heavy encirclements directly and utterly exterminate the bandits; thus, one naturally arrives at the world of purity.
Question: For one who cultivates the Way, what is valued? It lies in attaining total and complete realization—having nothing upon which to rely within the breast and being free from conditions.
Question: "Now, this frequent mindfulness of the Buddha involves a conditioned mindfulness and a reliance [upon something]. How can this be called 'thoroughly understanding all through one'?

Answer: "This is nothing more than using a wedge to extract a wedge, or using poison to counteract poison. It is because we see that people of the world are preoccupied with mindfulness of sounds and forms."
Those who pursue wealth and profit are bound by sensory objects and material gain, and are thereby ruined within them; this applies to all such things, even down to various thoughts.
Because the Buddha pities sentient beings whose mental inclinations they cannot relinquish, he uses a single phrase of Amitābha to replace the worldly sentiments of people.
This is what is meant by exchanging worldly thoughts for supramundane ones.
Contemplate: replace thoughts of karmic offenses with thoughts of merit; replace thoughts of entanglement and bondage with thoughts of liberation;

replace thoughts of danger and peril with thoughts of peace and bliss. Just as a skilled craftsman secretly replaces the beams and pillars, refine yourself until the various discursive thoughts of sentient beings are eliminated, so that even this single thought of mindfulness of the Buddha returns to the state of non-existence.

How true! As the ancients said: "To cross the river, one must use a raft; once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed. What further reliance, then, could there be on conditions or discursive thoughts?
Question: Many people say that Zen practice is the direct path, whereas reciting the Buddha’s name is a circuitous route. However...

"No. He replied: "In Zen meditation, one must let go deeply; in the recitation of the Buddha's name, one must maintain full awareness with every phrase. Although letting go and maintaining awareness differ, their efficacy is one and the same.
For those who practice skillfully, even the most circuitous paths become direct and immediate; for those who do not know how to practice, they remain so."
This means that even what is direct and straightforward becomes circuitous. The matter rests with the person; there is no need to doubt the relative superiority or inferiority of dharma-gates.
An ancient worthy said: "Hold up the single [phrase] alone; do not seek elsewhere. If one seeks, one will again find it. The path of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is easy to undertake;
why is it so direct? Please reflect on this carefully.

Question: Lately, there has been one who claims to be a man who "steps right through to the bottom," disparaging the practice of *nienfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) as merely the lifelong occupation of those with dull faculties.
What do you say to this? Answer:
He speaks with his mouth of "stepping right through to the bottom," yet as soon as he takes a single step, he encounters many entanglements and obstacles. Upon being touched by them, he is at a loss.
It is clearly manifest before you, yet you cannot be called a man who accomplishes the task. This is because you do not understand the power of a single phrase of Amitābha;
thus, you regard it as the lifelong practice of one with dull faculties. If you could truly comprehend it, you would quickly realize the state of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
The foundation of one's footing has only just become stable. How profound this is! Today is not like the past; it is no cause for wonder.

Question: For one who cultivates the Pure Land, having thoroughly studied and mastered all things so that the objects of contemplation are stored within the breast, is it possible to maintain mindful recollection?
Answer: As for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha yet fail to achieve samādhi, it is precisely because of this:

regarding objects that have not yet been mastered, they are unwilling to let go because they desire to cultivate mastery over them; regarding objects already mastered, they constantly fear losing them and thus engage in incessant recollection.

This fault is most profound; it extends even to the point where, when receiving kindness or encountering enmity from others, one feels compelled to repay them before ceasing, even unto the brink of death.
This is indeed what I am willing to accept with joy. If you can replace this recollection by holding fast to a single name of the Buddha,
and cast aside all that you have learned and practiced— the familiar objects of your mind— leaving them all to drift away like flowing water and passing clouds, then as days and months pass,
you will naturally achieve a state of unified integration within the Pure Land.
Question: When practicing mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land, is it permissible to study Buddhist scriptures and Confucian texts?

Answer: Although all Buddhist teachings and various philosophical principles are helpful for spiritual progress, if one does not clearly understand the profound depths of the Pure Land method or lacks earnest faith, one must urgently study the Pure Land sutras and treatises. This is because...
This determines the direction of one's practice. As for other scriptures, it is not appropriate to employ them indiscriminately;

otherwise, the mind will instead become a cause and condition for obstructing the Way. Therefore, "single-mindedness without distraction" is the fundamental principle of practicing the Pure Land, and it constitutes the great gateway to attaining samādhi.
Question: The Tathāgata teaches people to seek rebirth in the Western Land, yet he also teaches them to return to this Sahā world.
How can these scriptural meanings be reconciled? What is the reason for this?

Answer: Do you not observe the passage in the preceding text that speaks of not contradicting the state of being nurtured in An-yang? For one who has first resolved upon Bodhicitta is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss;

there, they are nurtured and perfumed for a long time until delusions and hindrances are completely exhausted, the gate of wisdom is widely opened, spiritual powers are radiantly manifested, and their rank reaches the stage of non-retrogression.
Only then do they go forth to transform sentient beings, moving between worlds without obstruction.
Therefore, those who dwell long in Sukhāvatī are further sent by the Buddha back into Saṃsāra to deliver sentient beings;

yet they do not thereby contravene their state of peace and nourishment, for they remain here with their spirits settled, manifesting emanations and returning in various forms to appear among all classes of beings. Thus it is known that:

Whether one exhorts others to abandon the Sahā world to be born in the Pure Land, or exhorts them to leave the Pure Land to enter the Sahā world, it is none other than observing their capacities and applying the teaching accordingly, refining them according to their faculties.
Thus benefiting both self and others, the path of the Bodhisattva is fully perfected.
What difficulty is there in the Buddha-way? This is the most exquisite and wonderful method for Śākyamuni and Amitāyus to deliver sentient beings.
Question: We have already heard your instructions regarding how this single Dharma-gate transcends the three realms horizontally.
However, we truly fear that sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age will create obstacles for themselves. We do not yet know what specific disadvantages there may be.
Answer: For those who cultivate the Pure Land, there are ten kinds of defects that serve as obstructing dharmas. First, their faith is not earnest. Second, their practice is not courageous.
Third, their aspiration is not profound. Fourth, they engage in idle and silent recitation.

Fifth, their minds are distracted by worldly affairs. Sixth, they have not eliminated attachment and aversion. Seventh, they extend their studies to both internal and external scriptures. Eighth, [the text continues...]
Fifth, one delights in composing poetry and allows the mind to be distracted. Sixth, one idly engages in miscellaneous talk. Seventh, one lacks single-mindedness and fails to remain undisturbed.

Eighth, one seeks to attain realization through the practice of stillness within a fixed period. If one truly applies oneself to the practice, one must certainly not allow even a single transgression to occur.

Raising the eyebrows, one should pursue the recitation with focused mindfulness. Thus, one will naturally perceive Amitābha Buddha as one's own original nature in the present moment; when this life’s retribution is exhausted, one shall return to the Western Pure Land.
The Lotus Ear.
Chan Master Zhenxie Qingliao of Changlu in Zhenzhou of the Caodong School (he was a dharma successor of Chan Master Danxia Chun).

The Master was a native of Anchang in Zuomian, Xichu, of the Yong clan. Having entered a monastery while still in his swaddling clothes, he was moved with joy at the sight of a Buddha, his eyebrows and eyelashes twitching.
At the age of eleven, he left the household life under the monk Qingjun of Shengguo Monastery. Seven years later, he ascended the lecture hall;

however, he soon abandoned lecturing to devote himself to meditation, practicing with an air of unconcern. Although both monastics and laypeople tried to detain him, he paid them no heed. Reaching Mianhan, he went to call upon Danxia.
In the abbot’s quarters, Yunxi asked, "What is your own self prior to the empty kalpa? As the Master was about to respond, Yunxi said, "You are making a fuss; go away for now.
One day, while ascending Potu Peak, the Master attained sudden and complete enlightenment. He returned directly to stand in attendance.

Yunxi struck him with his palm and said, "I thought you knew. The Master bowed joyfully. The following day, Yunxi ascended the hall and said, "The sun shines upon the solitary peak’s emerald heights."
"The moon hangs over the mountain stream, cold. The Patriarch’s profound and wondrous secret: do not seek peace within a single inch of the heart. He then descended from his seat.
The Master stepped forward and said, "Today you have ascended the seat; you shall no longer deceive me. Yunmen said, "Try to cite my words from today's ascent of the seat and see.
The Master remained silent for a long while. Yunmen said, "I thought you had suddenly awakened. The Master then departed. Later, he resided in Hangzhou.
At Gaotingshan Guangxiao Temple and Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou, he greatly propagated the Dongshan school, so that his Way nearly spanned half the world.

Furthermore, he widely disseminated the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation (*nianfo*) while simultaneously practicing it himself. He composed the *Jingtu shuo* (Treatise on the Pure Land), in which he stated:
"The single school of Dongshan all strives for esoteric cultivation. What is the reason for this? It is truly because the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is a direct path of cultivation."

[This] practice directly accords with the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) to engage those of the highest faculties, while also citing [scriptures] to guide those of middling and lower capacities. It further states:

"For those who have already realized the Dharma that is neither empty nor existent—great masters of the Chan school—and yet apply themselves with diligent resolve to the practice of purity (*śubha-karma*), is it not the case that their vision of the Buddha through pure practice is even more simple and easy than that of the Chan school? It further states: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs, within the Teachings..."
In dhyāna, all cultivate pure karma and return together to a single source. Once one enters this gate, one is able to enter all immeasurable Dharma gates.
It is further said that "one mind, undisturbed" encompasses both principle and phenomena. If it refers to the phenomenal aspect of one mind, everyone is capable of practicing it;
because by holding the name, the mind is not disturbed. This is like a dragon obtaining water or a tiger relying on a mountain. This is...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one recollects the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future;

one will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. This encompasses the meaning of both the middle and lower faculties. As for the principle of single-mindedness (*li yixin*), it is likewise not some other method;
one simply takes the four characters "A-mi-tuo-fo" (Amitābha Buddha) as a *hwadu* (critical phrase) and, throughout the two periods of six hours [day and night], directly...
Awaken from below. Do not contemplate with a mind of existence; do not contemplate with a mind of non-existence; do not contemplate with a mind that is both existent and non-existent;
do not contemplate with a mind that is neither existent nor non-existent. Cut off the boundaries of past and future. Let not a single thought arise.
Without traversing the stages, you directly transcend to the Buddha-ground.
Someone asked: "The Pure Land of the Mind alone is inherently possessed by every person. Why do you not simply accept this directly, instead seeking it beyond ten million *koṭi* lands?

The Master replied: "If you could truly realize the Pure Land of the Mind alone, then not only would ten million *koṭi* lands be no distance at all, even lands as numerous as motes of dust would not be far. Have you not seen how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra [traversed]..."
A single step taken through the air by a hair traverses worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Master Li said:

"In the ocean of boundless lands, self and other are not separated by even the tip of a hair; throughout the ten periods of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present thought-moment.
Therefore, the World-Honored One Amitābha directly points to that one thing within the mind. If one points to the mind—
The whole body. Not only is the Pure Land "mind-only," but even the hells and celestial palaces are manifestations of the mind alone. As the Sūtra says:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single fleck of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky."
Question: Since it is perfectly pervasive and unimpeded, why is the West specifically designated? The Master replied:
"Precisely because the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, every phenomenon does not depart from its original locus. He then composed the *Essentials of the Pure Land School*, stating:
"The Pure Land is not separate from the minds of sentient beings; these three are without distinction. Ultimate Bliss pervades all places; by mentioning one, the whole is encompassed."

It is like the jeweled net of a thousand pearls above the palace of Śakra: the light and shadows of the thousand pearls all enter into a single pearl, and the light and shadows of a single pearl pervade and enter into all thousand pearls.
Although each pearl pervades the others, this pearl cannot become that pearl, and that pearl cannot become this pearl;
they interpenetrate without being mixed, and they remain distinct without being divided. Each one manifests its pervasive presence, yet it has no fixed location.
The Pure Land of Amitābha is but one among a thousand beads. Within the hundred thousand Buddha-lands, each Buddha and each land is likewise one among a thousand beads.
Through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the Sage shows people that by single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha, one is directly pointing to one bead among the thousand.
To see one Buddha is to see all Buddhas of the ten directions, and it is also to see the sentient beings of the nine realms. Subtle...

The ocean of lands within the dust motes, throughout the ten directions and across all times, is instantaneously perfected by a single seal; there is not a single dharma remaining that is not understood.
For this reason, the Master devoted his mind exclusively to the Western Land. One day, he passed away without illness.
Chan Master Hongzhi Jue of Tiantong in Mingzhou (a successor of Chan Master Danxia Chun).

At eighteen, he began his travels as a wandering monk and arrived at Ruzhou, where he visited Cheng Kumu, who held him in high esteem. One day, while hearing a monk recite the Lotus Sūtra, he reached the passage:

I have a doubt regarding this work. It was composed for those of the Mahayana, a treatise that refutes existence and abandons emptiness, leaving not a single dharma remaining.
Yet, its final chapter speaks of fixing the mind on Amitābha and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

Because of this, my doubts remain unresolved. Later, I visited Xuefeng to ask Zhenxie, who said: "In the ground of ultimate reality, not a single speck of dust is admitted; yet the myriad practices..."

Within the gateway, not a single dharma is abandoned. You wished to destroy the marks of the world by discarding attachment to existence and clinging to emptiness, and only then would you have attained the Way.
At that moment, there was a sudden awakening in your mind, whereby you came to understand the Master’s instruction regarding the single gate of rebirth in the Pure Land.
This directly cuts across the essential path of birth and death.
