Their words thus accorded with one another, and he sent him off with this verse: "The mountain clouds are deep and black; the eye of the school has reached its limit.
Treading upon the silver mountain, a steep iron wall stands firm. When the groves are in full bloom and the single flower appears, A thunderclap resounds from the tip of the hare's horn staff.
Having received the seal of approval, he resided at Xiying Chan Temple on Mount Yang in the capital. Later, he lived at Baen Temple.
Retiring to Congrong Hermitage, he addressed the assembly: "Where the wheel of the pivot turns, even the eye of wisdom remains deluded; when the precious mirror opens, not a speck of dust can enter.
Opening the fist, it does not fall to the ground; responding to things, one must know the proper time. When two blades meet, how do you shift and avoid them? Addressing the assembly again:
"The single pivot above points toward the heavens, like a crane soaring into the void; the direct path before one is like a hawk flying to Silla."
"Even if one’s eyes were like shooting stars, one could not avoid having a mouth like a fan for carrying burdens. Now tell me, what is the underlying principle?

The Master had perused the Tripitaka three times and was conversant with the teachings of a hundred schools. He constantly cultivated the Dharma-gate of Pure Land and compiled the *Zu deng lu* (Record of the Lamp of the Patriarchs) in sixty-two fascicles.
Furthermore, he composed several works on the Pure Land to sever people's doubts regarding the practice of Buddha-recitation, thereby causing their three karmas to be reverent and sincere.
With a profound mind, he sought Amitābha, embarking on a journey to the Land of Bliss.
This was Master Guangen (who succeeded Master Guji Hui), whose secular surname was Jia.
His family had resided for generations in Zhanghua Village of Minghui. He received the tonsure at Fayun Temple in Jingzhen under the guidance of Master Jian.
Master Gōng received full ordination from Venerable Master Huī and simultaneously inherited the mind-seal.

He withdrew to Línchéng Mountain, where he shut his door and abstained from food, reciting and upholding the verses of the Great Compassion Mantra with diligent and tireless exertion. At that time, during the bitter cold of midwinter, a child of the Hò family went out to the outskirts to gather firewood among the thickets and brush.
There he found two peaches, fresh and lovely; he offered them to the Master, who ate them. From then on—

These were signs that his aspirations had been verified: fire could not burn him, and violence could not harm him. It reached the point where a rooster pecked at incense and set it ablaze, and an ox received the precepts and became docile.
He restored a well whose sweet water had long since run dry, and a single measure of rice provided food for ten thousand people.

At Ganling, while repairing the foundations of an ancient stupa, a stone inscription was discovered that foretold the Master’s name. There was a person who first conceived the resolve to practice giving; once [the work began]...
As for those who experienced transformation while still alive, upon returning home they opened their chests and found them filled with lotus flowers.

Filled with reverence and faith, people of the world, witnessing such spiritual wonders, all called him "The Bodhisattva Merchant. The Master established a Pure Land sanctuary and held the White Lotus Assembly.
The scale of the event was modeled after that of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu. At Wanshou Temple in the capital of Yan, the Great Precept Ordination Assembly was convened.

Chan Master Wansong specifically invited the Master to ascend the platform and recite the precepts, pouring forth the nectar of the Dharma so profusely that the fourfold assembly rejoiced, experiencing something they had never known before.
Chan Master Da Fang Ruchuan of Longgang in Huaqing (he was the successor of Chan Master Dashao Dazhang Shu). His alternative style name was Songgu.
He was born in Qishan County, Shaanxi, into the Li clan. From his youth, he delighted in the Buddhist teachings;

whenever he reached a Buddhist temple, it felt like his old home, and out of such affection, he would forget to return. At the age of seventeen, he left the household life and paid homage to Master Wuzong Ben.
Having shaved his head and donned the dyed robes, he resided there for three years. Feeling a sense of urgency and resolve, he traveled far to seek out spiritual friends.

He first visited Master Yue’an Xi, from whom he received full ordination and was instructed in the path beyond the ordinary. He devoted himself entirely to his investigation until he forgot both sleep and food.

Subsequently, he entered Mount Qingfeng, where he lived alone in solitude. There, he attained an awakening. Later, he visited Dazhang at Shaolin, where he received the master’s seal of approval. [He possessed] a needle...
The "Head-Jewel Sutra" and the "Iron Ox of the Ocean Bottom": having labored diligently day and night for years, one finally accords with the essential purport of the school upon reaching this point;
he was thus instructed to preserve it forever as the tradition of our house. One must surely await the convergence of the right time and conditions to propagate the declining ancestral Way.

Once the Master had attained the Dharma, he returned to the capital, where he frequented various lecture halls to profoundly investigate the principles of the Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) schools. Later, he arrived at...
In Huaiqing, Prince Letian of Zheng renounced the succession to the throne and cultivated pure deeds in seclusion. He established a vihāra and invited a master to dwell there in leisure.

At that time, scholars from all quarters heard of his reputation and traveled from afar to join him; their numbers increased daily. Later, he accepted an invitation to the Ciyun Hermitage in the Great Capital, where he vigorously propagated the spirit of the school.
He subsequently opened the Dharma hall at Qianfo Temple, surrounded by ten thousand followers. In the Gengyin year of the Wanli era, he served his Holy Mother...
By Imperial Edict of the Empress Dowager: At Daci Shousi Temple, the Pure Land Dharma-gate of Non-duality was opened.

Its transformation reached both near and far, and those among the clergy and laity who were steadfast in their faith and recitation of the Buddha’s name turned their hearts toward the Land of Bliss and attained rebirth there; this was truly due to the Master’s power.
Chan Master Zutong of Shunde Chong’en Dafang (Succeeding Chan Master Jinshan Bao):

He was the son of the Tang family from Neiqiu. In his youth, he attended a community school to study. There, he encountered a wandering mendicant with white hair and a long beard, yet whose complexion was like that of a young boy.
This man discussed with the master the arts of nourishing life (*yangsheng*) and, when the conversation turned to the study of characters (*zixue*), said: "In antiquity..."
Those who created these characters all understood the Way. Take, for example, the character *kòu* (thief/robber). It is composed of *wán* (intact) and *nǚ* (woman).
This signifies that when a person fails to guard their originally perfect and solid nature, they instead invite thieves to enter and plunder their own family treasures;

nothing is more extreme than this regarding women. Therefore, the compound meaning of "lacking in defense" combined with "woman" forms *kòu*. Upon hearing this, Master [Shenxiu] was immediately enlightened.

Upon hearing these words, his heart trembled with fear; he avoided women as he would a venomous snake. Later, when he heard that his parents had arranged a marriage for him, he fled in the middle of the night.
He went to Jiuxian Cave on Mount Que and received the tonsure under Chan Master Ming of Xinghua. From then on, his mind became settled and his will firm;
he focused solely on the matter of birth and death. Furthermore, lamenting that the Great Matter remained unclarified, he relied upon Master Xiaoshan at Kaiyuan Temple.

The Master was staying at Shaolin. Attending morning audiences and seeking instruction evening after evening, he was instructed by the Mountain Master (Huangbo) to contemplate the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree.
After a long time of study, the Master still had not attained realization. The Mountain Master said, "I only wish that you would practice for a long time and realize it slowly.

One day, while accompanying the Master and the Prefectural Governor Wu Pengyan to visit the Three Cypress Mountain of Hanfeng, the Mountain Master pointed to a cypress tree and said to the Master, "Ultimately, call it..."

"What are you doing? The Master suddenly attained realization, and sweat poured from his entire body. Yunshan said, "Do you have no more doubts? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master presented a verse, saying:

"The meaning of the Ancestor’s coming from the West, Is the cypress tree in the courtyard. It turns out it was always just this; Heaven and earth are but a single finger. Yunshan smiled and certified him.
The Prefect took the Master’s hand and sighed deeply, saying: [The Master’s name]... [The Master’s name]... [The Master’s name]. (The Master’s name is omitted in the source text.)
Our hometown has once again opened a gate of ambrosia. The Master had previously lived in profound seclusion and nurtured his practice deeply;

however, due to his mother’s illness, he returned to his native village to serve his parents with the full filial rites of a son. When these duties were completed, Mount Xiao (Xiaoshan) had already returned to the West.

Consequently, he succeeded the Dharma Master Bao of Jinshan and took up residence at Chong’en Temple in his own home district to open the hall for teaching. Those who sought refuge in him gathered like a market, and he generally instructed them in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
"Rebirth in the Pure Land" means that one has attained birth in the Pure Land; the great matter is naturally brought to completion, and there is no fear as to where one will go.
At a major crossroads, he constructed a thatched hut, opened his kitchen to feed the assembly, and when his disciples wished to acquire property for the community, he said:
The Master stopped him, saying: "Throughout my life, internally I have had the joy of the Dharma and the delight of Zen, no less than that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
externally I have possessed robes, bowls, scriptures, and books—a wealth and honor before my very eyes. This is the fundamental livelihood of a monk.
Beyond this, how could I willingly burden myself with family property or fetter my physical form? Moreover, the ancients lived in deep mountains, by their mattocks."
Cooking coarse grain porridge in a broken-legged cauldron, his wealth did not exceed contentment. For a lifetime he sought nothing from others; his nobility did not exceed quietude and leisure.

What need was there for seals as large as bushels? Now, with only a few thatched rooms to barely shelter him from wind and rain, he looked back upon those ancients who dwelt among graves or beneath trees and felt they had more than enough.
In the end, he did not comply [with worldly honors]. He lived to the age of seventy-three. This is a brief account.
He was slightly ill. A lay devotee dreamed that the Master was taking his leave and traveling westward; upon suddenly waking, he told his family, "The Great Master Fang has passed away.
When they entered the monastery to observe him, it was indeed true: he had passed away in a state of auspicious serenity.
Daguan Zhenke was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Zibo (who himself succeeded Chan Master Run of Shaoshi).
He was the son of the Shen family of Jiuqu. By nature he was fierce and bold, noble and vehement, and he took no pleasure in seeing women.

At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and traveled to study under various masters. Upon hearing the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse, reaching the line: "Cutting off delusive thoughts increases the illness," he rushed toward [the master].

"Even True Suchness (Tathatā) is false; this is a great doubt. One day, while at his midday meal, he suddenly attained enlightenment and said, "If I had been under the seat of Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me;
why resort to such 'how' and 'what'? He traveled to the capital, where Emperor Shenzong of the Ming dynasty held him in high esteem.
He restored fifteen monasteries, including Lengyan Temple, and oversaw the carving and publication of the Tripitaka and ancient texts.
The Venerable Elder spoke thus. Resolute and steadfast in upholding the Dharma, he incurred the jealousy of others. Suddenly, a seditious tract was circulated, and the Master fell into peril.

During his interrogation, his countenance remained composed and his principles were most upright. With his aged and infirm body, he endured every form of flogging and torture; yet until death, he did not yield.
When he was cast into prison and the judicial authorities sentenced him to death, the Master spoke this verse: "A single laugh has always been distinct."
"There is a cause. How could one know that a great mass of earth cannot contain a speck of dust? From this moment on, I shall gather in my mother-born feet;
the iron stake will blossom without waiting for spring. He also said, "Worldly dharmas are thus; what is the use of staying long?
Then, having requested a bath, he instructed his attendant, saying, "I am departing. Sitting upright, he passed away.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is the most simple and convenient.
Yet those who recite the Buddha's name today lack firm resolve; for this reason, though thousands or hundreds of people may recite, not even one or two achieve success.
This single phrase 'Buddha'—if any Bodhisattvas, devas, or humans are to be reborn in the Western Paradise, there are none who do not cross the sea of suffering by means of it."
However, as for the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha—whether it is genuine or not—the crucial point of examination lies directly in taking realization within the two states of joy and affliction.
Thus, the distinction between the genuine and the false mind can be clearly discerned.

Generally speaking, for one who recites the Buddha’s name with a true mind, there will necessarily be no interruption in their mindfulness amidst joy and affliction; therefore, neither affliction nor joy can disturb them.
Joy cannot move him; since neither can move him, he will naturally be free from fear and terror within the realm of birth and death.
Nowadays, when people recite the Buddha’s name, if even a slight amount of joy or anger arises before them, Amitābha Buddha is immediately cast aside behind their vexations.

How, then, could they obtain the spiritual efficacy of reciting the Buddha’s name? If one follows my method of reciting the Buddha’s name, one will be able to do so at the very crux of hatred and love.

If you do not realize this phrase—that Amitābha Buddha manifests before you—and yet fail to make use of it in your daily life, so that you cannot be reborn in the Western Land at the time of death, then my tongue will surely rot away.
If you do not practice according to my Dharma, then the lack of efficacy in your recitation of the Buddha’s name is your own fault; it has nothing to do with me.
The Master asked a monk, "Do you recite the Buddha's name without interruption? The monk replied, "When I close my eyes to sleep, I immediately forget.

The Master rebuked him with a display of majestic authority, saying, "If you forget as soon as you close your eyes, then even if you recite the Buddha's name for a thousand years, it will be of no use.

From this day forward, you must ensure that your recitation of the Buddha's name continues even within your dreams; only then will you have the possibility of escaping suffering. If, even in your dreams..."
If you forget to recite the Buddha’s name, as soon as you open your eyes, you shall weep aloud and go straight before the Buddha, prostrating yourself until your forehead bleeds.
Recite the name either a thousand times or ten thousand times, stopping only when your own strength is exhausted.
If you practice in this manner twenty or thirty times, then even amidst deep sleep, the sound of the Buddha’s name will naturally remain uninterrupted. Furthermore, in this world...
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha for thirty years, or even for the remainder of their lives, may find it of no use at the time of death.
This is because they lacked the true intent of mindfulness during their waking life, which was like a dream. Human life is like being awake;
human death is like dreaming. Therefore, those who have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha within their dreams will naturally remain undisturbed at the moment of death.
Furthermore,
the meaning of being born in the Western Land lies in maintaining mindfulness throughout one's life, so that at the moment of death, one’s mind remains undistracted.
One simply recognizes that this Sahā world is a realm of extreme suffering, while the Pure Land is a land of ultimate bliss— just like fish and birds [longing for their natural habitats].
Though the body is within the cage and bars, the mind is beyond the cage and bars. One recites the Buddha’s name, regarding the Sahā world as the cage and the Pure Land as the open sky and water.
Because one’s weariness with and longing for [the Pure Land] have reached maturity, at the time of death, the desires for the Sahā world within the mind—
There is not even a grain’s worth of reason [for doubt]; regardless of the gravity of one's offenses, one should simply abide in non-doubt.

Even if one has practiced *nienfo* for a lifetime until the moment of death, yet has not forgotten the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of this Sahā world and has not achieved uniformity in the visualization of the Pure Land—such persons are also said to be able to attain rebirth in the Pure Land while carrying their karmic burdens. This is determined by the underlying principle.

Rebirth [in the Pure Land] will necessarily be difficult. Therefore, at Mount Lu, he first composed the *Dharmatā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Nature of Reality) and subsequently established the White Lotus Society;
this was not without reason. For if the nature of reality is not clarified, the barriers of emotion will not be broken.

If the barriers of emotion are not broken, the grasping and attachment of body and mind can never be dissolved. Because this grasping has not been dissolved, regarding the desires for food, drink, and sexual relations—
The roots are severed yet cannot be uprooted; thus, one may recite the name of Amitābha with the mouth while the mind races toward the realm of desire.

If one first employs the method of breaking through body and mind, teaching them to practice gradually until they become proficient, then one will be able to understand that neither body nor mind belongs to oneself.
If this realization is achieved, then although the grasping of body and mind has not been suddenly shattered, compared to ordinary people, one’s clarity and loftiness are far superior.
As for the method, nothing is more expedient and essential than the first half-verse of the transmission of mind from Viśvabhū Buddha.
One should first recite it ten million times, five million times, or three million times; once the count is complete, one should gradually explain the verse to the practitioner.
Then, the deluded calculations of body and mind will naturally become greatly lightened. Once these calculations have been lightened, one may immediately...
Maintain the mind that upholds the gāthā, uphold Amitābha Buddha, and focus your thoughts exclusively on the Western Land.

When the time comes to relinquish your life, the desires of this Sahā world will naturally become empty without requiring deliberate effort. Why is this? Because you ride upon the power of understanding and maintain exclusive contemplation. As the ancient masters said:
First, one realizes that body and mind do not exist. Once this wisdom has opened, one focuses the mind on the Buddha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land.
When ordinary people practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), I dare to guarantee that not a single person among them will fail to be born in the Pure Land.

This principle is also based on the fact that [Huiyuan] of Mount Lu first composed the *Faxing lun* (Treatise on the Dharma-nature) to open the understanding of sentient beings, and subsequently established the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*) to perfect the practice of sentient beings. Thus it came to pass.
Thus it is said. The verse states: "The land is pure because the mind is pure; The land is defiled because the mind is defiled.
Since purity and defilement reside within the mind, Why seek the principle elsewhere? If you simply observe that the mind has not yet arisen, Where would purity or defilement be?

If this observation penetrates thoroughly, All transgressions will naturally be extinguished. Without waiting for the lotus to open, Fragrance and light will issue from your mouth. Namo Amitābha Buddha."

This is the awakening of one's own mind. When awakened, deluded emotions do not arise. When emotions arise, they create the conditions for "killing the Buddha. By killing the Buddha, one falls into hell and finds it difficult to be reborn in the Land of Lotus Flowers.
If one can prevent these emotions from arising, Amitābha will come to welcome them personally; with a lotus flower as their womb, they shall never again become sentient beings.

Although reciting the Buddha’s name is not difficult, it is difficult to break through the barrier of opposition and compliance. Only when this barrier of opposition and compliance is broken does [true practice begin].
Facing the countenance of Amitābha:
Chan Master Deqing of Caoxi (who succeeded Chan Master Shaoshi), whose courtesy name was Hanshan.
He was the son of Cai of Quanpao; his mother was surnamed Hong. From his youth, she made offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and prayed...

Please be born. His mother gave birth to him with a heavy caul. A neighboring woman was startled and informed others; they knew he was no ordinary child. When he had barely reached one year of age, he suffered from wind-fever and was on the verge of death.

His mother wailed out the name of the Bodhisattva and vowed to renounce the world for his sake. He subsequently recovered. She sent him to enter Changgan Baoen Temple, where Elder Xilin shaved his head.
He followed Master Yungu and resided at Tianjie Monastery. There, the Master [Yungu] posed the koan: "Who is the one who recites the Buddha's name?"

Gong’an. He practiced with intense diligence for ten days. A carbuncle broke out on his back, whereupon he offered prayers before the Buddha, vowing to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* ten times and requesting a leave of absence for one night.
When he rose at dawn, the carbuncle had healed. He redoubled his efforts and traveled north to Mount Song, visiting Biàn Róng, Xiào Yán, and Dà Qiān.
He visited the site where the First Patriarch sat facing the wall. Prefect Chen Gong carved the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* and entrusted it to him.

The Master examined the "Treatise on Non-Transmigration. For a long time he had harbored doubts regarding the passage, "A whirlwind topples mountains," but later, suddenly following the words of the Brahmin, "It is not the person of former times," he attained sudden, clear enlightenment, exclaiming, "How wonderful!
All dharmas truly have no coming or going. He immediately descended from his meditation seat to prostrate before the Buddha, yet there was no sign of movement.
When he lifted the curtain and saw the dancing leaves, there was no sign of shaking or motion. He then relieved himself.
Thus, the doubt regarding the shifting nature of birth and death, coming and going, was forever resolved.

He then wrote a verse: "Birth and death, day and night, Like flowing water and fading flowers. Today I have finally realized: The nostrils point downward. The next morning, his fellow practitioner Miaofeng saw this and remarked with surprise, "How joyful!
You have now secured the capital for staying in the mountains. Foga Guang of Mount Funiu said, "He has truly understood."

The Master possessed the functional mastery of the Chan school. When he requested further instruction, [the teacher] said: "There is nothing extraordinary; simply practice by remaining apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and learn by departing from the paths of sages and ordinary beings.
The Master went to reside at Mount Han. One day, after the morning gruel, while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), he stood in firm concentration and no longer perceived body, mind, or the world.
There was only a single, great, perfectly full radiance, within which the boundless mountains, rivers, and great earth appeared as reflections.
Within this state, he sought the body and mind through comparative awareness but found them utterly unobtainable. He then spoke in verse: "In a fleeting instant, the wild mind comes to rest;
The internal faculties and external objects are all transparently clear. Turning over, he strikes through the vast void; The myriad phenomena arise and perish together.
From then on, he passed his days in profound stillness. All sounds and forms were without obstruction, and his perceptions suddenly became empty. The Master—
He constantly took the essential methods for practicing the Western Pure Land as his teaching for the assembly.

Someone once remarked, "As for this single gateway of the Pure Land, it is often said that scholars and officials discuss it solely as being intended for those of inferior and middling capacities. He replied, "Little do they realize..."
This gateway universally encompasses the three faculties; there is no capacity that it does not include, making it most vast and expansive. Furthermore, it is simple and easy to practice.

Indeed, among the ancestral masters of old, there were many who, after attaining realization of the Way, turned their minds toward the Pure Land—such as the great Chan masters Yongming and Zhongfeng, who were by no means alone in this.
However, in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), there are three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
Because their faculties differ, the nine grades of the Pure Land also vary according to those faculties.
Furthermore, there are three types of Pure Lands: first, the land of eternal quiescent light; second, the land of true retribution and adornment; and third, the land of skillful means with remainder.

This last is the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Now, as for these three lands, because the causes cultivated are different, the resulting effects are mostly distinct. Let us briefly examine this.
To speak of it:

the first is the Constantly Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*), which is what the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Āryāvikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*) calls the "Great Treasury of Radiance" (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*). Within this realm, the holy and the ordinary are equal;

the environment and its inhabitants are undifferentiated. It is solely the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), profoundly still and eternally quiescent, that which all Buddhas have realized—the Dharma-body.

This realm is inhabited solely by those successive patriarchs who, through sudden awakening to the Dharma-body in a single thought-moment, have wondrously realized their identity with it and entered the Buddha-realm;
it is precisely the pure land for those of the highest capacity.
Second is the Land of True Reward Adornment. This is the twenty-fold Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), which is the dwelling place of the Sambhogakāya Buddha.

It is a pure land exclusively for the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). It is invisible and inaudible to those of the Two Vehicles, such as the Śrāvakas.
These are the individuals who received prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who await the cultivation of causes over many kalpas before—
This is what is brought about by past karma. A portion of this Pure Land is by no means easily accessible to ordinary beings.

Third is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, also known as the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages. This is precisely the nine grades of distinction; it is the transformation land of Amitābha.
Within the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng shìjiè*), there are twenty tiers; from the first tier to—
The thirteenth layer constitutes the Sahā world, which is the central principal realm among these thirteen layers.
That Land of Ultimate Bliss is exactly equal in extent to the Sahā world; from the center to the western edge of its flower petals, it is said to lie beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands.
As for its being listed alongside the Sahā world, this is because among all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, the Sahā alone [is the central one].

It is defiled and foul; filled with earth, stones, and various mountains, it is a place where the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties abound, a gathering of manifold sufferings, and is thus called "Endurance" (Sahā).
Its sentient beings are stubborn and fierce, making them most difficult to discipline and transform.

Therefore, although our Śākyamuni Buddha may employ the ten wholesome actions to guide humans and devas, they remain within birth and death and have not yet escaped the cycle of saṃsāra. Only by practicing Chan and awakening to the mind [is liberation attained].

Furthermore, because sudden enlightenment is difficult to attain, the single gateway of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land was established; this is called "transcending the three realms horizontally.
By relying on the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows made during his causal stage, any who recite his name will certainly be welcomed and guided by him.

Because one is born in that Pure Land, rebirth is easy. Although one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), by merely attaining birth in that land, one beholds the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and dwells on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
One never again falls into the cycle of birth and death within the triple world (*tridhātu*).

From this point, if one makes a vow to return to the triple world to save sentient beings, then one’s coming and going will be sovereign; one will not be detained by the suffering of birth and death. Therefore...
Master Yongming said, "If one can simply behold Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment? This is indeed so.
This Dharma door can be accomplished through a lifetime of sincerity; once one has attained birth there, one is suddenly liberated from birth and death and forever escapes the cycle of saṃsāra.

Moreover, while it is difficult to resolve birth and death through the practice of Zen meditation, it is easy to resolve birth and death through the recitation of the Buddha’s name. It requires nothing more than a single moment of genuine, sincere thought.
This is merely a sincere and earnest effort.

To demonstrate the essential point of mindfulness of the Buddha, there is this single gate of mindful recitation for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Its fundamental purpose is to resolve the great matter of birth and death; therefore, it is called "mindfulness of the Buddha."

To understand birth and death. People today take understanding birth and death as their reason for developing the aspiration [for enlightenment]; only then are they willing to recite the Buddha’s name. They simply say that the Buddha can bring an end to birth and death.
Yet, if one does not know the root and trunk of birth and death, after all, toward what will one direct the recitation?
If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot sever the root and trunk of birth and death, how can one bring an end to birth and death? What is birth?
The root-stump of death. An ancient said: "If one's karma is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha; if craving is not severed, one will not be born in the Pure Land.
Thus we know that the root of craving is the very root-stump of birth and death. That all sentient beings undergo the suffering of birth and death is entirely due to the fault of craving and desire.
Tracing back this root of craving, it is not something possessed in this present life, nor has it existed for only one or two lifetimes.

Regarding those who have undergone three or four births: from the very beginning, since the first arising of birth and death, throughout every life and every rebirth, the taking up and casting off of bodies has been transmitted solely through craving and desire, continuing right down to this day.

Reflecting back upon the past, when has there ever been even a single thought that momentarily separated us from this root of craving? Thus, the seeds of this root of craving have accumulated over kalpas until they are profound and deep.

Therefore, birth and death are endless. Only today have you finally resolved to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, yet you merely hope for rebirth in the Western Pure Land while remaining empty-handed;
even attachment to this very name is the root of birth and death. It is unknown when you will ever have a single thought that severs this clinging.
Since you do not know the root of birth and death, you practice mindfulness of the Buddha on one hand while the root of birth and death grows ever longer on the other.
In this way, mindfulness of the Buddha and birth and death are unrelated to one another.

No matter how you practice in such a state, when the time of death arrives, you will see only the root of craving for life manifest before you; it is only then that you will realize your mindfulness of the Buddha has been ineffective.

Yet they resent that their recitation of the Buddha’s name lacks spiritual efficacy; by then, it is too late for regret. Therefore, I exhort those who currently practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name:
first, you must understand that craving is the root of birth and death. As you recite the Buddha’s name now, in every thought-moment you must sever this root of craving.

Even when practicing the recitation of the Buddha’s name at home in daily life, regarding those things seen before your eyes—children, grandchildren, family affairs, and property—[you must realize they are all empty].
If there is not a single thing that is not love, then there is not a single matter or a single thought that is not the active pursuit of birth and death.

It is as if one’s entire body were within a pit of fire; yet, even while reciting the Buddha’s name, one does not realize that the root of attachment within the mind has never for a single moment been let go.
This is exactly like when one is not reciting the Buddha’s name—claiming only that one’s recitation is not earnest, without realizing that it is attachment itself [that is the problem].
Master: Reciting the Buddha’s name is merely the outer skin; thus, the Buddha hears only the recitation, while attachment hears only its own growth.
For instance, when the sentiments of a child for its parents manifest before you, turn the light back and look: can this single utterance of "Buddha" truly withstand such attachment?
Can it truly sever such attachment? If it cannot sever this attachment, how will you ever reach a final resolution?
Regarding birth and death, because one has become habituated through many lifetimes by taking craving as a condition, the mind is extremely callous when mindfulness of the Buddha is first aroused;
furthermore, it lacks earnestness, and for this reason, one gains no power from it. If one cannot maintain control over the objects of craving currently before one's eyes, then at the time of death—
Ultimately, it cannot be maintained. Therefore, I exhort those who practice the Buddha-remembrance: first, you must know that your resolve for birth-and-death is urgent;
second, you must sever the urge for birth-and-death with urgency. You must, at every moment of thought, cut through the very root of birth-and-death.
Then, every single thought-moment is a time of resolving birth-and-death. Why wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month before you finally achieve this resolution?
It is already too late. What is called "the present moment" is entirely the matter of birth and death.
If one can realize the emptiness of birth and death right now, then with every thought thus truly earnest, it will be as if "every stroke of the blade draws blood.

With such an application of mind, if one does not transcend birth and death, then all Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods. Therefore, whether lay or ordained, simply knowing the mind of birth and death is itself the transcendence of birth and death.
It is also the time of death. Could there be any other more wondrous Dharma than this? Upon arriving at Yunqi Mountain, he wrote a verse for the assembly, saying:
"The essence of Buddha-recitation is to transcend birth and death; first, one must recognize the mind of birth and death. Deluded attachment is itself birth and death."
Roots: If their roots are not uprooted, it is difficult to attain liberation. Delusion and craving are themselves the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha;
one uses the mindfulness of the Buddha to sever delusion and craving. If delusion and craving can be severed moment by moment, then Amitābha will manifest fully in every thought.
This is precisely what constitutes true diligence; one must not forget it for even a single moment. The Pure Land resides within the pure mind; do not seek it elsewhere.
He searched elsewhere and showed it to Jinggong and others from Western India.
Some said, "Ordinary people know only that under the Gate of the Patriarchs, awakening is held supreme; yet the original intent of awakening the mind is precisely to transcend birth and death."
Listen. Is not the recollection of the Buddha (*nien-fo*) not the very dharma for escaping birth and death? Among those who practice Chan meditation, many do not succeed in escaping;

yet for those who recollect the Buddha, there is no doubt they will escape birth and death. The reason for this is that Chan meditation requires the abandonment of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), whereas the recollection of the Buddha is focused precisely upon conceptualization.
Since sentient beings have long been submerged in deluded thoughts, it is truly difficult to abandon them. Therefore, rather than abandoning defiled thoughts, one transforms them into pure thoughts.

This is the method of "using poison to counteract poison," a practice of broad exchange. Therefore, while investigating through *chan* (Zen) inquiry is difficult to realize, reciting the Buddha's name (*nianfo*) is easy to accomplish.

If one truly possesses a sense of urgency regarding birth and death, then by reciting the Buddha’s name with the same mind applied to *chan* inquiry, what cause for concern would there be that one will not resolve the matter of birth and death within this lifetime?

If a person were truly to feel such urgency regarding birth and death that every thought-moment is like extinguishing a fire on one's head—fearing only that once the human body is lost, it may not be regained for hundreds of kalpas—they must firmly "chew" this single invocation of the Buddha's name, determined to confront all deluded thoughts in every situation.
Let it manifest in every thought-moment so as not to be entangled or obstructed by delusion. Only through such diligent and arduous effort can this be achieved.
After a long time of pure cultivation, one naturally attains resonance; thus, without seeking to form a unified whole, one spontaneously becomes a single piece.

Regarding the essentials of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' practice, there are only the two gates of Chan and Pure Land, adorned by the myriad practices—this constitutes the path of correct cultivation.
Lately, among students who study Chan, many have been led astray by the errors of false teachers into heterodoxy.

To see such a dense forest [of views], to fall under the power of the māra of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and to increase the seeds of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*)—this is truly cause for great anxiety.

How much more so when not even one person out of ten attains the state of liberation! Such a situation is not only a mistake for oneself, but also leads others astray; how can one not be fearful? Therefore:

The Elder vigorously maintains that the true practice of the Pure Land is the most essential and subtle method. Although reciting the Buddha’s name is easy, worldly people do not understand it and treat it with common indifference;
they fail to realize that it is the true and vital path for escaping birth and death.
However, they do not know that when reciting the Buddha’s name, one must first clear away all afflictions and delusive thoughts from within one's own breast.
Relinquish all at once the various disordered thoughts of greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment, until you reach the point where there is nothing further to relinquish.
Spend your days single-mindedly upholding the single phrase "Namu Amitābha Buddha.

If you can apply your mind in this way, reaching the state of "one-pointedness without distraction" at the moment of death, that is precisely the occasion for transcending birth and death and being born in the Pure Land.
Chan Master Shouchang Wuming Huijing (Dharma heir of Chan Master Zhong of Lingshan).

His name was Huijing; his style name was Wuming. He was the son of the Pei family of Chongren, Fuzhou. When his mother first experienced the difficulties of childbirth, his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereupon she was delivered.
Consequently, he was named Huijing. He was exceptionally gifted and stood apart from the common crowd; his physical appearance was ancient and dignified, as if...

Like a soaring crane ascending into the void, his innate nature was serene and free from worldly attachments or particular cravings. At the age of nine, upon entering the local school, he immediately inquired about the "vast and unyielding breath" (*hao-ran zhi qi*);
his teacher marveled at this. Constantly indifferent to the affairs of the mundane world, at seventeen he abandoned his brush and inkstone, resolving with great resolve to seek the Way.
One day, while visiting the residence of a lay practitioner (*jushi*), he saw the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on a table and read it.

He would invariably finish each scroll as if he had recovered a long-lost possession; his fellow students marveled at this. Consequently, he renounced meat and wine and resolved to pursue the path beyond the world.

At that time, Chan Master Yunkong was preaching the Dharma at Ling Shan, so he went there to rely upon him. For three years, he performed manual labor without ever failing to follow his master’s instructions.
I had long harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, I saw a verse by Master Zhuan (Chuanxiao) which read:

"If one discusses the four-line verse, it should never be separated from the body. The Master [Zhuan] was unconsciously moved to tears; there was a line that spoke of radiating light throughout the entire world.

Later, while casually browsing through the *Tripitaka*, I reached the "Chapter on the Eye of the School" (*Zongyan pin*) and only then realized the principle of the "separate transmission outside the teachings. As for...

Regarding the distinctions between the five schools, I have privately harbored doubts about them for eight months, feeling as bewildered and dull-witted as a rustic; others took me for one suffering from folly.
After a long time, I attained a realization. Thereupon, with a resolute will to investigate the matter, I took my leave of Rinzan and went to a secluded place on Mount Gakō.
There I cleared away the weeds to build a dwelling, vowing that until I had enlightened myself to the Great Matter, I would never leave this mountain. For three years, no one...
As for "The Knower": while reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), there was a monk who asked Xingshan, "What is the Way? Xingshan replied, "A magnificent mountain.
At that moment, the Master’s doubt suddenly arose, so much so that he forgot to sleep or eat. One day, while moving a stone, he found it stubbornly immovable.
With all his might, he gave a single push and attained sudden, great enlightenment. Impulsively, he spoke this verse:

"If one wishes to study the path of unsurpassed Bodhi, One must urgently clear away the great, fine mountains. Only upon knowing the Way does one realize the mountains are not fine; Turning the body around, one leaps out through the Patriarch’s Barrier.
He returned to present this to Linji (Im-san), who certified it for him. Later, while residing at Shouchang, he personally cleared the fields and provided three meals daily.
He gathered a hundred followers. At dusk, he returned and preached the essentials of the Dharma. Finally, foreseeing the time of his passing, he issued this admonition:

"The ancients cherished the permanent property of the Sangha as they did their own life-force. I, an old monk, have not spared my own body or life for the sake of securing the permanent property. From this day forth, I shall no longer lay stones.
He wrote by hand a farewell letter to all his companions, both near and far, exhorting them to seek the truth through self-inquiry. Thereupon, he sat upright...
He passed away while seated. Hanshan remarked: "The Master’s lofty integrity and solitary style are truly sufficient to inspire those of the degenerate age.
As for his diligence and power of endurance, one must seek them among the ancients. Although his shadow never left the mountains, his reputation reached far;
indeed, these words are not false. The Master taught: "Those who study the Buddha-way must, above all, not dwell in the stage of learning; they must practice."
Only upon reaching the ground of the Buddhas and Patriarchs can this be attained. Thus, when Sudhana visited over a hundred cities, he would always say, "I have first resolved to attain Bodhicitta;
how should I be instructed to study the path of a Bodhisattva? This is as it is said: "There is not a single dharma that can be obtained which is named Bodhicitta.
As for what has been attained by the successive Patriarchs of old, how could there be even the slightest dharma to be obtained? Therefore, a monk asked the Ninth [Patriarch]:
Fengqian said, "The patriarchs have transmitted it to one another; what, then, was transmitted? Feng said, "Śākyamuni was stingy; Kāśyapa was wealthy.
A monk asked, "What is Śākyamuni’s stinginess? Feng said, "He had nothing to give to others. The monk asked, "What is Kāśyapa’s wealth?
Feng said, "He is the Marquis Mengchang within the realm. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the matter that was transmitted? Feng said, "A hundred [pieces of gold]."
The Elder Sengren divided his night lamp [with others]. You must look closely: is this one in training (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Nevertheless, it is only by practicing to the end that one comes to know such a thing exists. If one practices but does not study, nine times out of ten one reaches the goal.

If one studies but does not practice, not even once in ten will one reach it. When study and practice are both complete, ten who cultivate will all reach the goal. Thus, Śākyamuni practiced austerities for six years.
Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years; Mazu did not open his mouth for twenty years; and Zhaozhou was still traveling on foot at the age of eighty.

Those throughout past and present who have attained this essential meaning are beyond the capacity of pen and tongue to fully describe; each and every one of them was established through actual practice.
In a single moment, break through the lacquer bucket; then, naturally, everything will accord with the head and every object will be clear.

That which has been used exhaustively throughout antiquity and the present—once it reaches your hands, when you wish to employ it, it is truly like a poor woman’s *lanca* grass: you simply pick it up as it comes to hand.

Do not merely practice study; even if you have passed through the belly of the Tripitaka and brought forth the seventeen hundred koans, when the time for fixed karma arrives, you will inevitably face a scene of frantic turmoil. Have no other thoughts—there is simply "A-ha! (or "A-ya").

What, then, is fixed karma? It is precisely the realm of habitual patterns that have matured since beginningless time. Although one recognizes this fault and exerts every effort to clear it away, things become even more chaotic;
the power of practice does not endure. Thus, despite making progress in cultivation, one unknowingly and unconsciously merges everything into a single, indistinguishable mass.
If you wish for the enemies of fixed karma to disperse, the first thing you must not do is strike them.
Bury them all. Simply take up this "head-word" for confronting birth and death and place it directly before you;
then, inevitably, these idle spirits, wild ghosts, foxes, and various strange and demonic beings within the cave of deluded thoughts will not dare to approach.

Long ago, the Venerable Panthaka held a broom for twenty years until his mind regarding birth and death was shattered, and he realized the patience of the non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Rest in peace.
Are there not those who practice with exhaustive effort yet fail to glimpse the ground? Do not, under any circumstances, indulge in the arrogance of claiming it is easy;
for even this mountain monk, having applied myself to earnest practice for thirty years, still stumble and falter—how much less can one achieve success without exerting oneself to the death?
Thus, Fengyang said: "The ancients required twenty or thirty years before they finally accomplished it; how much more so in these present times?"
Whenever I am before others, I do not dare say that [Zen] is easy. It is not that I lack the strength of true practice;

rather, have I ever truly grasped the core of the ancients? How would I dare speak such words? This is certainly not idle chatter intended to deceive people. The sin of deceiving others is by no means a light matter.
If you all are willing to resolve your minds, you should apply yourselves to the essential practice of Sudhana, using the *huatou* (critical phrase) of the various masters.

Pressing forward with resolute determination, do not calculate whether it takes years or months; you will surely reach the day when, like clouds parting to reveal the moon, the entire earth is bathed in radiance.

Having thus resolved to turn toward the Buddha, even before reaching your destination, you must establish checkpoints and set up camps to block the wild foxes, discern right from wrong, and enter the realm of equality, so that you are no longer led astray by the six teachers into the fires of worldly attachment.
This faction seduces and ruins future generations and defiles the former sages. A true lion cub turns at a single stroke; one must decisively determine their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Unless it is the seal transmitted separately by Kāśyapa, even if one treads upon lotus flowers, wears a jeweled canopy atop one's head, possesses eloquence like a cascading river, or spans the universe with one’s body—once confronted directly, they will surely vomit [their falsehoods] out. Why? It is simply because one must select [the authentic].
He takes up one [method], possessing the skillful means to settle heaven and earth and a heart free from dross. He revives the ancestral style and acts as an eye for the future.
The Buddha-dharma is rarely encountered in a thousand lifetimes; the Way of the Patriarchs is difficult to meet in ten thousand ages. By fortunate karmic conditions, I have now met it once.

It was as if I had obtained an iron hammer without a hole; my body and mind were bewildered and distressed for many years. Suddenly, passing through a magnificent mountain, it was like finding a supreme treasure.

My joy and exultation have not yet ceased, and even until this present moment, its utility remains inexhaustible. I prostrate myself in hope that you will cherish and value this "Good Heart" in the future.
The Master constantly taught the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land to others, and his verse on reciting the Buddha’s name says:
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must purify their minds; with a pure mind they recite the Buddha’s name and with a pure mind they listen.
When the mind is pure, the mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the mind. To attain Buddhahood is nothing other than the purity of the mind.
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must be diligent; when pure mindfulness continues without interruption, one will first achieve Buddhahood.
The Buddha-mind fills the entire Dharma-realm; In a single thought, without deviation, is the mind of the Supreme Vehicle.
Reciting the Buddha’s name cuts off all doubt; When doubt is purified and exhausted, that is Bodhi.
If every thought does not arise, there is no bondage or entanglement; Throughout the ten directions and the three realms, all shine with universal radiance.
Mind is Buddha, and Buddha is mind; all phenomena return to the single spark of life.
From within this radiant spark, a unique sprout emerges, naturally transcending all expedient means.
The mind that recollects the Buddha is itself the Pure Land; within the abode of the pure mind, all Buddhas dwell.
The mind that recites the Buddha’s name surpasses all things; with an empty mind, one enters the path of non-arising.
Those who recite the Buddha’s name must keep their minds upright; an upright mind is like a crystal mirror, wherein the ten directions are bright and pure, and no object can escape.
The myriad phenomena of the universe are the seal upon the ground of the mind.
Those who practice the mindfulness of Buddha must be sincere; With a sincere heart they mindfully recite the Buddha’s name, and the wild mind comes to rest.
Once the wild mind has ceased, the Buddha appears before one; His radiance is like the moon in a clear pool, where the vast surging waves remain unmixed.
The manifestations of the holy and the ordinary are free from birth and extinction.
When listening with a mind focused on the Buddha, at the moment the time arrives, the heart is naturally gladdened;
it is as if encountering a net that shatters the Great San Pass, or like losing a pearl and emptying the Yellow River to search for it.
To see such inconceivable benefit is not for the sake of idle chatter, but is spoken for your sake.
In the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, one must investigate with fierce intensity; Directly within this mindfulness, pursue that which is originally possessed.
One does not become a Buddha by virtue of mindfulness of the Buddha; The Buddha-nature is pervasive and eternally imperishable.
Raising the eyebrows, you must look for yourself; In a sudden flash of realization, personally forget all prior faults.
People who practice Buddha-remembrance have their own reasons; Their faith does not take the Dharma as its peer.
They disregard both Zen meditation and scriptural exegesis; Only when the mind is suddenly enlightened do they rest.
A cow on open ground plows across the vast earth; A net cast across the heavens gathers in the fierce tigers.
Capturing the living and seizing the vital, he brings awe to the world; Transcending his ancestors and surpassing his predecessors, he stands on a path apart.
I universally exhort those who recite the Buddha’s name and practice Zen: Do not treat your own kin as enemies!
Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian of Gushan, Fuzhou (Dharma heir of Chan Master Shouchang Jing).

The Master was the son of Cai of Jianning. While he was a student in the local school, he lived in a mountain monastery and happened to hear a monk’s verse, which stirred in him a desire to transcend the mundane.
He went to visit Shouchang at Dongyan and presented a verse on Nanquan’s Beheading of the Cat. Shouchang said, "This matter cannot be grasped through a single trigger or a single circumstance;
it requires passing directly through with hands extended, layer upon layer, a hundred times over a thousand folds. Only then might one encounter it.
A person is one who, though their body is already beyond the clear blue sky, still further enters their body into the various treasuries; this is the eye of study.
Consequently, he was urged to contemplate Yunmen’s "dry shit-stick. At the age of forty, he abandoned his home and took refuge with Shouchang to receive the tonsure.
One day, he encountered Chang in a field. Upon returning, the Master went to meet him and asked, "What is the pure, luminous body?
Chang shook out his robe and stood there. The Master said, "Is that all? Is there anything else? Chang brushed off his robe and walked away. The Master entered the abbot’s quarters and prostrated;
before he could even open his mouth, Chang struck him three times with his staff and said, "Henceforth, you must not be so careless. The Master then performed a formal bow.

[The master] withdrew. One day, he happened to hear a monk reciting: "All Buddhas, with a cough and a laugh, together snap their fingers. At this, he suddenly saw through the point of Shouchang’s application.
He composed a verse: "The golden rooster pecks through the azure lapis lazuli; Ten thousand cessations and a thousand restings are known only to oneself.
Reclining peacefully on a single sail under a clear sky, On the mountain ahead, the rain-birds no longer cry. While residing at Gushan, he still believed in the six characters.
Amitābha is the bridge and raft for the Dharma-ending age; thus, following the tradition of Yunqi, I have extracted the essential points of the practice of *nianfo* to show them to all.
Regarding the source of the Pure Land teaching:

in the past, the Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of the "great cause and condition" (*mahāntam artham*), preaching various teachings to universally accommodate the capacities of all sentient beings.
It is merely to remove the filth of habitual tendencies and restore my original purity. However, since capacities are not uniform, the teachings are also a thousandfold.
If one seeks that which is easiest to practice, most stable for entering the Way, and swiftest in achieving results, nothing compares to the single gate of the Pure Land.
What is this Pure Land? It refers to a land within the vast expanse of empty space.

They stand in dense rows; some are pure and some are defiled. If the minds of sentient beings are pure, they will be born in a pure land; if their minds are turbid, they will be born in a turbid land.

Being born in a turbid land, one's obstructions and burdens deepen daily, making it difficult to accomplish wholesome dharmas. Being born in a pure land, one's obstructions and burdens are cleared away day by day.
Wholesome dharmas are easily accomplished; therefore, those who study the Way must distinguish between the pure and the defiled.
Even within the Pure Lands, there are various degrees of distinction. That which is most preeminent is the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
This world has been accomplished through the immeasurable power of vows and the immeasurable merit of Amitābha Buddha;
thus, its meritorious adornments are so vast that they cannot be matched by any other direction. Within it, there are both phenomena and principle.
The practitioner should not neglect either aspect. What is meant by "phenomena" (事)? It refers to all the phenomenal characteristics of the Pure Land enumerated in the sutras.
What is meant by "principle" (理)? It refers to the realization that all phenomenal characteristics do not transcend the single mind.
Although it is said that the Pure Land is "mind-only," this does not preclude the existence of the World of Ultimate Bliss, for that world is precisely what is manifested by the single mind.

Although it is said that Amitābha is one's own original nature (*prakṛti*), this does not preclude the existence of the Lord of Sukhāvatī, for the Lord is precisely what is accomplished through one's own original nature.
Although he is quiescent and without birth, this does not preclude his manifest and vigorous manifestation of birth, because the act of being born in the Pure Land is fundamentally non-arising.
Among the highly intelligent, many delight in discussing abstract principles while deriding and laughing at practical conduct. This is a common failing.
Those of inferior capacity mostly cling to phenomenal practices and remain deluded regarding the true principle.
They do not realize at all that there is no principle outside of phenomena; rather, phenomena are the phenomena within the principle.

To cling to the principle while abandoning phenomena leads to the calamity of falling into emptiness, whereas to cling to phenomena while remaining deluded about the principle still possesses the benefit of rebirth. How can one covet empty talk and thereby incur actual calamity?
Second, regarding the cultivation of this dharma-gate through the correct faith of mindfulness of the Buddha: correct faith is the primary requirement.

It is by means of this faith that the Buddhas of the three periods, the great Bodhisattvas, and the successive patriarchs were able to enter [the path]; without this faith, one will be hesitant and indecisive.

It is settled that [the mind] is frivolous and lacks reality. Regardless of whether one is unwilling to practice, or even if one is willing to practice, if one is inconsistent—sometimes present, sometimes absent;
starting and then stopping—one will lack the resolve to "drive a nail through iron" or the intent to "shoot an arrow through stone or sink it into feathers.
How, then, could such a person achieve this rare merit? This is because the minds and consciousnesses of us ordinary beings are dark and obscured.
Inferior beings are constrained by their immediate associations; they are unable to comprehend vast realms or subtle states.
Upon seeing even a single extraordinary phenomenon, they immediately become suspicious and dare not believe it. Therefore, ordinary people should simply and resolutely follow the Buddha’s words.
With a heart of great compassion and a heart of great wisdom, the Buddha speaks truthful words that are entirely free from falsehood or deception. To disbelieve the Buddha’s words—
What is it that can be trusted? That which is trusted is the word of the Buddha. There are generally two gates: first, trusting its principle; second, trusting its facts.
To trust its principle is to believe that one's own mind is itself the Pure Land, and that one's own nature is Amitābha.
To trust its facts is to believe that there truly exists a Pure Land in the West, and that there truly exists Amitābha in the West. Although...
Principle gives rise to phenomena while fully embodying principle, just as the ocean-seal (sāgaramudrā) can manifest all myriad phenomena.

Although these phenomena exist, they are entirely principle, just as the myriad phenomena do not depart from the ocean-seal. To believe and understand in this way—neither one nor two, yet both one and two—is called right faith (*samyakśraddhā*).
Conversely, to believe in principle but not in phenomena, or to believe in phenomena but not in principle, is not right faith.

This is called biased faith; it is not right faith. If a practitioner has not yet attained such right faith, they must extensively consult those who have prior knowledge and thoroughly examine the sutras and treatises.
Then, all doubts will naturally melt away like ice, and right faith will naturally manifest before them.
Only then can one give rise to great vows and exert great practice to directly attain Bodhi, rather than leaving it for after death.
There are those of exceptionally refined natural talent who, upon merely reading the sutras and treatises, claim to have attained right faith;

yet they are pulled down by the weight of habitual afflictions and cannot move a single step forward. One must realize that this is merely superficial understanding and not true right faith. It is like [the case of] faith...
A tiger can devour a person; how could one dare to provoke it lightly? If one believes that a poisoned cup can kill a person, how could one dare to taste it lightly?
Now, to willingly suffer the calamity of being devoured or poisoned and yet feel no regret—what lack of faith could be more extreme than this?
If you are a man of exceptional character, then please set this matter aside from this moment forth.

Third, regarding the practitioner of the pure karma of the correct practice of mindfulness of the Buddha: having already established right faith, one should cultivate correct practice. As Zhenxie said: "Take this phrase 'Buddha'..."

Take up this critical phrase (*huatou*). Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, maintain it directly and immediately. Do not contemplate with a mind of existence; do not contemplate with a mind of non-existence;
do not contemplate with a mind of both existence and non-existence; do not contemplate with a mind of neither existence nor non-existence.

Cut off the boundaries of past and future; let not a single thought arise. Without traversing stages, one transcends to the stage of Buddhahood. This is the maintenance of the principle. As for the practice...

As for "holding" [the name]: concentrate your will and unify your thoughts. Solely take up the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," relying upon it as if it were Mount Sumeru—unshakable and immovable.
Recite it thus in the morning; recite it thus in the evening; recite it thus while walking; recite it thus while sitting;
and even when responding to conditions or interacting with others, recite it thus. Even if you encounter favorable circumstances...

When encountering adverse conditions, one should likewise maintain this mindfulness. As pure mindfulness continues in succession, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind (*citta-vivaraṇa*).

This is not in the slightest different from the aforementioned method of maintaining the principle. Even if one has not yet attained the opening of the mind, at the time of death one will certainly be reborn in that land;
such a person is certainly not of inferior or middling capacity. Should one’s strength be insufficient or one’s practice not yet perfected, one must necessarily cultivate according to one's ability.

Whether performing recitation and prostrations at dawn and dusk, or ten recitations at early morning, one accumulates merit and virtue, gradually cultivating the seeds of wholesome fruit. The essential requirement is that faith and aspiration be firm;
then, at the moment of death, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. However, if one's rank is somewhat low, the vision of the Buddha will be somewhat delayed.
Nevertheless, it is like ranking at the very bottom of the examination; even so, it is not necessarily a bad thing.

Fourth, for those practitioners who cultivate various merits and pure deeds concurrently, they must extensively cultivate all manner of blessings while single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, taking these as their foundation.
...to assist [them]. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit.
First, filially supporting one’s parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous actions.

Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating dignified decorum. Third, generating the bodhicitta, deeply believing in cause and effect, and reading..."
Reciting the Mahāyāna sutras and exhorting practitioners to advance—these three types of karma are the primary causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Master Sengzhao said: "Though the conditioned is false, if one abandons it, the Buddha-way is difficult to accomplish; though the unconditioned is true, if one clings to it, the nature of wisdom will not be bright.
If you now wish to cultivate the *nien-fo* samādhi and seek rebirth in the Pure Land to swiftly achieve Buddhahood, [you must practice these].
To attain the fruit of Bodhi, one must exclusively take the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as the primary path, while further cultivating merit as a supplementary practice.
Morning and evening, one should constantly and diligently make offerings to the Triple Gem, perform prostrations and repentance, practice giving and uphold the precepts, and purify the three karmas.
One further cultivates pure conditions; all roots of goodness thus cultivated are entirely dedicated toward the Pure Land to accomplish the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha.
This may be called rowing with oars while sailing downstream.

The Compassionate Illuminator and Guide, Master Nianfo Zhengyuan, said: "If there is practice without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary; if there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty.

Only when practice and aspiration support one another can one ascend to the Jewel Ground. Therefore, all who recite the Buddha's name must give rise to the correct aspiration. This correct aspiration..."
This is not a vow for the karmic rewards of human or celestial realms; it is not a vow for the minor fruits of the provisional vehicles;
nor is it a vow that I alone shall be born in the Pure Land and realize Bodhi. Rather, it is a vow that all sentient beings together shall be born in the Pure Land.

It is the same as realizing bodhi. Once this vow is made, one is immediately able to possess immeasurable merit, to eliminate immeasurable defilements of karma, and to shatter immeasurable nets of Māra;
it serves forever as the true seed for attaining Buddhahood. This is what is called the bodhicitta.
Therefore, practitioners should generate it thus every day and at all times, so that the power of their vow remains firm and unshakable.
If there is transformation, then all myriad virtues will be fully accomplished—the true cause for the Pure Land and the sublime practice of Bodhi.
What need, then, is there to worry about not being reborn there?

Sixth is the merit of right mindfulness and pure karma at the time of death. Although these may have been accumulated during one's ordinary days, the final thought at the moment of death is the most critical.
This is because whether one is born into purity or defilement, or enters the state of a sage or an ordinary person, it is solely this single thought that effects the transformation. Every...
I have observed those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha; though they constantly speak of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, at the time of their death, most lack right mindfulness.
Either they crave life and fear death, being attached to this physical carcass, or they look back upon their wives and children, finding it difficult to bear the pain of separation.
Some are bound by their household wealth and refuse to let go; some, due to unfavorable circumstances, end their lives harboring resentment;
others, oppressed by the pains of illness, depart while drinking in agony. Having lost right mindfulness, they willingly follow the path of downfall. I now exhort you:

When the practitioner reaches this point, they need only have sincere faith in the scriptural text, maintain firm and concentrated right mindfulness, relinquish all things in every way, and recite the Buddha’s name until the end.
Alas! The matter of the gate of death is great; in an instant one enters the next life. A single moment of error leads to suffering for kalpas on end.
How can one not be cautious!
This was Chan Master Zhànrán Yuánchéng of Yúnmén in Xuānshèng (he was a successor of Chan Master Niàn of Dàjué).
He was the son of the Xià family of Huìkěi. His mother conceived him after dreaming of a monk. When he grew up, his parents passed away; being extremely impoverished, he served as a postal guard.

Because he had mistakenly submitted a public petition, he was summoned for interrogation. Fearing disgrace, he fled to Yinfeng, who instructed him to contemplate, "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?
After three days and nights, he attained realization. He then went to Master Miaofeng at Tianhuang Mountain to shave his head.

Coincidentally, while listening to monks discuss the Dharma-body verse of the Great Master Fu (Bodhisattva Fotuo), he was able to memorize the scriptures and commentaries, understanding all their meanings and principles. He subsequently went to Yunmen...

After receiving full ordination, he returned to close himself in seclusion at Baolin. Recalling the dialogue between Qianfeng regarding "raising one" and "not being able to raise two," he attained a great awakening.
He composed this verse: "To raise one or to raise two is to distinguish the outward signs; Within this very self, there is fundamentally neither right nor wrong."
The melody of the "Snow Song" is sublime; few can comprehend it. Only Shaoyang was granted permission to harmonize with it in perfect accord.

How could these two elders have ever moved their tongues? Yet throughout the various quarters, people needlessly knit their brows. To deliberate upon this is like a hawk flying to Silla; to mark the boat while searching for a sword is fundamentally delusion.
At Yunqi, he raised the story of High Peak’s “mud ox at the bottom of the sea. The Master pushed out a monk standing nearby and said, “The assembly shall bear witness.”
Xiqian took up residence there. Later, when the monk Huo returned from a ritual bathing ceremony, Xiqian asked, "After a deceased monk has passed away and undergone transformation, where does he go?

The Master stepped forward and said, "Thank you, Preceptor, for your concern. Xiqian then withdrew. When Chan Master Cizhou Nian came from Beijing to preach the Dharma at Fengtu, the Master presented his realization for verification by offering a verse.
[Cizhou] confirmed it with his seal of approval, and thus their relationship as teacher and disciple was established.
He ascended the hall at Kai Fayunmen Guangxiao Monastery. Yunmen’s fan leaps and bounds; today, picking it up, it is quite laughable.
He said, "How is it that a pillar conceives and gives birth to a son? He called out loudly to the assembly, "Tell me, what sound is this?
Is there anyone who knows the news? If no one knows, I, the mountain monk, shall announce it for you."
He made a "wa-wa" sound and said, "If you people still understand how to laugh, nothing has ever been lacking.
If you wish to ask further, it is as if you were to go back to the year of the donkey. He continued, "The matter is not yet resolved; is there anyone in the assembly who wishes to pose a question?

If anyone comes forward, I shall merely strike the grass to startle the snake. As soon as a monk stepped forth, the Master said, "Truly, this is a field of karma. Seize him! and he grabbed hold of him.
The Master descended from his seat with his staff. Throughout his life, he had diligently cultivated pure practices.
He composed a song of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) which says:
"Among a hundred deeds, none is as good as mindfulness of the Buddha; Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha have little affliction."
Whether busy or at leisure, do not let your practice falter; In days to come, you need not fear the examination of King Yama.
Whether walking or sitting, maintain mindfulness; Within every action, apply skillful means.
Every dharma, in every circumstance, is fundamentally perfected— Why need one further inquire after the face of one's mother?
Whether sitting, one is mindful; whether lying down, one is mindful.
Scattered thoughts and dullness merge into a single sphere of purity—a bright pearl illuminating the great thousandfold world-system.
Having traversed this realm and all others, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away; In a single moment before one's eyes, one may transcend it all at once.
Falling blossoms and flowing waters proclaim the True Dharma; sentient beings delusively claim it is separated from them by clouds and sky.
Seven layers of jeweled trees are interspersed, with lapis lazuli for the ground and golden pavilions.
Fragrant breezes blow, making the body comfortable and warm; once the meal is finished, celestial music is played.
I shall compare Sukhāvatī to this Sahā world; though there are eight sufferings in the Sahā world, people do not believe what I proclaim—let me count them for you one by one from the beginning:
first, birth; second, old age; third, many illnesses; separation from what is loved, and a lack of long life.
How can one escape meeting with the hated and the resentful? How can one avoid the failure to obtain what is sought?
These eight sufferings persist through all time. To be liberated from them, one must realize non-arising;
otherwise, even if you dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, how could you escape the encroachment of birth and death?
I shall compare this Sahā world with the Land of Ultimate Bliss; when the two are set side by side, this land truly cannot match that one.
Here, every matter is subject to impermanence, while there, every phenomenon is the realization of perfect awakening.
Upon the golden terraces of the nine grades of lotus flowers, Amitābha has come forth through the vows made over vast eons.
If there are sentient beings who invoke my name, In a single thought they shall grow as noble embryos within the flowers, Reborn in Sukhāvatī, not from any other realm.
Do not concern yourself with whether Amitābha is busy or idle;
When your practice reaches maturity, the flower of the mind will blossom, And the great earth, mountains, and rivers will all radiate light.
One must practice the mindfulness of the Buddha early; do not let the passing moments be wasted in vain.
Counting the days on one's fingers and bowing the head to discuss the ancients—how many heroes have been buried beneath the green grass?
Have you not seen Wang Longshu, who throughout his life exhorted others to recite the name of Amitābha?
Manifesting miraculous efficacy at the moment of death, a divine pearl appeared upon the tip of her writing brush;
yet the Lady of Jing was no longer seen. At that time, she recited the True Sutra together with her maidservants;
though her body had not yet departed from the Sahā world, her name was inscribed upon the superior grade lotus.
