By Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai of Boshan in Guangxin (Dharma successor of Chan Master Jing of Shouchang).
The Master was the son of the Sha family in Shucheng. From birth, he wore lay clothing yet maintained a profound purity; pungent foods, blood, wine, and spirits never entered his mouth.

At sixteen, he traveled to Jinling to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*. He sighed deeply and said, "To seek it, one must look within oneself; how can one merely follow the words and chase the phrases?
Thereupon, he paid homage at Wutai Mountain and received the tonsure from Jing’an. He attended Shouchang for several years, after which he resided at Yi...
In his room, he heard that the Dharma-protecting deity had fallen to the ground; suddenly, his mind opened. He presented this verse: "A single word from Mount Jade induced me;

my mind expanded and the path of speech was cut off. How many profound understandings have there been? Like pouring boiling water upon snow. The golden needle has no handle; it is a favorable cause and condition at the right time.
Plum blossoms bloom on withered branches; peach flowers open in the ninth month. Upon contact with the eye, all is as if debate has ceased. Farewell.
"Cast the sounding pole at the head of a rapid rapids; it drowns countless heroic travelers. Chang E-zhi then recorded the master’s instruction on the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land.
He would frequently address the assembly, saying: "Hold up the single phrase 'Amitābha' alone. One should take faith, practice, and vows as one's provisions.
Believe that your own mind possesses the seed for attaining Buddhahood; believe that a Pure Land exists where one may be reborn; believe..."
"I shall certainly see the Buddha in the future; I shall ultimately attain Buddhahood.

The practitioner should maintain this mindfulness without interruption, just as a person walking along a path must go straight until they reach their destination. As for vows, one should vow that oneself be born in the Pure Land, and further vow that all people throughout the entire world be born together in the Pure Land.
Practitioners who recite the Buddha’s name should properly cultivate the vow to be reborn in the Pure Land; they must not merely seek to perceive the Pure Land before their eyes.

How can those of a broad and great disposition remain confined to a single corner? To claim that "the mind is pure and the land is pure" is precisely what is meant by one who rides upon the great ocean yet mistakes a bubble for the entire tide—is this not delusion?
Master Yunqi said: "To cling to the literal while turning one's back on the principle is like..."
A young child reading the books of the ancient sages grasps the principles while turning their back on the facts; this is like a poor man obtaining a promissory note from a wealthy householder.
Although a child reading books does not yet understand their meaning, there will eventually come a time of illumination; whereas for a poor man who obtains a note...
Even if [karmic offenses] were piled up like mountains, there would ultimately be no way for them to govern one’s destiny.

If one takes up a single phrase of Amitābha and practices recitation—not reciting for others, but for oneself—until one reaches the ultimate state of "single-mindedness without distraction," then the principle of "mind-only" will be understood without the need for further explanation.

Furthermore, what harm is there in making a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land? Having realized the realm of mind-only, though one is born throughout one's entire life, this does not hinder the realization of non-arising.

Throughout the day there is no birth, yet this does not hinder the process of rebirth. How much more so when one contemplates emptiness as true emptiness, such that birth is thoroughly realized as non-birth?
—Chan Master Xueguan Zhiyin of Guangxin Yingshan (successor to Chan Master Boshan Liaoyuan)
The Master was the son of the Fu family of Shangrao. At the age of eight, he took leave of his widowed mother and entered the monastic life under Master Zhuan of Jingde Temple.

Master Zhuan, pitying the Master’s frail physique, instructed him to perform prostrations to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Suddenly, he dreamed that [the Bodhisattva] stroked his head with his hand, whereupon his limbs and bones gradually grew strong.
He read through various books extensively, yet his understanding remained superficial. One day, upon seeing the phrase "fire burns the bottom of the sea" in the *Platform Sutra*, he felt doubt.
While at Mount Boshan, he silently investigated the "Case of the Boatman’s Hiding His Body. One day, seeing an ox pulling a millstone at the stable, the ox suddenly snapped the nose-rope.
He immediately attained realization and presented this verse: "At the very moment of meeting face-to-face, There has never been any concealment."
"The tongue is originally but flesh; chewing it to pieces does no harm. Shanke approved of this. The layman Yujisheng asked:

"I do not inquire further regarding the four selections of Chan and Pure Land by Yongming. However, as for the phrase 'if one possesses both Chan and the Pure Land,' should one engage in formal study?"
The ceremony concluded, and we immediately returned to the West. Alternatively, one might directly and solely uphold [the practice], secretly continuing pure mindfulness;
within this, there is certainly no lack of mutual challenge and response. We beg the Master to specially open up a path for the assembly gathered here before you.

The Master replied: "Master Yongming deeply lamented this matter and extended his hand to rescue and uplift [beings], so that they might know that the true Chan school is itself the true Pure Land, and that apart from the mind alone there is no separate Buddha; the true Pure Land is itself the true Chan school."
Apart from the Buddha, there is no separate mind; for mind and Buddha cannot be bifurcated or divided into two.
Chan and Pure Land cannot be separated or treated as distinct. Thus it is said: "One who possesses both Chan and Pure Land is like a horned tiger;

in this life they serve as a teacher to humanity, and in the future they shall become a Buddha or Patriarch. If one sees the true tiger, it seems unnecessary for it to have horns—it is still capable of devouring people.
If one awakens to true Chan, it seems that one need not necessarily cultivate Pure Land practices to become a Buddha;

yet, when a tiger is both fierce and horned, its majestic power becomes even more formidable. When Chan is realized and is further combined with Pure Land, the brilliance of Chan becomes even more manifest.

Therefore, a "withered Chan" that sinks into emptiness and clings to stillness is not as good as being roused to mindfulness while reciting the Buddha’s name, for this too can attain samādhi. Thus, he further distinguishes them by saying: "Without Chan..."

There is the Pure Land; of ten who practice, ten go there. Because this Pure Land is relied upon and firmly established, it far surpasses wild intellectual understanding that loses the mind—what has such understanding to do with true enlightenment?
Therefore, he further distinguishes: "If one has Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray."

Those who possess neither meditative concentration nor purity are, by their very nature, ordinary beings of the "hair-path" (mārga). Since they forever lack the potential for awakening, they further lose sight of the path to rebirth in the Pure Land.
It is only fitting that they undergo suffering amidst iron beds and copper pillars, bringing saṃsāra upon themselves.
The Buddha is likewise difficult to save. Therefore, the Buddha opened the single gate of the Pure Land to gather all beings in their entirety and encompass them universally.

If one possesses the three elements of faith, practice, and aspiration, then even if they do not realize that "mind-only" and do not perceive the True Buddha, provided they are willing to hold the name and recite the Buddha’s name—merely by invoking the Precious Name, one casts the seed into the womb of the lotus;
with the first arising of faith, one's name is already inscribed upon the Golden Ground.
By virtue of the goodness of their precepts, even those of inferior grade can surpass others in enjoying the blissful rewards of celestial palaces;

by the light of the Buddha, even the tiny bodies of crawling insects can be touched. At the moment of death, a single recitation of the name leads even a *caṇḍāla* to be reborn with his karmic burdens;
a parrot’s tongue produced lotus flowers, and its miraculous passing was extraordinary. Thus we know that through the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation), one attains such results.

Universally encompassing the three faculties, where both sages and ordinary beings alike traverse the four lands; casting a net across the heavens to haul in the myriad spirits of the great earth, and building a bridge over the sea of suffering to ferry all those with karmic affinity—Yongming has passed away. Who now shall serve as the ladder and the vessel? I say: [The following is the continuation of the verse: The wind and moon are the boatman, The clouds and mist are the oarsman. The ten directions are the fishing net, The three realms are the fish basket. The five aggregates are the hook, The six sense bases are the bait. The four elements are the water, The eight consciousnesses are the fish. When the hook catches the fish, The fish is caught by the hook. When the hook releases the fish, The fish is released by the hook. If you can understand this, Then you will know the meaning of Yongming’s words. If you cannot understand this, Then you will never know the meaning of Yongming’s words. I say: The wind and moon are the boatman, The clouds and mist are the oarsman. The ten directions are the fishing net, The three realms are the fish basket. The five aggregates are the hook, The six sense bases are the bait. The four elements are the water, The eight consciousnesses are the fish. When the hook catches the fish, The fish is caught by the hook. When the hook releases the fish, The fish is released by the hook. If you can understand this, Then you will know the meaning of Yongming’s words. The Great Master Yunqi possessed a compassionate mind and vast wisdom; having fulfilled his vows, he returned once more to this world.
He integrated Chan and Pure Land as a single, unbroken thread and synthesized the various teachings and schools into a perfect vehicle.

Formerly, the scholar Song Jingliao of Jinhua realized that his previous life was that of the Elder who transcribed the scriptures at Bantang—namely, Master Shou—who had manifested through a rebirth. Thus, for over two hundred years...

O Venerable Master, how could you have long remained hidden, concealing your transformative traces? Were you weary of acting as a bridge for sentient beings that you suddenly ceased to let even a whisper of your influence be heard?
Now, observing the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, one sees its vast gathering of materials and wide-ranging research;

it extracts the essence of the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) to brew a sublime flavor, and shifts the stylistic tone of the Chan school to revitalize the Lotus School. This is what is meant by "even at the brink of a world-flood, one still acts with compassion."

A boat that sinks only at the end of the great night still serves as a precious torch. This is Yongming who withdrew to Yunqi, concealing true Chan within the Pure Land, and transposed Shaoshi to Donglin.
Were it not for those with discerning eyes, how could one distinguish the origins of his coming or understand the scope of his methods?
It may be said: "The wild landscape is no longer cut off by mountains; the heavenly light flows directly through the waters. Buddha.
Is it not said: "If one can bring [the mind] under control in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished"?

This may serve as proof. Master Juelang Daosheng of Mount Jing in Hangzhou (who succeeded Chan Master Dongyuan Jing)—a native of the Zhang family of Jianyang—was twenty-nine years old when he saw his grandfather pass away. He then questioned himself, saying: "This single point..."
"Where has the spiritual luminosity gone? One day, upon hearing a cat cry, he attained realization.
He subsequently went to Ruiyan to shave his head and received full ordination from Boshan at Dongyan.

That winter, he visited Dongyuan, who minutely investigated the points of his lifelong practice and realization, as well as interrogating him on the distinct principles of the five houses' monastic regulations. The Master freely expounded upon his insights.

Master Yuan sighed in admiration, saying, "I did not expect that you would be able to penetrate so deeply into this secret Dharma-gate. This branch of the life-force of wisdom from me, Shouchang, is now entrusted to you for dissemination. He then bestowed upon him his robe and whisk. The Master vowed to broaden his compassion and rectify the times to remedy their deficiencies. He frequently presented the six-character koan and propagated the Pure Land Dharma-gate, instructing the assembly as follows:

[The Master’s instruction on the six-character koan: "Namo Amituofo. [He explained: "This is the single phrase that encompasses all Buddhas and all dharmas. It is the root of all practice and the source of all realization. To recite it with a sincere heart is to enter the Buddha-mind directly. It is like a great medicine that cures all illnesses; there is no ailment it cannot eliminate.

Therefore, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should constantly chant it. Do not seek for it elsewhere; it is right here within your own mind. If you can maintain this single thought without interruption, you will naturally attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus he showed it to the multitude.

The Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha (Nianfo Zhizhi Tu) explains why Buddhas and Patriarchs differ from ordinary people: it is because they skillfully employ their minds, do not occupy fixed positions, and maintain a correct orientation.
Among the essentials of the Buddha-dharma, none surpasses Chan meditation and mindfulness of the Buddha;

while reciting mantras, practicing contemplation, studying the sutras and treatises, and observing the precepts are all virtuous practices, the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha is the most sublime and distinguished. This is because a person possesses only a single mind.
Since this single mind fully encompasses both the mind and the Buddha, all deluded thoughts and miscellaneous discursive thoughts are gathered back into undistracted right mindfulness.
The seeds of the beginningless *karmic consciousness* are entirely dissolved and transformed into the uniquely manifest true mind.

Without separately investigating public cases (*gong'an*), the *hua-tou* (critical phrase) naturally becomes intimate; without minutely scrutinizing the precepts, the Brahma-conduct naturally becomes pure. Not...
Without practicing the methods of contemplation, the principle of truth is spontaneously realized; without reciting mantras, divine efficacy is spontaneously manifested;
without discriminating between names and meanings, the ultimate intent is spontaneously attained; and without traversing the successive stages, the final ground is spontaneously reached.

This is precisely because the mind and Buddha are fully presented, and all phenomena take refuge therein; without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously achieves sudden transcendence, with no further glancing aside or secret deviation.
The mind can be divided and its swiftness robbed away by this Dharma-gate.

Since the founding patriarch [Huiyuan] established his school in the distant past and formed a society on Mount Lu, countless individuals—such as the eighteen eminent worthies—each experienced spiritual resonance;

at the moment of death, they beheld the Buddha, the sacred realm manifested before them, and attained rebirth in the Pure Land. All of these achieved their goal in a single lifetime, without waiting for future lives to practice again.
What is called "a single phrase" means to clearly transcend ten billion kalpas and attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Following him were: Śānadao (Dharma Master Guangming) of Chang’an; Chengyuan (Upādhyāya Banzhou) of Mount Nanyue; Fazhao (Dharma Master Wuhui) of Yunfeng; Shaokang (Dharma Master Taiyan) of Xinding;
Yan-shou (Chan Master Zhijue) of Yongming; Shengchang (Dharma Master Yuanjing) of Zhaokong; and Zongze (Chan Master Cijue) of Changlu.
Reaching our own Great Master Yunqi Lianchi, he revitalized the practice of Pure Land Buddhism and synthesized its various traditions into a great whole, becoming the eighth patriarch.

This is precisely what I mean when I say that he brought together hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates of samādhi and pointed directly to the essential principle of the single phrase of Buddha-recitation as the ultimate goal.

Donning the six perfections to adorn the Dharma-body and gathering all capacities for awakening to lead them toward perfect enlightenment—the grandeur of such edification truly illuminates both past and present.
For to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of the mind is like entering the womb of a sovereign; one is immediately a prince and immediately ascends the royal throne.
The perfection of their application of mind, the loftiness of their station, and the sublimity of their aspiration are not at all like those of common ministers.
One advances gradually through the ranks of the civil service examinations before finally attaining proximity to the honored and noble. Therefore,
I have specially created this diagram to manifest the true decree of the "Directly Above" (xiàngshàng) as fully upheld by Master Baizhang, and to clarify the fundamental tenet of Mazu—
that "mind is Buddha"— which synthesizes the direct pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature of the two Tathāgatas of Vulture Peak and Sukhāvatī.
This is the secret essence of attaining Buddhahood.
During a New Year’s tea talk, someone asked:
"Can the method of reciting the Buddha's name also lead to seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood? The Master said: "In this case, you should call out to awaken the host."
This is the complete presentation of the fundamental principle for directly pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha.

Although Zen meditation (chan) is a direct approach, those who attain realization through it are rare. Only the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name (*nianfo*) is the truly perfect and sudden method.

When ancients referred to *nianfo* as a "shortcut," they had not yet fully exhausted its excellence. While a shortcut differs from a winding path or a forked road, it still cannot avoid entering through a gate.

From without, one enters within. Now the host is manifestly seated upon the imperial throne; having called himself and awakened himself, how could the person atop the Hanyuan Palace seek another shortcut to Chang’an?
Therefore, by taking the recitation of the Buddha’s name as the recitation of the mind, the eternally abiding true mind will become perfectly luminous and pure illumination.
When one does not rush outward in pursuit, one transcends the categories of sage and ordinary, good and evil.
This transcends all dualities—good and evil, right and wrong, great and small, partial and perfect. People today do not realize that their own minds are themselves the Buddha;
instead, they arbitrarily establish numerous names and characteristics for the Western Paradise.

Consequently, they cause this sovereign mind to engage in conceptual inference and calculation among the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), which is like forcing the Emperor on the throne to descend the steps and debate with his ministers and commoners.

This concerns the distinction between the noble and the humble. It further causes the sovereigns and kings within the palace to turn toward the ranks of the scholar-officials and commoners, seeking through the examination system and advancement before finally ascending once more to the royal throne.
Now, this inner succession of the fundamental principle does not enter by means of the merits or services of ministers and officials;
it is what is called the King of Samādhis among all samādhis. Since it is called the "King of Samādhis," how could it [be attained] otherwise?
How can one compare this to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), various names and signs, the six perfections, or the myriad practices of cultivation?
Today, there are none who truly practice *nianfo*; those who claim to uphold the Lotus School have all erred regarding this Buddha, the King of Mind.
It is merely being adrift in a foreign land. It is like a host sitting at home when suddenly a guest arrives from outside and asks, "Is the host at home?
If one is truly the host, one should rightfully reply, "Why do you call for me?
If, at that moment, one cannot act as the host but instead wanders aimlessly about, the guest will call out again, "Host, come back!"
"Come home! Let me speak with you. When the master hears this urgent call, he runs even further away, like a man pursued by a thief;
the more he is called, the faster he flees, disregarding thousands of mountains and ten thousand rivers as he abandons his home and native land.
How could he possibly realize that the master has been dwelling constantly right within his own house all along? Alas, the multitudes of beings upon this great earth!
All those born [into this world] are ignorant of their own master and abandon their homes to wander aimlessly. Only my Compassionate Father, Amitābha, regards these sentient beings as his only child;
in every thought-moment, he desires to call them back to dwell and sit within his home, lest they continue to rush outward in pursuit of things elsewhere.
Question: Now that people have already abandoned their homes and fled abroad, calling out to them brings no return.
Is there not, then, a swift path to be established through skillful means and analogies, so as to cause them to return home?
The Master said: "Excellent. This too is a metaphorical expression. When a person travels to a foreign land, it requires years and months before they can return home.
Have you not seen that Bodhidharma said, 'A single thought-moment turning the pivot is identical to attaining the original state'?
These sentient beings have their minds deluded and wander outside the home, like a person sleeping on a bed who dreams of galloping ten thousand *li* away, perhaps seeing the heavens."

They may see the ultimate bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; or they may see the extreme suffering of the hells; or they may see the calamities of war, water, and fire, or the plundering and slaughter of bandits;
or they may be deluded by wives, children, fame, wealth, and affectionate attachments; or they may face the karmic obstacles of enemies and offenses that have come upon them;

or they may be overwhelmed by grief, sorrow, and affliction regarding matters of great state, such as the imperial court or the frontiers. Their souls are startled and their spirits terrified, and they cry out in a great voice for rescue.
"Alas! Amitābha Buddha has startled me from my great dream. It turns out my body is still upon the bed;
though my entire frame is drenched in sweat, I have not moved a single inch from my native land. How can one take that foreign land to be the true Dharma assembly?
Therefore it is said: 'Moment by moment, call out to awaken those within the dream; realize for yourself that the mind is fundamentally without birth or death. People of today..."
Deeply asleep and intoxicated, one cannot awaken by oneself; it is necessary for kinsmen and close friends to call out to them, push them, prick them with awls, and stab them.
A clever person awakens at the first call, but a heavy person requires further pushing and calling.

If they remain in a state of death-like sleep and delusion, like a man whose skin is devoid of blood, there is no avoiding deep pricks and painful stabs that penetrate to the very marrow, until the matter is thoroughly investigated.
Even for a terminal illness where one might die and never return, this single mind of nianfo is sufficient to serve as a nine-fold elixir of transformation, reviving the dead and restoring life;
it can turn white bones to flesh and bring back the soul. It is a pity that worldly people do not realize that the spiritual efficacy of nianfo is such as this.
Question: My teacher has not grudged the use of his broad and long tongue to speak this Dharma with such poignant urgency for the sake of those deluded throughout past and present.
Now, as for "reciting the Buddha's name," this is precisely the recitation of the mind. Why does he not lead people to recite the mind itself as the direct pointing?
The Master said: "The minds of sentient beings are mostly impure. It is because they are led astray by much deluded thought and craving that they are drawn into the cycle of birth and death.
These deluded thoughts and craving minds are either the mind of hell, or the mind of a hungry ghost;
they are either the mind of an animal, or the mind of an asura; they are either the mind of the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds, or they are the mind of greed and anger."
Envy and delusion; arrogance and conceit; killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying; and the mind of usurpation, rebellion, and chaos—how could such thoughts ever be entertained?

Among all things in this world most worthy of concern are one's parents; yet there are times when they fail to provide care, or when illness reaches its peak, such that even though one cries out "Father!
Mother!", their suffering cannot be avoided. As for the affection of wife and children, or brothers and friends...

These cherished things—children, jade, silks, precious treasures, chariots, horses, palaces, and lands—even the dignity of a ten-thousand-chariot sovereign or the highest rank of nobility—can offer no salvation at all when faced with the calamities of life and death.
Yet, if one seeks what is most dear, nothing is more intimate than oneself;
one’s own hands, feet, head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and tongue are mutually protected. Should one day one’s vision grow dim...
The ears become deaf; the hands contract and the feet stiffen; the throat becomes rigid and the tongue is knotted; the breath is obstructed.
Consequently, the will and the spirit are all overturned and deluded, such that one can no longer maintain self-mastery. How much less, then, can one attend to matters external to the body?
Since matters external to the body cannot be attended to, as for matters pertaining to the mind—such as being able to compose prose or verse on ordinary days—[one is likewise unable].

One is able to apply principles of reason; one is able to manage worldly affairs; one is able to clarify the subtle meanings of the scriptures and teachings; and one is able to engage with public cases (*gong'an*) and their critical pivot points (*jīfēng*).
Yet, when the moment arrives where not even a single breath remains, ultimately the power of thought cannot reach it and deliberation is impossible.
Only this mind of reciting the Buddha's name remains as its own sovereign; only then does one attain freedom and spontaneity, transcending even the sages.
Beyond all good and evil, and the deluded karma of birth and death, is this not what Baizhang called the "spiritual light shining alone,
utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects, its essence revealing the true and eternal— this very Tathāgata"?
This single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha is the king of all samādhis.
Just as Prince Siddhārtha, having entered the womb of Queen Māyādevī, was already the sole honored one above and below heaven and earth as soon as he took birth upon the ground.
This is precisely the Prince, the Son of the King. The father-king’s entire realm, state, and nation are all already the possession of the prince;
why must he act like a common subject, attaining fame, merit, rank, and title one degree at a time until reaching the highest grade, only then finally possessing a territory?
It is simply this single thought—the wondrous, perfect, true mind—which is naturally noble and sublime, utterly transcendent.

Furthermore, how could one be willing to follow the gradual gates of the various minor teachings—cultivating a single merit, establishing a single practice, severing a single delusion, and advancing a single stage—gradually accumulating merit and traversing the rungs of a ladder before finally reaching the ultimate ground?
If you say, "I have never practiced the six perfections and myriad deeds;
how then could I achieve the adornment of a buddha-land?"—you do not realize that when a single drop of water is cast into the great ocean, it absorbs the flavors of a hundred rivers.

When the single mind is cast into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), it unifies all virtues and becomes fully complete. It illuminates the masses of darkness while shining alone, like a single needle piercing the Great Void.
Reaching the ultimate, it encompasses heaven and earth without exceeding them; it completes the myriad things in their particularity without omission.

This is what is meant by "dissolving my eons of inverted thoughts," attaining the Dharma-body without passing through kalpas of *asaṃkhyeya*, and perfectly accomplishing the eighty thousand gates in the snap of a finger.
Regarding "directly transcending to enter the stage of the Tathāgata," only this supreme, singular vehicle of the wondrous mind is sufficient to correspond to this principle.
This Dharma-gate of my *nien-fo* samādhi exclusively takes the pure essence of the one mind;

it is like the six lines of the Qian hexagram in the *Great Changes*, where every aspect—above and below, inner and outer—is nothing other than that same pure essence, devoid of any further generation, overcoming, restraint, or transformation.
As for the various transformations, reversals, and composite forms, that which is called "pure" (*chún*) does not manifest the beginning and end with excessive clarity.

When one mounts the six dragons to govern Heaven, as soon as one sees the dragon in concealment, or in agitation, leaping, flying, or at its zenith, there are already six heads, and thus one cannot employ the nine.
Only when one does not see the six dragons as having heads is there pure unity governing Heaven. This is...

To see that the Way of Heaven is unmixed—this Dharma-gate of the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi—is uniquely great, easy, and weighty like the hexagram Qian (Heaven). It is sufficient to serve as a metaphor.
As for the remaining six sons [of the trigrams] and the sixty-four hexagrams of the Eight Trigrams, they all involve the intermingling of yin and yang in six ways;
their substance is broken and not pure. Thus, one cannot say of them, "Riding the six dragons at the proper times to govern Heaven. This applies only to the King Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance.
This Dharma gate may be correlated with the pure and unadulterated mind of the youth Sudhana, which is able to enter the samādhi of the body of Vairocana within the one true Dharma-realm.
For this reason, Amitābha Buddha manifests as Immeasurable Light in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, he is the sovereign lord within the King of the Dharmadhātu-garbha-body.
In the Gate of the Patriarchs (the Chan school), he may be paired with the "natural nobility" where returning home consists entirely of one's descendants, yet the grandfather has never left the door.
Furthermore, regarding the Pure Dharma-body in the Land of Constant Tranquil Light, there is no need to push for the father to be inside it either. Is this not the celestial realm?
This is the wondrous principle of the total upholding [of the Way] throughout the world.

As for the essential point of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), the Buddhas have always been awakened and never deluded; they are like the sun’s orb in the sky, with no further confusion or obscurity. Sentient beings, however, have always been deluded and not...
Awakening. Just as when one awakens from a dream of forms and perceptions, there is no further deluded clarity; therefore, mindfulness of the Buddha is the most direct and expedient method.
By awakening the Master of one’s own house with every thought-moment, one will no longer be deluded by the cycle of birth and death within the realms of sense organs, objects, and consciousness.
As it is said: "If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; if the mind does not waver, the myriad dharmas are one."
This is because reciting the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and without distraction is like the roar of a lion or the trampling of a king elephant.
What foxes or monstrous beasts could withstand such power and not be destroyed? However, in the practice of nianfo, it is essential that every thought-moment be uninterrupted, pure, and unmixed.
If one can thus become the master of oneself and is not swayed by delusive thoughts, then the spirit will reach its ultimate purity.
Through transformation, one swiftly accomplishes samādhi.
By means of nianfo (buddha-recollection), one fully brings forth the single mind to accomplish the Pure Land and preach the Dharma for all sentient beings within the dharma-realm.
Originally, they are of one and the same mind-nature; it is only because of the movement of a single thought of delusion that one has [strayed].

Each thus forms its own distinct path. Therefore, if one contemplates the good, one follows the good; if one contemplates evil, one follows evil. If one contemplates existence, one falls into existence;
if one contemplates emptiness, one sinks into emptiness. If one contemplates the delusory, one pursues delusion in saṃsāra; if one contemplates the true, one returns to the True and dwells eternally.
Therefore, sentient beings, because their thoughts move toward objects, flow outward; the Buddhas, likewise because their thoughts move toward objects, return inward to themselves.
Those who gallop far away become increasingly scattered and increasingly deluded; those who turn back toward what is near increasingly gather themselves and increasingly awaken.
Thus, there are degrees of depth among the deluded, and there are both sudden and gradual modes of awakening; so too is it with those who gather themselves.

There are provisional and ultimate [teachings], and those who seek them likewise differ in their speed or slowness. In establishing various forms of transformation according to individual capacities, there is nothing that does not involve immediate guidance at the very moment of thought.

Yet among the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and dharma-gates, none is more swift, more sudden, or more direct and total than the method of the self-mind contemplating the Buddha within itself, and the Buddha within itself contemplating the self-mind;
for this constitutes the non-duality of cause and effect, wherein the fundamental and the initial are identical.
This is the wondrous source. Moreover, for a person, the single mind is the foundation and the myriad dharmas are its function.
If one can simply maintain the single mind, contemplating oneself as the Buddha, then in every thought-moment one will suddenly transcend to the self-awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvidita-āryajñāna*).

Furthermore, what dharma is there that is not manifested from the Buddha of our own mind? Even the hundreds of thousands of skillful means (*upāya*) that involve mutual refutation are none other than [the desire to manifest this].
It causes sentient beings to give rise to true realization and return to the source, so that they are no longer turned by delusive thoughts.

As for the preaching of the Amitābha Sūtra, it does not further distinguish between the real and the delusive; when comparing the ultimate and the provisional, there is nothing to be constrained by in terms of sudden or gradual, partial or perfect.
Furthermore, there is no distinction to be made between beginning and end, or large and small; it is simply the complete presentation of the Dharma of pure liberation—
the single mind without distraction— which enables all those ordinary people, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, heterodox practitioners, and outsiders—

whether they hold views of existence or non-existence, permanence or annihilation— to each suddenly awaken to their own minds, transcend both mundane and supramundane dharmas, and achieve [enlightenment].
This concerns the inconceivable merit. Among the people of the world, who knows the great purport of this sutra?
Its subtlety lies in its not establishing the doctrine of "relying on the true to give rise to the false," nor the discourse of "returning to the true by reversing the false.
Rather, it simply describes that Buddha currently preaching the Dharma, as well as the environment and the inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) of his Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therein...

Such pavilions, stairways, water-birds, and rows of trees, as well as these assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—all are produced by the Tathāgata’s single-minded, pure vows and practices.

If there are those with roots of goodness who aspire to be born there, they should hold fast to the Name; whether for one day or seven days, provided they can maintain single-mindedness without distraction.
Chaos. Spontaneously and suddenly severing the life-root of birth and death, there is immediate response and manifestation;
at that very moment, one personally beholds that Buddha and the assembly of sages. Is this not the Western Pure Land appearing clearly before one’s eyes at the time of death?
Is it not the merit and adornment accomplished through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the Buddha-nature within one's own mind? Yet, the Buddhas of the six directions fear...

The sentient beings of this land lack such deep faith. This is because they have always heard it taught that one must first observe and practice the six perfections and myriad deeds as instructed by the Buddha, and only then can one finally attain the realm of the Buddha.
How is it, then, that in this assembly we are taught only to single-mindedly hold the Name, without relying on expedient means, yet immediately achieve such majestic adornment? Therefore...
Extending his broad and long tongue, with one voice and in unison, he praised this method of single-mindedly holding the Name of our Buddha:
"This is a teaching difficult for sentient beings to believe; this is a practice difficult for all Buddhas to perform. You sentient beings, always believe in single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha;
you are those who have already been protected and remembered by all Buddhas through the accomplishment of inconceivable merit."
Furthermore, if one can maintain the name with single-minded, deep faith, then every thought will be pure and every moment of mindfulness will bring liberation.
Every sense faculty and every sensory object will pervade the entire Dharma-realm, all becoming adornments of the Pure Land. Is this not the beginning and end of the ten ages of past and present?
Without departing from the present moment, the oceans of lands as numerous as atoms—self and other—are not separated by even the tip of a hair.

Our Buddha precisely addresses the sickness of all sentient beings: that they possess excessive knowledge and views; thus, rather than establishing further knowledge and views, he seeks to destroy them.

On the contrary, they produce views and knowledge, yet they are afflicted by those very views and knowledge. For this reason, he teaches them only to single-mindedly hold the Name, without relying on contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Thus, the merit of contemplative practice is spontaneously accomplished; without relying on refutation or establishment, the causes for refutation and establishment are spontaneously accomplished.
If, within the state of single-minded non-distraction, one further engages in the understanding that "thinking is no-thought" and "no-thought is thinking," and so forth, [it is not so].
Is this not also a great loss of the essential principle of "one mind undisturbed"? Furthermore, by using the dualistic terminology of subject and object regarding stillness and illumination,
or the conceptual distinctions of "cessation" and "contemplation," right and wrong, do you instead provoke the false views and conditions of sentient beings in the five turbidities,
thereby misleading them from the true Dharma of their own mind’s pure direct perception?
The method of Buddha-recollection I have described is perfected in its total integration with one's own fundamental mind and self-nature.

Through its inconceivable power, it causes every thought-moment to be fiercely intense and every occasion to reach the mark of reality. Thus, one naturally transcends the mundane world to attain sovereign and sublime excellence.
Is this not in accord with the principle of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" that does not rely on words and letters?
Indeed, some may believe these words, thinking that this direct pointing is so sublime it can universally encompass those of the three capacities and lead them to perfect enlightenment.
Why, they might ask, should there be a ninefold gradation of lotuses in the Pure Land?

Although this Dharma-gate of the self-awakened noble wisdom of the one mind is fundamentally without hierarchy, how can it be otherwise when the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ in their degree of greatness or smallness?

If one can thoroughly comprehend the essential principle of this "total presentation" (*quan ti*) of the single mind, then one will know that the myriad hues of red and purple are no different from the springtime, and that the ten thousand streams and a thousand currents all share the same nature of moisture.
As for the saying, "when the water rises, the boat floats higher;

when the mud is deep, the Buddha is greater," this depends upon the diligence or indolence of one's practice, as well as the depth or shallowness of one's faith and aspiration. △ One should know that ordinary beings of the six realms must...
One must contemplate this Buddha of the mind; only then can one swiftly bring an end to birth and death. Those of the Two Vehicles, the Śrāvakas, must contemplate this Buddha of the mind;
only then can they swiftly transcend limited emptiness. Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas must contemplate this Buddha of the mind; only then can they swiftly transcend the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, even the eldest son, Samantabhadra, must contemplate this Buddha of the mind; only then can he achieve the perfection of the Flower.
This is the adornment of the *Avataṃsaka*. Alas! Thus, when contemplating the Buddha within one's own mind, one must have deep faith in this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation;
only then can one attain the single path of turning the body, which is the vital mechanism for exiting through the gate within the body.
Otherwise, it is best to investigate and study the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* by the Great Master Yunqi, wherein the ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* is harmoniously integrated and penetrated.
It thoroughly transforms the capacities of sentient beings, encompassing all that is vast and great, reaching the ultimate perfection in every respect.
As Master Foyi Shiyu (who succeeded Chan Master Zhanran Cheng), it is said:
"There are many ways of reciting the Buddha’s name: there is the gradual, the sudden, the gradual within the sudden, and the sudden within the gradual. As for example:
People today recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths lubricated by oil; yet, though they do so, they neither contemplate the Buddha’s marks nor recognize the Western Pure Land.
When the time eventually comes that their good and evil karmic retributions are exhausted, this single phrase of the "oil-mouthed" Amitābha will indeed prove useful.
However, for those who practice sudden recitation, they directly hold the name for one day or seven days until they achieve single-mindedness.
It is not only after death that one attains rebirth; rather, Amitābha appears in this very life, manifesting his entire body.

Furthermore, there is a crucial point to recognize for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: with every thought, strike the bell; strike until there is nowhere left to strike, and suddenly you will encounter him.
This refers to those who practice the gradual within the sudden. As for those who practice the sudden within the sudden:

they do not care whether you are in the Western Land or the Eastern Continent, nor do they care whether your mind is in a state of stillness or distraction; they only require that one phrase be recited with mastery, and then one is a true adept.
It is said: "If a person, with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and utters 'Namo Buddha' but once, they have all already attained the Way of Buddhahood.
Nevertheless, why did the ancients also say: "Recite the Buddha's name once; rinse your mouth for three days"? Study this!
The layman Qi Jingtiao (dharma heir of Chan Master San-yi), surnamed Qi and styled Jichao, lived in Yuezhou.
While residing within the school system, he harbored thoughts of transcending the mundane. He sought out spiritual friends and investigated the matter of the self for many years.
Having attained realization beyond words, he subsequently received the seal of his heart from Master San-yi. Alas, the ancestral temple is in autumnal decline.

Among those who succeeded him later, there were many who possessed understanding but lacked practice. Consequently, he compiled the *Zongmen Chongxing Lu* (Record of Venerating Practice in the School Gate) to encourage them.
He consistently took the single method of the Pure Land as his final word, reciting the Buddha’s name morning and night and seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise.

He established a Pure Land Society (*jing-she*) and composed its *Yuanqi* (Prolegomenon), stating: "The gateway of the Pure Land was proclaimed by our Buddha in the past, and has been cultivated by the various holy sages."

Subsequently, its role as a precious raft for crossing over birth and death became manifest and clear. However, since the decline of the Dharma-vehicle, those of "mad wisdom" have arisen to sweep it away.
They pride themselves on being lofty, profound, and transcendent, unaware that they have already entered the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, and no one comes to their rescue.
Allow me to explain this briefly. Those who sweep away the Pure Land generally cite the principle that "the mind is pure because the land is pure."
This teaching holds that there is only the pure land of the mind; how could there be yet another land to which one might be reborn?
This is because [such views] take the mind to be a stream reaching into empty space, thereby falling into the error of nihilism (*uccheda*);

and they take the land to be a truly existing realm external to the mind, thereby falling into the error of eternalism (*śāśvata*). They fail to realize that when one speaks of the mind, mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all it.
It is to rectify one's own mind. When the mind is pure, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the rectification of one's pure mind.
This is what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," for when the mind is pure, the land is pure.

If one were like those who follow the path of wild wisdom, they would merely allow for a pure mind that is empty and void, yet refuse to allow for a Pure Land that is identical to the mind; this is to push the land outside of the mind.
Is this not the view of the non-Buddhists? Those who disparage the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha generally cite the doctrine that "with thought one becomes deviant;
without thought one becomes a sage," asserting that it is sufficient for not a single thought to arise. Why, they ask, add this further thought of upholding the Name?
They consider this merely a state of dull emptiness or extinction, and thus fall ill with the affliction of nihilism.
To regard mindfulness as having a truly existent intrinsic nature is to be afflicted by the notion of permanence;

it is to fail to realize that wondrous non-existence is fundamentally not annihilation, and thus that wondrous existence is itself wondrous non-existence. Since all thoughts are originally devoid of intrinsic nature, seeing one's nature is itself non-thought.
This is what is called the distinction between the sage and the heterodox: it lies within the interval between existence and non-existence. If, like those of "mad wisdom,"...
To speak thus is to know only that the cessation of thought constitutes non-thought, while failing to realize that non-thought is inherent within thought itself;

this is to negate existence by seeking it outside of non-existence. Is this not, indeed, the view of the heterodox? Now, there was one who took pity on those followers of these two types of thought and spoke to me with deep regret:
"In this world, there truly are not a few who practice the Pure Land blindly, without awakening to the fact that the land is but the mind."

Nevertheless, his illness was still relatively easy to treat. However, he merely gathers the leftover spittle of the Chan school, is oblivious to the skillful means of Great Compassion, and bears the wild and reckless views of a heretic;
having entered the snare of external paths, his illness has reached the vital organs and the diaphragm, making it more difficult to cure.
Therefore, its treatment must be urgent. I intend to unify dhyāna and purity, harmonize principle and phenomena, restore the declining wind, and repay the Buddha’s grace.
May you, sir, act as the *pratyaya* for me and announce this to the assembly of virtuous ones. I replied: "This has been my long-standing aspiration.
The Buddha taught that the single gate of the Pure Land is a great skillful means, a wondrous Dharma for swiftly escaping birth and death. If one can truly believe in this mindfulness..."
The Buddha is the entire body of the Dharma-realm of Amitābha; he is the entire body of the Dharma-realm of all infinite Buddhas.
Thus, the power of Amitābha’s vow to welcome and guide is precisely the power of our own mindfulness of the Buddha; the power of our own mindfulness of the Buddha is [the power of Amitābha].
This is precisely the power of Amitābha’s vow to welcome and guide beings; fundamentally, there is no distinction between self and other, nor is it a matter of stimulus and response.
It is like bubbles in the great ocean: as one vanishes in the east, another surges up in the west. What interval could there be? What journey must be traversed?

Indeed, this single thought-moment inherently possesses such inconceivable supernatural powers and wondrous functions. Alas, though everyone possesses them, they remain unaware of their own nature. If...
Regarding the knowledge of birth and the place of death, one cannot help but have doubts; one must urgently cultivate deep faith.
This single gatekeeper and single phrase of Amitābha should be relied upon as firmly as Mount Sumeru.

If one remains unmoved by the eight winds and myriad conditions, then every thought-moment is Amitābha radiating light, and at all times Amitābha is preaching the Dharma. Yongming said: "Ten thousand practice..."

Ten thousand people have departed; it was not that I deceived you. Suppose, by some chance, one were to lose their grip and push over Mount Sumeru with a single shove, causing the great earth to subside and the void to shatter into dust.
Tell me, where would the Buddhas and Amitābha and the great assembly stand as they smile? Smile! Smile!
The Layman further wrote a brief preface to the *Verses on the Pure Land*, saying: "I often observe those of wild wisdom who rely upon the Chan school to disparage the Pure Land.
People say this is because they do not understand the purport of the Pure Land; I, however, say it is precisely because they do not understand the subtlety of the Chan school.
For one who truly knows the Chan school, even brothels and wine shops are nothing other than sites of practice (*dōjō*); how much more so the adornments of the seven jewels?"
Yan, is it not the case that even solitude is a *bodhimaṇḍa*? Are the songs of woodcutters and the chants of herdsmen not all expounding the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
How could it be that the proclamation from the Golden Mouth alone is not the *Prajñāpāramitā*? Whether coarse words or subtle speech, they are all the *paramārtha*.

How could it be that the holding of the Name alone is not the *paramārtha*? As for the great elders of old, even if they occasionally rebuked those who recite the Buddha’s name, did you not see them ever rebuke the Buddha?

To revile the Patriarchs! If one sees their censure of mere recitation of the Buddha's name and immediately claims they are sweeping away the Pure Land, then one is also reviling the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
this is likewise to sweep away the Chan school. All such people are those who have died within the words and phrases of the ancients.
Therefore, I say that one who has truly awakened to the Chan school must surely perfect the principles of both Chan and Pure Land, and not fall into partial views. Those who cling to partial views—
They are certainly not of the lineage that has awakened to Zen.
Onehezi said: "The conduct of a patch-robed monk is like the tracks of a bird in the sky or the traces of a fish on the water.
At times, he swallows a thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas in a single gulp; at other times, his myriad voices do not depart from this one Buddha."
Its mechanism and its function are divine and subtle, beyond the reach of thought.

Like the Old Man of Boshan, who received the Dharma-voice of Lianchi and sang the melody of ignorance, those who harmonized with him included Xueguan Yin, Juelang Sheng, and others, down to Sanmu Zhiyi, whose single branch covered the world—each a wondrous tree.
Their noble counsel and profound understanding of the ultimate meaning are seen in every realm.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s statement that “the Nāga is always in samādhi,” Mount Ying further explains: Reciting the name of the Buddha with single-mindedness and without distraction is a method that takes this as its core principle;
it is a form of practice that is both rigorous and direct. Its excellence lies in grasping the beginning and knowing the end, returning home by way of the very path one travels.
Though the journey may span billions of miles, it can be completed in seven days; through a single thought of rebirth, [one attains it].

This should be the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. One is then called a Buddha. This may be described as "seeking the dragon by grasping its pulse" or "capturing the thief by eliminating the ringleader";
it is the path within paths. Linggu said: "If in every thought one gathers the six sense-faculties, when purity reaches its limit, light will penetrate through.
If every thought does not pass in vain, one can extinguish all suffering of existence. Every thought is a wondrous lotus flower; cause and effect are entirely identical. Thought...

Contemplating the patience of non-arising, body and mind are like illusions and transformations. In every thought-moment, the flowers of the heart bloom; in the nine grades, all see the Buddha simultaneously.
In every thought-moment is Amitāyus, who fundamentally does not abide in nirvana. In every thought-moment is the King of Dharma, eternally sovereign over all phenomena.
In every thought-moment, I fully manifest the teaching; there is none like the Buddha. Alas! The wind of Linggu sweeps across the vast [ocean].
Waves! The snow on Mount Ying fills Chang’an. Those within the realm of learning will surely break out a cold sweat that penetrates their very bones and drenches their hearts.
Their merit and virtue are by no means trivial.
Chan Master Shouyi Fazhen of Benjue Temple in Xuzhou of the Yunmen School (he was a successor of Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben).
He was the son of the Shen family from Jiangyin. In his "Record of the Jingtu Dharma Hall at Chengjiang," he wrote: "Master Feng of Tiantai..."

The teachings of Master Xuezhi were transmitted to Ren Chengjiang. Once he had passed away in accordance with the Dharma, [Ren] reflected upon the various gates of liberation in this world, wondering which was the most skillful and direct path.
He concluded that only the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land would lead to the ultimate destination.
Thereupon, he utilized his resources for acts of generosity, reverently adorned sacred images, established a *bodhimaṇḍa*, and taught others to practice the *nienfo samādhi*.
I shall record this as requested by the assembly. I say: the teaching of the Pure Land is ancient, established in the sūtras and śāstras;

the expositions and analyses of the various masters are likewise already detailed. That its rewards and responses manifest from time to time is not a deception of us. Yet there are still those in the world who harbor doubts;
this is likely because they obstruct themselves with ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus fail to harmonize principle (*li*) with phenomena (*shi*). According to the *Lotus Sūtra*, if a person scatters...
Even those with distracted minds who enter a stupa or temple and once call out "Namo Buddha" have all already attained the Way of the Buddhas;
how much more so for one who seeks birth here with a single-minded, undistracted heart—how could it alone not be so?

Furthermore, if one's perception of the good is unclear and the application of the mind is inconsistent, then even regarding the myriad dharmas of the mundane world, where would one go without doubt, and what practice could lead to attainment? It is only I...
This is indeed the teaching of the Buddha. In short, one should simply believe and accept it; one ought not to doubt whether it exists or not.
If so, does the Pure Land truly exist? He said: "No. Does it truly not exist? He said: "No. Does it both exist and not exist?
He said: "No. Is it neither existent nor non-existent? He said: "No. If this is the case, then where, indeed, does the Pure Land reside?
To be free from these various views is itself called the Pure Land; it is to see the Tathāgata.

If, upon hearing this teaching, one is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid, you should know that such a person will certainly attain birth—yet there is no birth, for they are adorned with that which is non-adornment.
With the purity of faith, in a single thought-moment the flower blooms and the entire body manifests before them, complete with all marks. This is the mind.
Since he is the Buddha’s successor, how can there be any doubt? He has already transcended birth and death and attained immeasurable life.
Should anyone be unable to believe and understand this, the nine grades [of rebirth] are fully present within other skillful means (and so forth).
Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou (who succeeded Chan Master Xuedou Xian).

His family occupation was fishing. His mother dreamed that a star fell upon her house, and shortly thereafter she conceived. When the child was young, he would sit at the stern of a boat and release every fish he caught as soon as he obtained one.
His father scolded and whipped him for this, but he paid it no mind. Later, he traveled to the capital and eventually took refuge at Jingde [Monastery].
He left the temple to become a monk. He visited Jinluan Shan, but there was no accord. He then visited Xing at Yexian, yet again there was no accord.
Traveling eastward, he arrived at Cuifeng and visited Mingjue. Mingjue asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Yihuai. Mingjue said, "Why do you not simply call yourself 'Huai'?"
Yi said, "I attained it at that time. Jue asked, "Who gave you this name? Yi replied, "It has been ten years since I received the precepts.
Jue said, "How many pairs of straw sandals have you worn out on your travels? Yi said, "Master, do not deceive people. Jue said, "I myself am without measure;
what about you? The Master was speechless. Jue struck him and said, "You are a liar and a talker of falsehoods!"
Han went out. Shortly thereafter, while acting as a water-carrier, he broke his carrying pole while drawing water and was suddenly enlightened.

He composed a verse of spontaneous realization, saying: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on one foot atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak. Seizing the bright pearl from beneath the chin of the black dragon."
With a single word, he thoroughly penetrated the meaning of Vimalakīrti. Juewen clapped his hands on the desk and praised him, saying, "Excellent!
The Master once cultivated the Pure Land and diligently encouraged others to do the same. In his quarters, he asked his students:

"If one says to abandon the defiled and take up the pure, or to loathe this world and rejoice in that, this is a sentiment of acceptance and rejection—the deluded conceptualization of sentient beings. If one says there is no Pure Land..."
This would contradict the Buddha’s words. "How should those who cultivate the Pure Land practice? When the assembly remained silent, he answered himself:
"To be born is certainly to be born; to go is truly not to go. He further said: "It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its reflection sinking into the cold water.
The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain the reflection."
Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben of Hui-lin Temple in Tokyo (who was a successor of Chan Master Tian-yi Huai).
He was the son of the Guan family of Wuxi. He visited Tian-yi, who then cited the story of Vasubandhu descending from the inner palace of Maitreya.
Asanga asked, "Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for those devas.

In a single period, Maitreya brings five hundred billion devaputras to the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). I do not yet know what dharma he teaches.
Vasubandhu replied, "He teaches only this very dharma. [Asanga asked,] "What is this dharma? After a long time, the Master attained awakening; his nature was inclined toward joy.
He slept with his snoring so loud that those who heard it were weary of it. When they reported this to Master Yì, Yì said, "This child is the banner of diligence for my house.
You all shall rely upon him in the future. Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty held the Master in the highest esteem and once summoned him for an audience.

The Master remained composed and natural, showing neither elation nor dejection. On the day he departed from the capital, carriages and horsemen of princes and high officials followed him in a continuous stream.
The Master instructed him, saying: "Time and months cannot be toyed with; old age and illness do not wait for anyone.

Only through diligent cultivation without indolence can one truly act as a true disciple. Those who heard this were moved without exception. On the day he ascended the hall, auspicious light appeared in the world.
He gathered the assembly and struck the drum; the drum spun upon the ground, revolving and emitting a thunderous resonance. The multitude was startled and retreated.

A monk stepped forward and said, "This is an auspicious sign that the Dharma-thunder of this Master shall shake the earth. As soon as he finished speaking, the monk vanished. From then on, the Dharma seat flourished daily, with the assembly constantly numbering five hundred.
In his daily life, the Master secretly cultivated the Pure Land practice. Once, when the Dharma Master Cai of Leifeng traveled in spirit to the Pure Land...
At Tushi, he saw an exceptionally beautiful flower and inquired about it. [The attendant] said, "It awaits Chan Master Ben of Jingci.

Furthermore, when Master Xi of Zifu went to Huilin Temple, he prostrated at the feet [of the abbot] and gave him gold before departing. When people questioned him on the reason for this, he said, "In my meditative concentration, I saw a golden lotus flower;
others say it was to await Master Ben. Someone asked, "The Master’s transmission is the Direct Pointing. Why did you use the realm of the lotus as a designation?"
The answer was: "Although he belonged to the Chan school, he also practiced the Pure Land method concurrently. Later, when his end approached, he passed away while sitting peacefully.
He was posthumously titled Grand Master Yuanzhao."
The Master Yunqi’s eulogy states: "There are two senses of 'simultaneity. Simultaneity in the sense of standing foot upon two boats is indeed impossible;
however, what impossibility is there in simultaneity that is unimpeded and all-pervasive?
Moreover, since there is no Pure Land outside of Chan, the land is identical to the mind; they are fundamentally not two separate things. This is what is meant by 'perfect illumination.'"
Chan Master Qisong (posthumously titled Furi Mingjiao), a successor of Chan Master Dongshan Cong, was a native of Tanting in Tengzhou.

His secular surname was Li. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and received ordination at thirteen; the following year, he received full precepts. At nineteen, he began his travels to seek instruction.
He would often spend the night venerating an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, reciting the Bodhisattva’s name. It was his constant practice...
He ceased writing only after reaching one hundred thousand words. From that time on, he was able to master the chapters and sentences of worldly scriptures without formal study.

Having received the Dharma from Dongshan, he composed the *Yuanjiao lun* (Treatise on the Source of the Teachings) in over one hundred thousand words to refute the arguments of Han Yu and others who sought to exclude Buddhism. Those who read it were awestruck and submissive.

Later, while residing at the Yong'an Aranya, he authored the *Chanmen dingzu tu* (Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs of the Chan School) and the *Chuanfa zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma). He assisted...

He compiled the *Jiaobian* (Compilation of Teachings) and presented it to the throne in a ten-thousand-word memorial. Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty praised it highly and ordered him to edit and arrange the Eight Tripitakas.
He was granted the title Great Master Mingjiao. In his later years, he resided at Mount Furi and composed a poem on longing for the Pure Land, which says:
Delighting in leisure by the green depths, soaring high while playing with fragrant bait— For what reason do you despise kings and lords?
Your mind transcends heaven and earth. The imperial Way of the ancient sovereigns is vast; why do you toil in life, binding yourself?
It is better to go back and return: ride the wind and brush the sleeves of your robe.
The Golden Immortal’s White Jade Capital— As one departs, how ethereal it seems!
Twelve tiers of towers and pavilions, Luminous and exquisite, floating above the clouds. The silver river has the moon for its waves; Ten thousand acres are but a single pond.
Lotus flowers bloom with extraordinary blossoms, And the kalaviṅka birds sing their auspicious songs. Suddenly, all this is far removed from the human world.
The thoughts drift into a vast void, empty and desolate, where the mist clears into a distant clarity. The colors of the clearing sky embrace the autumnal scene;
as my reflections deepen, I linger and gaze upon the summit of the western peak. There, the bright moon is perfectly full, capable of illuminating the silhouette of a beautiful woman.
Whether the beauty comes or not, the clouds and mists are vast over the forested ridges.
On the fourth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Xīníng era, he rose at dawn and wrote this verse: "The moon is bright in the night to come;
I shall now walk alone. I will not follow the old man of Dàméi, Who was greedy to hear the cries of the flying squirrel. He passed away at midnight. His body was cremated.
There are five items that do not decay: the crown, the ears, the tongue, and the youthfulness; as well as the rosary he constantly held.
From his cranial bone emerged śarīra relics, crimson-white and crystalline pure, shaped like large beans.
Chan Master Fayun Fashu of Dongjing (who was a successor of Chan Master Tianyi Huai) saw that Li Bo-shi was skilled at painting horses and rebuked him, saying:
"You are a scholar-official who has gained fame through painting; moreover, you paint horses, seeking to be praised for your exquisite skill.
Yet such exquisite skill leads one into the belly of a horse—this is truly enough to cause alarm. Thereupon, Bo-shi ceased his brushwork. Thus did the Master exhort him.
Huang Lu-zhi was skilled at composing erotic poetry. The Master also rebuked and scolded him for this. Huang laughed and said, "Will you then place me in the belly of a horse?
The Master replied, "Because you stir up the lustful hearts of people throughout the world with your licentious words, it will not stop at the belly of a horse;
I fear you will instead be born in the hells. Huang was struck with awe and repented, apologizing profusely. He then gained faith and sought the Way.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "For those who study the Way, it is difficult to attain clarity of mind and realization of one's nature. Yet they must still practice buddha-recitation and prostrate to the Buddha;
why is this the livelihood of one who has accomplished their task? It is because for one who has mastered the practice, the recitation of mantras causes karmic obstructions to be further purified."

Obstructions become increasingly empty; emotional consciousness becomes increasingly parched; the mind-ground becomes increasingly tranquil. Amitābha of one's own nature becomes increasingly luminous;

its functioning becomes increasingly vast; the turning of the wheel becomes increasingly alive; preaching the Dharma becomes increasingly unimpeded; the Pure Land of Mind-only becomes increasingly manifest, increasingly expansive, and increasingly consummate in its enjoyment.
This is indeed reaching the ultimate field of the Buddha-fruit. It is simply because it is perfect that one attains this self-...
The nature is Amitābha; the Pure Land is one's own mind. There is nothing else added to this.
The Chan Master Datong Shanben of Fayan Monastery in Dongjing (who succeeded Chan Master Huilin Yuanzhao), was of the Dong clan, descendants of Dong Zhongshu of the Han dynasty.
His grandfather Qi and his father Wen both served as officials in Yingzhou. Subsequently...

He was a native of Ying. His mother prayed to the Great Being clad in white (Pītavāsas), and thus she obtained him as her son. Upon reaching adulthood, he read extensively across all branches of literature;

he maintained a pure and austere life, having no intention of pursuing official service. Together with his younger brother Shansi, he went to Dizang Monastery in the capital, where he selected scriptures for ordination and studied the Vinaya.

He traveled east to Gusu, where he paid homage to Yuanzhao at Rui Guang Monastery. Yuanzhao took a special interest in him, and thereupon they reached a profound accord regarding the essential meaning of the teachings.
After five years, he ascended further into the subtle and profound mysteries. He was instructed by Master Yuan-tong Xiushu, who again exhausted the essentials for him.

During the Yuanfeng era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Fayun Monastery and was granted the title Dadao (Great Penetration). A monk asked, "The precious stupa is originally without seams; how can one point this out to people?
The Master said, "Mist and clouds arise upon its front and back; stars and moon circle its eaves and rafters. The monk asked, "What is it like within the stupa?"

The monk asked, "As for the time before black and white were yet distinguished—how was it then? The Master said, "I will grant you one move.
A monk asked, "How does one advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole? The Master said, "Dangerous. The monk said, "And how does one go forth from there? The Master added, "Furthermore—"
"How is it? The Master said, "A hundred fragments. Ascending the hall, he said: "Above, no heaven; below, no earth.

It fills the void, leaving no place to evade. To explain it clearly for you would be ineffective; instead, look toward the South Mountain at the turtle-nosed snake. He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
Later, he returned to Xiangwu in Hangzhou to cultivate the Pure Land practice. While in meditative concentration, he beheld Amitābha Buddha.
He manifested a body of golden hue. One day, he told his disciples, "Only three days remain. When the time arrived, he sat cross-legged reciting the Buddha's name and passed away while facing west.
Chan Master Huishen of Cishou at Hui-lin Temple in Tokyo (who succeeded Chan Master Xun of Changlu). His secular surname was Xu, and his given name was Shou-xun.
At birth, auspicious light appeared within his mother’s chamber. When Chan Master Wen-shu Jian heard of the Master’s birth, he went to visit him; upon seeing Jian, the Master smiled.
His mother permitted him to leave the household life, and at the age of fourteen, he severed worldly attachments and shaved his head. Thereafter—
For four years he traveled seeking the Way among those outside the conventional world. He relied upon Jingzhao at Zisheng Temple in Jiahe.

Jingzhao cited the kōan concerning Liangsui’s meeting with Magu and asked, "What is the place where Liangsui has realization? When the Master had thoroughly clarified this, Jingzhao sent him forth to reside at Zifuku.
The doors were filled outside. Chan Master Fojian Qin of Mount Jiangshan was traveling for alms when he arrived at Chatei.
The Master led him on a tour of the quarters, arriving at the "Thousand-Man Ward. Fojian asked, "Since this is the Thousand-Man Ward, why is there only one person?
The Master replied, "Excessive emptiness is not as good as meager reality. Fojian said, "Is that so? The Master felt abashed and requested further instruction. Fojian said, "Zi..."
Fuzhi thought this was a matter that could be settled there and then, but the Master said, "I am truly not yet at ease; I hope you will not exclude me from your discernment.

He then raised the story of the "Soul Departing from the Bride" (*Qian-nü li-hun*) and examined it thoroughly from every angle. Fuzhi’s doubts and obstructions were greatly cleared away, and he presented a verse, saying:
"It is only the place where I have walked for all these years; Yet when casually brought up, it becomes a riddle. Last night a sudden gale arose, Blowing down the peach blossoms."
"How many flowers do you know? Jue struck the table and said, "Is this not the living intent of the Patriarchs? Shortly thereafter, he resided at Mount Jiao.
The Master maintained that there is no shortcut to spiritual cultivation that surpasses the Pure Land, and he established a Western Paradise practice hall, exhorting the assembly with earnest words.
He once composed a hymn on *nianfo*.

The Minister of Rites, Yang Jie, known as the Layman Wúwéi (who was a successor of Chan Master Tiānyī Huái), whose courtesy name was Cìgōng, traveled extensively to study under various renowned masters. In his later years, he followed Tiānyī, who frequently cited the Elder Páng.

This was a "turning word" (jigū) intended to lead him toward profound investigation. Later, while serving as a shrine priest at Mount Tai, one day at the first crowing of the cock, he beheld the sun rising like a great platter;
he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse for the Elder Pang, saying: "When a man grows up, he must marry; when a woman grows up, she must wed.
What leisure do I have to further discuss talk of the unborn? He wrote this and sent it with his robe. The Elder praised it highly. Subsequently, he met the Chan master Furong Kai.
The Master asked, "How many years has it been since you parted from me? Rong replied, "Seven years. The Master asked, "Have you been studying the Way?

Have you been practicing Zen? Rong replied, "I do not strike these drums and pipes. The Master said, "In that case, you have traveled through mountains and waters in vain, accomplishing nothing at all.
Rong replied, "It has not been long since we parted; you are well able to discern this clearly. The Master laughed heartily. He once said: "Generally speaking..."
Those who study the Way must constantly maintain vigilance throughout the twelve periods of the day.
Have you not heard Nanquan say: "For thirty years, I have been tending a water buffalo. If it should trample the crops, I would pull its nose and drag it back.
Now it has become a white ox in the open field, stark naked; even if I let it go, it will not leave. Everyone must always exert their utmost alertness; you must not—
When speaking of the Way of Chan, there is the principle of "maintaining awareness" (*zhàodài*). Even when washing vegetables or performing manual labor, one must not be devoid of knowledge.
It is like a hen brooding her eggs; if she leaves them unattended, the warmth will not be sustained, and they will fail to become seeds.
Now, as the myriad phenomena array themselves before us and the six sense-faculties are in constant agitation, even a momentary lapse in care leads to ruin.
To lose one's life is no small matter. You, sir, have widely expounded the teachings and contemplations of the Western Land to guide those of the future;
you have left behind many dharma discourses for posterity.

In his later years, the Duke painted an image of Maitreya Buddha sixteen feet tall. He practiced mindfulness and visualization while traveling with it. On the day of his passing, he was moved by the vision of the Buddha coming to welcome him;
he passed away sitting upright. His verse of departure from this world says: "In life there is nothing to be attached to; in death there is nothing to be abandoned."
In the vast void of space—*zhi-hu-ye-zhe*. Someone asked, "Where are you going, Master? The Master replied, "I am going to be born in the Western Land.

The person challenged him, saying, "If you are to be born in the West, then you are mistaken. The Master said, "Let the mistake be the mistake; the Western Land is the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*)."
The Great Master Yunqi’s eulogy states: "Reading the verses of the Master Wuweizi, one sees that he advocates investigating Chan to realize one's nature while taking Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.
As for the phrase 'to take what is mistaken and make it right,' it contains profound and subtle implications."
Alas! How could it be that all the talented scholars of the human world have fallen into this single error?

The Layman Wen Zheng Gong, Fan Zhongyan (who succeeded to the Dharma from Zongdao), whose courtesy name was Xiwen, was reading among the Longbai Mountains when he discovered a cache of buried gold in a temple one day; he covered it back up.

He did not accept it. Later, while serving as a State Councillor for Confidential Affairs (Shumitsu) and Participant in Government (San-chi-cheng-shih), he instructed a monk to provide gold for the restoration of a temple.
