While staying overnight at an inn, the official discovered an ancient scroll consisting of one fascicle titled *The Verses on the Causes and Effects of the Sixteen Arhats* (*Jūroku Rakan In'ga Ju*).

As this was not recorded in the Tripitaka, he had it carved into printing blocks and wrote a preface, stating: "In these verses, each of the venerable ones has seven stanzas, all concerning their realization of the fundamental nature and attainment of Buddhahood."
He said, "I have read it; with each verse I attained awakening, only then realizing that there are boundless sacred teachings within the human world that had been left behind in the Great Canon.
While the Master was serving as governor of Wu, Chan Master Langye Jue visited him. After staying for several days, the Master presented him with a verse, saying:

"We have discussed the 'dissolving the doubt-mass' together for consecutive days; who would have thought that in this floating life there would be half a day of leisure? I truly wish to remain in leisure with you, Master, until we grow old."
"Completely gathering the nature of consciousness to enter the Mysterious Pass. At that time, there was one named Zongdao who, after meeting Xuedou, became transcendent and free as he pleased.
Later, he suddenly withdrew to reside in Shouchun, where he did not go out. He constantly recited the name of Amitābha and used a broom to personally cleanse his dwelling.
When the Master went to visit him, he asked, "Having lived in the mountains for many years, what is your essential purpose? Zong replied, "I dwell in the mountains."
Alone behind the closed wattle gate, there was no other pursuit. Three pieces of firewood were being toasted over a brazier. Without needing to wield a brush, the literary brilliance was revealed.
The Duke asked, "What is the great meaning of the Westward Journey? Zong said, "Clouds part and the mountain moon is revealed; rain falls and the bamboo wind is cool.
He asked again, "If one recites the Buddha's name all day long, what does one transcend? Zong raised his broom and made a dancing gesture. The Duke—
Suddenly he attained profound understanding of the teaching. He constantly cultivated the practice of purity to nurture the holy embryo.
On the day of his passing, he said to his family members, "Last night I dreamed that the lotus flowers in the pond all turned golden; I shall now follow my teacher to the West.
Thereupon, he passed away in serene stillness.
Chan Master Yongming Yizhao Yanshou of the Fayen School (he was a successor of National Teacher Tiantai Shaokang).

He was the son of the Wang family of Yuhang. His character and appearance were extraordinary, and he was fully endowed with both types of discipline (*dvividha-śīla*). He practiced Chan and Pure Land cultivation concurrently. He once compiled...

The profound essentials of the Buddhas and Patriarchs were compiled as the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles. Within it are four types of "discriminatory selection" (*liaojian*).
The first says: "If there is Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray. When the realm of the shadows manifests, they will instantly follow him away.

This means that if one clarifies only the principle of nature (*li-xing*) without aspiring for rebirth in the Pure Land, one will transmigrate within the Sahā world and suffer the consequence of falling back.

Regarding the "affliction of the aggregates" (*skandha*): within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the māras of the aggregates manifest. As clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, fifty kinds of demonic activities arise regarding the objects of the five aggregates.
Such a person initially fails to perceive that they are possessed by a demon;
furthermore, they claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Thus, deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell—this refers to such individuals.
The second is: "There is no need for dhyāna, yet there is the Pure Land; if ten thousand practice, ten thousand shall go. Once one has seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?

This means that although one has not yet clarified the principle of nature, by merely wishing for rebirth and relying on the power of the Buddha, one will swiftly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.

The third point: To possess both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the Pure Land is like being a horned tiger; one becomes a teacher of humanity in the present life and a Buddha or Patriarch in a future life.
Having attained profound mastery of the Buddha-dharma, one is fit to be a teacher for humans and devas;
furthermore, by vowing to be reborn there, one swiftly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression—like one who, girded with a hundred thousand strings of cash, rides a crane to Yangzhou.
The fourth says: "If there is neither meditation nor the Pure Land, there are only iron beds and copper pillars; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one will have no one to rely upon.
Having failed to clarify the Buddha-nature and having no aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land, one will sink into samsara forever—by what means can such a person escape?"
Those who wish to transcend birth and death and swiftly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression should select and practice the good deeds among these four types.

Throughout his life, the Master boarded the great ship of his vows to extensively deliver all classes of beings; the world universally revered him as the crimson banner of the Chan school and the white-browed elder of the Pure Land tradition.
He once recited the *Lotus Sūtra* thirteen thousand times and composed ninety works, including poems, gāthās, and prose rhapsodies.
He produced seven fascicles [of writings]. He ordained one thousand seven hundred disciples and conferred the precepts upon approximately ten thousand others.

He printed and distributed forty thousand copies of the *Amitābha-tantra* and encouraged people to pay homage and recite the Buddha’s name. The lives he spared were beyond counting. His reputation spread to foreign lands;
the King of Koguryo dispatched a monk with a letter to express his devotion as a gate-disciple, to inquire after the Master’s well-being, and to receive his seal of transmission.

There were thirty-six such individuals who, at the time of their death, knew in advance that the hour had arrived. Rising at dawn, they burned incense and addressed the assembly before passing away while sitting in the lotus posture.
After their cremation, the *śarīra* relics were arranged like fish scales, and a stupa was erected among the mountains of Jingci. Later, a monk came from Linchuan.
For years he circumambulated the stupa. When people asked him the reason, he said: "I was ill and entered the realm of the dead.

There I saw a statue of a monk enshrined in the left hall of the palace, to which the King paid diligent homage and respect. When I inquired closely about this person, they said: 'This is Chan Master Yongming Shou of Hangzhou.'"
"Generally, all who die pass through the Netherworld; however, this Master has already been reborn directly in the Western Land in the highest of the superior grades.
Because the King values his virtue, he pays him such reverence. He lived seventy-two years in the world and spent forty-two summers in seated meditation.
Regarding the Master, it is said that he formerly composed the "Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in Peaceful Nurturing" (*An-yang fu*), which states:
The precious realm of Amitābha bears the auspicious name of An-yang (Peaceful Nurturing). Abiding in this land of retribution, it is supremely blissful; among the ten directions, it is most pure.

Through the two sets of eight contemplations, one cultivates the concentrated mind to proceed in silent union with the Buddha. By means of the forty-eight great vows, even those with distracted minds are transported to be born there through transformation.
Thus, one shall uphold [the teaching] throughout one's entire life and take refuge for a whole lifetime.

As the immortal seers ride upon clouds to listen to the Dharma, and the deities of the void realm offer hymns of praise and chanting, one ascends the body upon a purple-golden terrace; thus, the original vow is not in vain.

Within the white jade *ūrṇā*-hair, divine transformations occur, and with a single mind, one rejoices. Consider the praise from the broad and long tongue: it is proclaimed simultaneously across ten lands; yet, by merely directing the mind—

All these are in accord with the truth; they are not mere fabrications based on personal whims. As the axis of the earth turns and celestial flowers scatter before them, a single thought causes the flowers to bloom, and upon beholding the Buddha, all attain the wondrous fruit.
A thousandfold radiance shines forth, and through realizing the Dharma, they all rank among the former sages.

Examining the past and inferring the present, those who have attained rebirth are not few. When the time arrives, celestial music fills the sky, and when the moment comes, extraordinary fragrances pervade the chamber.
Within the realm of the single truth, manifestations appear; though these rely upon the Buddha’s majestic power, the visions beheld within the pools of the seven treasures all emerge from the mind.

Thus we know that the Sage’s intent is unfathomable and his responsive resonance is enduring. He transforms the mundane into the sacred in an instant, and clarifies delusion into awakening in a flash.
To unearth this secret scripture is truly the art of longevity; it points the way back to the Pure Land.

They dwell forever in the land of the deathless. Furthermore, there are transcendent worthies and great bodhisattvas amidst the dust of the world who practice through such acts as burning their bodies or arms;

they establish their conduct by hanging their stomachs or holding their hearts aloft. They do not follow when celestial music comes to welcome them, nor do they rejoice when heavenly youths offer them invitations.
Whether atop the mountain of blazing fire or within the realm of radiant light, they never again hear the name of the evil realms. Forever...
Casting off the baseness of the womb-prison, one’s eyes open and the tongue becomes firm as proof is established; the bull’s charge and the rooster’s peck suddenly cease.

Dwelling within the Iron City, one must resist the king’s decree and follow one’s sincere heart; sitting upon the Lotus Throne, one relies on the Buddha’s grace and finds it difficult to abandon the ultimate truth.
Should one ever slander the Triple Gem or violate the precepts, then at the moment the winds and knives dissolve the body, one shall face the retribution of karma.

When a mirror reflects one's form, if one suddenly encounters a spiritual friend who manifests inconceivable wonders—the forest of swords transforms into seven rows of jeweled trees, and the chariot of fire changes into a lotus pond of eight virtues—then the hells vanish; in profound stillness, the heart of fear completely subsides.
Celestial flowers flew down to lead him away; in an instant, the transformation-Buddha welcomed him. His wisdom-eye became clear and his mind enlightened; the incense burner fell from his hand.

In accordance with the prophecy, the lotus flower did not wither; having received the prediction, the Jewel Forest would not remain for long. How marvelous! The power of the Buddha is inconceivable, such as has never existed before in antiquity or today.
Question: A sutra states: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha likewise. When not a single thought arises, the celestial truth is suddenly clarified.

How can one chant the names of other Buddhas and extensively recite other sutras? With high and low [tones], with samsara, and with the arising and ceasing of before and after, these hinder meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) by merely following sounds.
When water is stirred, the pearl becomes dim; how could this ever lead to profound union?
Answer: Sound is the treasury of manifold meanings; every word is a gateway to liberation. All sounds that proceed from any source are the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
As a sutra says: "Within each and every phenomenon, all phenomena are contained. Thus, we know that within a single utterance, [all things are present].
Encompassing all without exception, the ten realms are fully present and the principle of the three truths is perfect. How could one fail to value this while disparaging that?

To abandon appearances in search of truth is to fail to exhaust the source of movement and stillness, thereby leading to errors regarding speech and silence. Thus, the Sūtra says: "When a single thought first arises, it has no initial mark;
this is true protective mindfulness. It does not necessarily mean that one must cease thought and eliminate sound to merge with the true mark. This is...
Within the gateway of adornment, the myriad practices remain unimpaired; within the ocean of True Suchness (*tathatā*), not even a single hair’s breadth is forsaken.

For instance, regarding the recitation of the Honored Name, the teachings provide clear evidence: by chanting a single invocation, sins as numerous as grains of sand are extinguished; by completing ten recitations, one’s form dwells in the Pure Land.

It rescues those in peril and uproots those in distress, banishing hindrances and dissolving grievances—not merely providing temporary extraction from the depths of suffering for a single lifetime, but [enabling one to] entrust oneself...
By means of these causes and conditions, one will ultimately cast oneself into the ocean of enlightenment. Thus, the Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra states: "Sentient beings are dull and ignorant;

they cannot understand through contemplation. However, if they merely cause the sound of recitation to continue uninterruptedly, they will naturally attain rebirth in the Buddha-land. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"For example, suppose there were a person who, as soon as they were born and fell to the ground, immediately traveled a thousand *li* per day for a full thousand years, and filled [the path] with the seven treasures."
To offer [this] to the Buddha is not as meritorious as for someone in the future evil age to utter the name of a single Buddha; the latter’s merit surpasses the former.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If there are sentient beings whose virtuous minds continue uninterrupted and who recite the name of the Buddha for the duration of a single cow's milk being milked, the merit obtained will surpass the inconceivable, such that no one can measure it. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

Abide in the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha through the mind of mastery. Know that according to whatever desires and inclinations exist within one’s own mind, all Buddhas manifest their forms accordingly.
Thus, the *Ratnarāśi-śāstra* says: "One who bathes in the great ocean has already utilized the waters of the hundred rivers; so it is for one who recites the name of the Buddha."
One will certainly achieve samādhi. It is just as when a clear pearl is cast into turbid water; the turbid water cannot help but become clear.
When mindfulness of the Buddha is applied to a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot help but become the Buddha. Once this accord is reached, both mind and Buddha vanish together.

This simultaneous vanishing is concentration (*samādhi*); their simultaneous illumination is wisdom (*prajñā*). When concentration and wisdom are balanced, what mind would not be the Buddha? What Buddha would not be...
It is not the mind. Since the Buddha is the mind, then the myriad objects and myriad conditions are none other than samādhi. Who, then, would suffer from this?

Why should one raise their voice to recite the Buddha’s name upon the arising of thoughts or mental stirrings? Therefore, the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states that there are ten kinds of merit in chanting the Buddha’s name and reciting the sūtras with a loud voice:
first, it can dispel sleep; second, the celestial māras are struck with terror; third, the voice...
1. Pervading the ten directions; 2. Ceasing suffering in the three miserable realms; 3. External sounds do not enter; 4. Causing the mind not to be distracted; 5. Courageous and diligent effort;
6. All Buddhas rejoice; 7. Samādhi manifests before one; 8. Rebirth in a pure land. The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) asks:
"If the nature of names is empty and cannot fully express all phenomena, why does the teaching instruct people to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name?"

[Question: Does a different explanation satisfy hunger? [Answer: If one were to say that names are useless and cannot express the essence of all phenomena (*dharmas*), then one might as well summon fire and water by name.
Thus we know that the trap and snare are not in vain; once the fish and the rabbit are caught, they serve their purpose.

Therefore, the Brahma King requested the turning of the Wheel of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakra*), and the Great Sage responded to the capacity of beings to widely proclaim the sublime intent. Humans, devas, ordinary beings, and sages alike have all received this True Teaching.
It is said: "The five paths and four modes of birth all follow these bequeathed instructions; hearing, reciting, and chanting them brings profound and vast benefit.
By invoking the Buddha’s name, one is reborn in the Pure Land. Furthermore, one must not claim that names are merely false and devoid of explanatory power."
Question: Regarding the merit of mindfulness through walking (*cankrama*) versus mindfulness while seated (*āsana*), how do they compare?

Furthermore, is there merit in prostrations as well? Answer: It is like sailing against the current; one might still say that progress is being made, yet if one sails with the wind and the current, the speed is easily understood.
A single utterance of mindfulness while seated can already eliminate the sins of eighty billion kalpas; as for the merit of mindfulness while walking, how could it be fully known?

Regarding the measure [of prostration]: if one performs a prostration, one humbles and subdues ignorance and deeply enters the ground of awakening. This is the ultimate form of reverence, like a tree falling or a mountain collapsing.
The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "In a single prostration to the Buddha, from the knees down to the vajra-realm (the earth)," [one purifies all karmic obstructions].

For every single mote of dust, one attains the rank of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and acquires ten kinds of merit: first, obtaining a sublime physical form; second, having one’s words believed by others; third, being fearless when among the multitude;
fourth, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; fifth, possessing great dignified deportment; sixth, being closely approached and attached to by the masses;
seventh, being loved and revered by the devas; eighth, possessing great karmic rewards; ninth, being reborn in a favorable realm at the end of life; tenth, [swiftly...]

One realizes nirvana and penetrates the emptiness and unobstructed nature of one’s own mind. According to the direct perception of the mind, to pay homage to a single Buddha is to pay homage to all Buddhas;

to pay homage to all Buddhas is to pay homage to a single Buddha. Because the essence and function of the Buddha-Dharma body are interpenetrating, a single prostration pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
All various offerings, such as incense and flowers, are to be understood by this same principle.

Regarding the six realms and four modes of birth, one should regard them all as the Buddha. Mañjuśrī said: "Because the mind is neither born nor extinguished, I pay homage to that which is without an object of observation.

Internally practicing equanimity and externally conforming to the cultivation of reverence, when the internal and external merge in darkness, it is called "equanimous homage. I have briefly cited the teachings of the Patriarchs;
the principle and its phenomena are clearly distinct. One must not suppress the intent of the Buddhas to disparage the golden scriptures, nor rely on biased views to harm the Perfect Teaching.
The Master said:

Question: "If the Pure Land of Mind alone pervades the ten directions, how can one entrust one's substance to a lotus pedestal and lodge one's form in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, thereby giving rise to thoughts of acceptance and rejection?
How could this be reaching the gate of non-arising? If feelings of longing and aversion arise, how can equanimity be achieved?"
[Question: "The Buddha-land is mind-only. [Answer: It arises only upon the realization of the mind. As the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time are non-existent; they exist solely in dependence upon their own minds. If a Bodhisattva can thus understand all...

The Buddha and all phenomena are solely the measure of mind (*cittamātra*). By attaining the Patience that Accords with Truth (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), or by casting off the body upon entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one is swiftly reborn in the pure Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī.
Thus, one knows that it is only through the awakening of the mind that the Pure Land of Mind-only arises;

to be attached to objects is merely to fall into the realm of perceived objects. Since cause and effect are clearly seen to be without discrepancy, one realizes that there are no phenomena outside the mind. Furthermore, [this is] equality.
Regarding the gate of non-arising: although one may look up to the teachings and give rise to faith, one must acknowledge that one’s capacity is as yet insufficient.

With shallow observation and a floating mind, and with external conditions being powerful while habitual tendencies are heavy, it is necessary to be born in a Buddha-land to rely upon superior conditions; there, the power of patience will easily be perfected, and one will swiftly practice the Bodhisattva path.
The *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "When sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek correct faith, their minds are timid."
If there are those who are weak— dwelling in this Sahā world, fearing that they may not constantly encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings,
and apprehending that their faith may be difficult to perfect, and thus intending to retreat— one should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain their faith.
That is to say, by means of the causal conditions of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one shall, according to one's vow, attain birth in the lands of other Buddhas.
One will constantly behold the Buddha and forever leave the evil realms behind. As stated in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward the vow to be born in that land, they shall immediately attain rebirth there; because they constantly behold the Buddha."

There shall never be any regression. If one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā*-dharma-body and constantly and diligently practices, one will ultimately attain birth there, because one abides in right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states: "Those who sport at the gates of hell are born in that land;

having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the realm of birth and death to teach and transform those in hell, rescuing sentient beings from suffering. By these causes and conditions..."
Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
Question: If one has practiced evil throughout a lifetime, such that the accumulated causes are profound, how can ten recitations at the moment of death suddenly dispel them?
Answer: Although this state of mind lasts for only a brief moment, its mental power is fierce and sharp; like fire or poison, though small in quantity, it is capable of great effect.
This is a momentous occasion. At the time of approaching death, the mind is resolute and courageous; therefore, it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice.

This final mind is called the "Great Mind" (*mahācitta*), and because the affairs of the faculties are urgent, it is like a person entering battle who does not spare their own body or life—this is what is meant by being "courageous.
Thus we know that good and evil have no fixed nature; their essence is empty, yet their traces involve ascent and descent, and their manifestations are distinguished as superior or inferior. Truly.
A single *liang* of gold surpasses a hundred *liang* of layered flowers; a tiny spark from a torch can burn away ten-thousand-fathom stacks of grass.

The Master further remarked: "I deeply lament that in this degenerate age, people deceive themselves by speaking of 'Chan' while merely learning empty verbiage, possessing no real understanding at all.

Step by step they follow the path of existence, yet mouth after mouth they discourse on emptiness. They do not reproach themselves for being dragged by the power of their karma, and furthermore, they teach others to deny the existence of causes."
Consequently, it is said that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi; committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder Prajñā.
Yet, in life one encounters the laws of kings, and at death one falls into Avīci Hell.

Having received the retribution of hell, once the karma is exhausted, one enters again among animals and hungry ghosts for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, with no time of liberation in sight—unless, in a single thought-moment, one turns the light back within, immediately transforming the heterodox into the orthodox. If...
If you do not repent and reform yourself, if you do not save and cultivate yourself, then even if all the Buddhas were to appear, there would be no place for them to rescue you.
(It must be like the moment of impending death; only when the mind is resolute and courageous can it be so.)
Question: If merely seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way allows one to transcend birth and death, what need is there to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in another land?

Answer: A true practitioner should examine themselves with care; as the saying goes, "When a person drinks water, they know its coldness or warmth for themselves. Now, consider the metaphor of the tortoise...
A mirror, used to shatter many delusions. O virtuous ones, you should examine your own conduct and understanding: have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way?
Have you received the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the position of the Patriarchs? Can you be like Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna?

Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*? Can you be like Tiantai Zhizhe? Are you proficient in both the doctrine and its exposition, and do you cultivate both practice and understanding? Can you be like...?
Zhongguoshi, is it not so? These great beings have all clearly bestowed their teachings and deeply exhorted others toward rebirth in the Pure Land.

This is surely for the sake of benefiting both themselves and others; how could they ever intentionally mislead others or deceive themselves? Furthermore, the Great Hero [the Buddha] has praised this with earnest words from his golden mouth.

We should follow the examples of the sages of old and reverently obey the Buddha’s command; our realization will certainly not be erroneous. Moreover, as recorded in the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth), these are the eminent figures of past and present.
The deeds of these gentlemen are numerous and manifest; you should diligently examine them to reflect upon yourself and gain self-knowledge.

Furthermore, you must evaluate for yourself whether, at the moment of death, you will certainly attain mastery over the departure from or remaining within this life. Since beginningless time, your heavy obstacles of evil karma have been accumulated.
The meditative state will certainly manifest before you. Will this single *saṃbhogakāya* certainly liberate you from saṃsāra?

Moving among the various species within the three miserable realms and the evil paths, will you certainly be free from suffering and affliction as you appear and disappear at will? In the heavens, among humans, and throughout the worlds of the ten directions, will you certainly encounter no obstruction as you take up residence wherever you please?
If you can understand this clearly and attain such self-confidence, what could be more excellent than this? If...
If you fail to do so now, do not let your temporary arrogance lead you to sink into eternal samsara; do not lose the benefit of the good for yourself—then whom will you blame?
Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now?

Question: Outside the mind there is no Buddha; seeing the Buddha is seeing the mind. Why, then, do the teachings speak of transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) coming to welcome one and lead one to birth in the various Pure Lands?

Answer: The true Buddha of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. From that truth, transformation bodies arise to guide and receive those with deluded faculties. Since the transformation body is...

Reality is suchness; suchness should be a single realm, which is neither coming nor going. Yet, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, the body of transformation is itself reality, and thus it is said to have no coming or going.
Flowing forth from reality as transformation, it appears to have movement and return. This is "coming while not coming," and "seeing while not seeing.
Coming without coming is like the moon’s reflection suddenly appearing in water; seeing without seeing is like passing clouds.
Suddenly, [a vision] appeared.
He asked: "As stated above, the true essence is tranquil and unmoving, while its manifestations appear as if coming from nowhere.
This is precisely the external mind perceiving another Buddha coming to welcome one. How, then, can one realize that one's own mind is the Buddha?"

Answer: This is due to the power of the merit of his original vow, which causes those sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection to focus their thoughts and mindfulness so that they are able to see the Buddha coming to welcome them within their own minds.
It is not that the Buddhas actually dispatch transformation bodies to come and receive them.
However, when the conditions are met and the timing is right, one’s own mind can perceive the Buddha coming to welcome them.

In reality, the Buddha’s body is profoundly still and eternally quiescent, neither going nor coming. It is through the power of the Buddha’s original vow that the consciousness of sentient beings undergoes a transformation in a single thought-moment.
There is going and coming, like reflections on the surface of a mirror; it is like the activities in a dream. The forms within a mirror are neither internal nor external;
the events within a dream are neither existent nor non-existent. These arise solely from the mind and have nothing to do with the transformations of the Buddha.
Question: Since there are no phenomena external to the mind and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, how can there be such things as seeing the Buddha or being welcomed by him?
Answer: It is through mindfulness of the Buddha based solely on the mind (*cittamātra-buddhānusmṛti*). By means of the contemplation of mind-only, one encompasses all phenomena.

Having realized that objects are nothing but mind and that the understanding of the mind is itself the Buddha, whatever one brings to mind is none other than the Buddha. As the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who sees [the Buddha] in a dream..."
The seven treasures and his kinsmen were filled with joy; yet upon waking, he could not recall where they were. In this way, one should recollect the Buddha.
This metaphor illustrates that which is produced by mind alone: it exists yet is empty, and thus has no coming or going. Furthermore, like an illusion that is not real, both mind and Buddha vanish;
yet because the illusory appearance is not non-existent, neither mind nor Buddha is destroyed. Where emptiness and existence are unimpeded, there is no departure.

Come! It is not an obstacle to universal seeing; yet seeing is itself non-seeing, for one is always in accord with the Middle Way. Therefore, the Buddha truly does not come, and the mind likewise does not go.
When the path of resonance and response intersects, it is the mind alone that sees itself. The Buddha-land of Vairocana is not restricted to east or west.

If right understanding is clear and lucid, habitual defilements are simultaneously extinguished. With both principle and knowledge fully prepared, one personally realizes the Unborn. Having thus traversed the stages of the sages, one attains liberation.

Abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, one does not yet feel weary of the suffering of birth and death, and thus transforms sentient beings within the six realms. This is like having just begun to possess faith while the power of patience (*kṣānti*) is not yet perfected;

though one desires to rescue those submerged in the depths of saṃsāra, it is truly difficult to save them all at once. It is like having no boat to save the drowning, or having weak wings when attempting to fly high.
It is like lying bedridden with a chronic illness while wishing to leave one’s skilled physician, or being in one’s swaddling clothes while intending to abandon one’s compassionate mother.
Having long suffered such a fall, death is certain beyond doubt. Yet, while there is the peril of sinking oneself, there is as yet no capacity for benefiting others.

Furthermore, according to various sutras, those born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) do so through powerful conditions and superior ground; they are born by transformation from lotus flowers, instantly entering the family of the Tathāgata. All...

They receive the prediction of enlightenment. Their ears are constantly touched by the hearing of the Mahāyāna Dharma. Shoulder to shoulder, they are all neighbors to those in the stage of "one more birth" (ekajātipratibaddha).

Moment after moment, they dwell in the profound and empty; thought after thought, they remain in meditative concentration. The flames of affliction are extinguished, and the springs of craving are dried up.

Since even the name of the evil realms does not exist, how could there be any matter of saṃsāra? Thus, the benefits of the Dharma have been briefly described above as being boundless; such is the sacred realm.

It is not false; it speaks directly and is without error. Yet why is it that you drown without concern at the bottom of the waves of the river of craving, and burn without fear amidst the flames of the house on fire?
You weave a dense net of delusion, such that the blade of shallow wisdom cannot cut through it;

you plant deep roots of doubt, such that the power of superficial faith cannot uproot them. Consequently, you submit your will with a willing heart, taking misfortune as your fortune and calamity as your joy, while turning away from purity.

In this world, they look back with longing upon an age of fear and dread; like moths scorched and cocoons consumed by fire, they remain amidst their own lingering calamities. Like caged birds or fish in a cauldron, they paradoxically claim to be happy.
Thus one knows that the power of the Buddha does not equal the power of karma; it is difficult to approach the True Cause through false causes.

Furthermore, as long as one has not escaped the karmic body, one will ultimately remain entangled in the three obstructions. Since they do not desire a transformed body upon a lotus pedestal, they must instead receive form within a womb.
If one receives a physical body, the whole body is suffering. Having sunk into the three realms, how can one avoid the cycle of rebirth?

Now, among the eight sufferings, I shall briefly indicate two: birth and death. First, regarding the suffering of birth: taking up semen and blood as its substance, it dwells within the receptacle for undigested and digested food;
through forty-two transformations, it becomes this illusory form. Above, it is pressed by foul food; below, it is perfumed by a stinking pit. When drinking cold [liquids]...
If it were an ice river, swallowing one as if in a furnace of glowing coals; one would writhe in confusion and distress beyond description. Upon birth, the myriad sufferings are immeasurable:
touching the hand or falling to the ground is like having the skin of a living ox flayed; the confinement and difficulty are like being born from a tortoise shell.

Clutching grievances and harboring resentment, the infant seeks to harm its mother’s body; yet, upon merely touching the warm breeze, the conditions of suffering are suddenly forgotten. Thus is the state of an infant.

Foolish and deluded, they perish violently by water or fire. Even if they manage to attain human form, they cultivate the seeds of the body. Once the field of karma has ripened, it is frequently moistened by the waters of craving;

ignorance arises, and the sprouts of suffering grow. Adhering like glue to the seven consciousnesses and enshrouding the nine abodes, they revolve like a whirling firebrand, never ceasing their cycle.
Regarding the suffering of the two deaths: the winds of the "knife" dismember the body, and the element of fire burns the physical frame. The sounds are hollow...

Internally trembling, the *po* spirit quivers and the *hun* soul is startled; extreme suffering arises all at once as evil karma suddenly manifests. A thousand sorrows press down with melancholy, and ten thousand fears cause frantic alarm.
Finally, when life ends and the breath ceases, one departs alone in silence. The netherworld is dark and gloomy; the path to the underworld is vast and boundless.

Facing their former enemies with stark clarity, they cry out to heaven and strike the earth, yet find no way to escape. According to the depth and shallowness of their karma, they pass through the various realms of existence;
some are born upside down in the hells, while others secretly assume the forms of ghosts.

For long kalpas they endure hunger and thirst while wailing, and suffer the pains of punishment until their entire bodies are scorched and rotted. Having not yet escaped the twenty-five states of existence, the karmic seeds of good and evil remain.
Nothing perishes; one receives retribution for the body one has received, never failing to do so. The ocean of birth and death is vast, and the paths of karma are difficult to exhaust.
Even Śrāvakas remain dim-sighted regarding the emergence from the womb, and Bodhisattvas are still obscured by the "separation from the corpse" (the transition after death).

How much more so for ordinary worldlings at the lowest level, bound by all fetters—how could they not be ensnared by the suffering of birth and tethered by the demon of death? This is solely because they do not believe in the Buddhist scriptures; [otherwise], they would become humans in future lives.

Their afflictions become even deeper and more severe, such that they are unable to be reborn in the lands of the thousand Buddhas. For this reason, I say that the land of Amitāyus Buddha is easy to reach and easy to attain;
it is the single gateway to the Pure Land through which one may enter the path. You should know that while it is difficult to perfect one's own practice, [this path is accessible].

Relying on the power of others (*tārala*) is easily accomplished; it is like a person of inferior station who, by attaching himself to the might of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), soars and wanders through the four continents.

Or like an ordinary person who, by borrowing the efficacy of immortal elixirs, ascends to the Three Isles. This is truly a path easy to practice, through which one may swiftly attain realization. Your compassionate instructions are earnest and repeated;
I must engrave them upon my very bones.

Question: Although the dharma-gate of the six recollections and the ten types of contemplative signs are called "aids to the path," they involve pursuing thoughts and conditions within sensory objects;
since these arise fleetingly and deviate from the truth, how do they compare to pure mindfulness?
Answer: The single dharma of non-thought (*amanasikāra*) is the source of all practices. When both the subtle and the coarse have vanished, only a Buddha can purify it. Thus, a sutra says:

"The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in the retribution of their fruits; only the One Buddha dwells in the Pure Land. How much more so for one dwelling in the realm of ordinary beings, especially at the initial stage of the path?
If there were no gateways of auxiliary practice (*sambhāramārga*), the True Path could not manifest on its own. Furthermore, the method of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) is able to...
It dispels illusory demons, increases merit, and supports the roots of goodness. Through the ten gates of contemplation, one skillfully detaches from greed and attachment;
turbid thoughts are silently purified, and one secretly accords with the true source. These are all essential forries on the Way and the sublime tracks for practicing dhyāna.

Like a staff that possesses the power to support those in peril, and like a boat that achieves the feat of reaching the shore, when strength is fully prepared and merit is consummated, both the boat and the staff [are cast aside].
Renunciation. Question: Layman Pang said, "To speak of the Buddha-land from this shore, it is a hundred thousand li away. The great ocean stretches boundlessly;
stir it and a black wind arises. Though millions have set out, not one or two in a million reach their destination. Suddenly he encountered his own...
Question: "The person who comes does not exist within causes and conditions. How can one understand this thoroughly and realize rebirth? Answer:
"If one extracts the fundamental principle and examines the root, one does not even say that there is a Buddha or a land; how then could one speak of reaching it or not reaching it?"

Therefore, the celestial nature is spontaneously possessed; it does not involve causes and conditions, nor does it stir so much as a hair’s breadth, yet it is eternally in harmony with the true essence.
If discussed in terms of phenomena, there are thus not uniform levels: those of the nine grades of rebirth reach both the upper and lower realms;

some travel to the Land of Transformation to behold the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while others are born in the Land of Reward to perceive the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*). Some may ascend to the higher stages in a single night, while others...

It may take an eon before one realizes the Lesser Vehicle; there are those of sharp or dull faculties, those with concentrated or distracted minds, and those who awaken slowly or quickly—thus their capacities and dispositions differ.
There are differences in the timing of when the flower blooms, and variations in the limits of time. These matters are fully recorded from ancient times to the present;

ordinary beings and sages are born together, and their modes of conduct are clearly manifest. This is evident proof and direct observation. Therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha personally prophesied that Mañjuśrī would be born [in this world].
In the land of Amitābha Buddha, one attains the first bhūmi. As the Great Sūtra states:
Maitreya Bodhisattva asked the Buddha, "I do not yet know how many non-retrogressive bodhisattvas in this world-system will attain birth in that land. The Buddha replied, "In this Sahā world..."
There are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who all attain rebirth there. At the jeweled trees of the Fragrant Terrace, it is easy to reach and no one is there to hinder you.
Even those who encounter the chariots of fire and manage to repent for a single thought can still attain rebirth;

how much more so for those who cultivate the power of the path through the熏 (perfuming) of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—their practice shall never be in vain. The Buddha’s Brahma-like voice never deceives anyone. Thus concludes the *Sutra of Praise for the Pure Land*.

It is said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extend their broad and long tongues, covering the entire trichiliocosm, to certify that rebirth [in the Pure Land] is attained;
how could this be a mere fabrication?"
Question: The *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies that the sixteen gates of contemplation all consist of concentrating the mind to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Only by contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs until they are clearly and perfectly realized can one ascend to the Pure Land. How, then, can one with a distracted mind be able to be transformed and go there?
Answer: The scriptural texts of the nine grades naturally possess degrees of elevation and descent; though they encompass both high and low levels, they do not transcend two types of mind.

First is the concentrated mind, such as when one cultivates meditative concentration and practices contemplation, leading to birth in the highest grade. Second is the single-minded mind, which consists merely of reciting the Name, with all manner of good deeds serving as supportive cultivation.
Regarding the dedication of merit and the making of vows, one must attain the final stage; furthermore, throughout one's entire life, one must take refuge and practice with diligent cultivation.

Whether sitting or lying down, one should always face westward. When performing circumambulation and prostrations, or when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, one should be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts, as if facing execution, imprisoned in a jail, pursued by enemies, or drowning in water.

Pressed by the fires [of suffering], one should single-mindedly seek salvation, vowing to escape the wheel of misery, swiftly realize non-arising, extensively deliver all sentient beings, perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude.
With such sincerity of will, this resolve shall certainly not be in vain.

However, if one’s words do not accord with one’s deeds, if the power of faith is feeble, and if there is no mind of continuous mindfulness but rather a disposition toward frequent interruption—relying on...
This indolence leads one, at the time of death, to hope for rebirth; yet, being obstructed by karmic hindrances, one fears it will be difficult to encounter virtuous friends.
As the winds and fires of dissolution press in, right mindfulness cannot be established. Why is this? What exists now is the cause, and what occurs at the moment of death is the fruit.
If the cause is genuine, the fruit will not be in vain. For when the sound is harmonious, the resonance follows suit; when the form is straight, the shadow is upright. Thus it must be.
If one achieves the ten recitations at the moment of death, it is simply because one has prepared the ferry and bridge in advance by gathering and dedicating merit;
if at that time every thought remains unimpaired, then there will be no cause for anxiety.

Now, the two wheels of good and evil and the two retributions of suffering and joy are all created by the three karmas, produced by the four conditions, accomplished by the six causes, and subsumed within the five fruits. If, even for a single thought-moment, the mind harbors anger or wrong views...
Lust is the karma of the hells. Stinginess and greed without giving are the karma of hungry ghosts. Ignorance and delusion are the karma of animals. Arrogance and pride are the karma of asuras.
Firmly upholding the five precepts is the karma of humans. Diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions is the karma of devas.
To realize the emptiness of persons is the work of the devas; to know that the nature of conditions is detached is the work of the śrāvakas;

to cultivate the six pāramitās in equal measure is the work of the bodhisattvas; and for true compassion to be impartial is the work of the Buddhas. If the mind is pure, one is born by transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees;
if the mind is defiled, one receives a physical form in a defiled land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines—all of these are equal.
The fruit of ethical discipline is able to evoke superior conditions; therefore, apart from the source of one’s own mind, there is no separate entity. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, like a sovereign jewel, various colors appear according to the mind; because the minds of sentient beings are pure, they perceive pure lands.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "If you wish to purify your realm, simply purify your mind. Thus, we know that all things return to the mind.
The mind is the master of all phenomena. If you wish to obtain pure fruits, simply practice pure causes.
Just as the nature of water is to flow downward and the nature of fire is to rise upward, such is the law of natural tendencies; why should there be any doubt?
The Elder Yunqi praised him, saying: "Yongming bore the mind-seal of the direct pointing from the West and devoted himself to the Pure Land.
His vast vows for self-benefit and the benefit of others have shone brightly throughout ten thousand ages.
Is he not Maitreya descending to be born among us? Is he not a rebirth of Shandao?"
The Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi of the Guiyang School (a successor of Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun and the lineage of Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai), of Hangzhou:
his native place was Yuxi in Jiahe; his secular surname was Zhu. From birth he possessed extraordinary aspirations; at the age of seven, he left home to become a monk and constantly practiced...
He followed the instructions of the Vinaya. Later, he went to pay his respects to Zen Master Xingkong of Mount Daci. Xingkong said, "Why do you not travel extensively to seek instruction?
The Master proceeded directly to Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai. Upon arriving at the Vajra Cave, he paid his respects.
There he encountered an old man leading an ox who invited him into the temple. The old man called out, "Guṇḍi! and a boy responded by coming out to welcome him. The old man released [the ox].
Niu led the Master up into the hall; the entire building was radiant with a golden light. The old man sat upon his couch and, pointing to an embroidered cushion, bade him sit.
The old man asked, "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, "From the South. The old man asked, "How is the Dharma maintained in the South?

The Master replied, "In this age of the final dharma, monks rarely observe the precepts and regulations. The old man asked, "How many followers do you have? The Master replied, "Sometimes three hundred, or..."
[The Master] said, "Five hundred. The Master then asked, "How do you maintain the Buddha-dharma here? The old man replied, "Dragons and snakes are mixed together;

ordinary people and sages dwell side by side. The Master asked, "How many followers do you have? The old man replied, "Three times three before, and three times three after. The old man then called to his attendant boy.
He served tea along with some *sukha* (butter) and curd. The Master ate it and felt his mind and spirit become clear and refreshed.

The old man picked up a glass cup and asked, "Is there anything like this in the South? The Master replied, "No. The old man said, "What do you usually use to drink your tea? The Master was speechless.
As the sun’s light grew late, the Master asked the old man, "I wish to stay for one night; would that be possible? The old man—
The monk said, "I have a mind of attachment; I cannot stay overnight. The Master said, "I have no mind of attachment. The elder asked, "Have you received the precepts?
The Master replied, "I received them long ago. The elder said, "If you have no mind of attachment, what need is there for you to receive the precepts?"
The Master took his leave. The old man ordered a youth to escort him. The Master asked the youth, "What is the meaning of 'three before and three after'?
The youth called out, "Virtuous One! The Master responded, "Yes. The youth said, "How many is that? The Master asked again, "Where is this place?
The youth replied, "This is the Prajñā Temple at Vajra Cave. At this, the Master was moved with sorrow and realized that the old man was none other than...
"It is Mañjuśrī. He cannot be seen again," he said. He then prostrated before the youth and requested, "I pray you grant me a single word as a parting gift.
The youth spoke a verse, saying: "When the face is free from anger, it is an offering vessel; When the mouth is free from anger, it emits wondrous fragrance;

When the heart is free from anger, it is a precious treasure; Stainless and undefiled, this is the true permanence. Having finished speaking, Junti and the temple both vanished. Only [the verse] remained visible.
Amidst clouds of five colors, Mañjuśrī was coming and going, riding upon a golden-haired lion. Suddenly, white clouds arose from the east and covered him, so that he could no longer be seen.
The Master consequently took up residence at Mount Wutai. Later, he visited Yangshan, where his mind and realization were suddenly in accord.
Yangshan appointed him as the steward of the kitchen. Once, when Mañjuśrī appeared above the rice-pot, the Master struck him with the stirring ladle and said, "Mañjuśrī!"
Wenzi was truly Wenzi; Wenhui was truly Wenhui. Wenzi then spoke a verse: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip;
The sweet melon is sweet from stem to end. Having practiced for three great kalpas, I am instead criticized by this old monk.

One day, a strange monk came seeking alms food. The Master set aside his own portion and gave it to him. Yangshan, having foreknowledge of this, asked: "Was that just now someone of the fruit-position?"
[The Master] arrived. "Did you provide food? The Master said, "I have already set it aside to offer in return. The Master said, "You have brought great benefit.
The Master studied the sutras and śāstras, and admiring the *Vow Verses of Mañjuśrī*, he said: "May at the time of my life's end, all obstacles be extinguished;
may I behold Amitābha and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. He resolved his heart upon the Pure Land and would always instruct others, saying: "Investigate! (參)

Chan is the awakening to and illumination of the mind-ground. Once my own mind-ground is illuminated, it is identical to illuminating the mind of the Buddha; this is precisely to first attain the mind of Amitābha.

Thereupon, one should cultivate the various gates of practice to seek birth in the Pure Land, perfecting its adornments and fully realizing its enjoyments—this is called attaining "subsequent wisdom" (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Only then does one become a venerable ancient Buddha. For true principle is realized through awakening, and...
Sudden perfection is like a newborn infant whose limbs are already complete in a single day;
gradual cultivation is like a person growing into adulthood, whose character and spirit are only firmly established after many years.

Therefore, those who are able to speak horizontally and vertically before their eyes, employing staffs, shouts, and perfect gestures with spontaneous eloquence, may encounter circumstances that are either adverse or favorable.
The realms. Without knowing or perceiving, the mind arises in response to objects; thus, habitual tendencies are difficult to forget, and one cannot avoid leakage.
As it is said, "Even after forty years of applying my mind, there are still places where I wander"—this is the truthful word of the ancients, spoken without deceiving themselves or others.
The height of realization lies precisely here. To wish to transcend the adverse conditions of birth and death, one must recognize [the nature of the mind].
The shortcut to Bodhi is to focus the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha; this is the essential ford for the journey ahead and the pivotal juncture at the end.
Therefore, I shall briefly clarify its meaning in two parts.
First is reciting the name and mindfulness. As stated in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*:

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "I recall that in past lives I was always born in pure lands and attained hundreds of thousands of billions of gates to the Buddha-recollection samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"One who wishes to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi* should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and not grasp at external appearances."

Fixing one's mindfulness on a single Buddha, reciting His name with single-minded devotion, and facing Him directly in the direction where He dwells, one is able to maintain a continuous succession of thoughts focused upon that one Buddha.
Within this very mindfulness, one is able to see all Buddhas of the past and present. Why is this?

Because the merit of mindfulness toward one Buddha is no different from the merit of mindfulness toward immeasurable Buddhas; they all constitute a single suchness and achieve the most perfect correctness.
Awakened. Thus, he fully knows that the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is without marks of distinction.
In every thought-moment, he contemplates the mark of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which curls to the right in graceful spirals like the autumn moon;

it is transparently luminous inside and out like a tube of white lapis lazuli, and also like a bright star in the darkness. Whether the contemplation is perfected or not, ninety billion nayutas [of obstructions] are extinguished.
The heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will constantly be brought under his guidance and protection;
how much more so for one who clearly understands every word and reflects back upon every thought? Second is the mindfulness of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Neither arising nor ceasing, neither departing nor arriving, neither name nor mark—this is called the Buddha. It is like observing the true mark of one's own body."
"Contemplating the Buddha is likewise so forth. One contemplates the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas; among all roots of goodness, this practice is most supreme.
The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body. When one recollects a single Buddha, one recollects all Buddhas;
there is not a single land that is not pure.

The Master said: "In the family of patch-robed monks, those who possess great spiritual capacity and have attained profound enlightenment yet further seek birth in the Pure Land do so to fulfill the myriad practices of Samantabhadra and to pray for the early realization of Buddhahood. As it is said in the teachings:

'First realize the Dharma-realm of Vairocana, and subsequently enter the gateway of Samantabhadra’s practices. This is like Sudhana visiting Mañjuśrī, where Mañjuśrī performs the lion’s gaze of the elephant king."

Under these words, Sudhana attained sudden and thorough penetration. Finally, he beheld Samantabhadra, who expounded for him the Ten Great Vows of the King, guiding him back to the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) to fulfill the ten thousand practices;
this is a supreme model. Therefore, even those who have attained awakening must still practice mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in An-yang (Pure Land).
Those born in An-yang attain the stage of non-retrogression and immediately realize the various great samādhis.
They manifest various supernatural powers and display immeasurable bodies. Carrying immeasurable incense and flowers,
they travel to immeasurable worlds to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, praise immeasurable Buddhas, prostrate before immeasurable Buddhas,
repent for all karmic obstructions, rejoice in all merits, request the turning of all wheels of Dharma, and exhort all...
The Buddhas dwell long in the world; they constantly follow all Buddhas to study the profound Dharma and always accord with all sentient beings so that all may obtain benefit.
All the merits they perform are universally dedicated. Thus, these gates of Samantabhadra’s practices are all brought to full completion.
They then establish the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdue the armies of Māra, become great Kings of Dharma, and deliver beings according to their various types.
He is born resembling the youth Sudhana, manifesting countless hundreds of koṭis of emanations;
his wisdom is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions, universally benefiting the entire realm of sentient beings. How does this compare?
As the Master was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he informed the assembly, sat cross-legged, and transformed. A white light illuminated the room, and the bamboo and trees took on the same color.
His stupa was erected in the western valley of Lingyin Mountain. Later, it was plundered by bandits, yet the Master’s physical body remained undecayed, with his nails and hair having grown long.
King Qian Wusu was struck by this and reinterred him with great honor.
This is a brief biography of the ancient venerable master, written by Bai Juyi, the Layman of Mount Xiangshan.
The Duke’s courtesy name was Lètiān. He had long attended upon Fǎguāng, having attained the Dharma and simultaneously received the Bodhisattva precepts.

While serving as the governor of Hángzhōu, he visited the Venerable Niǎocháo and asked, "The place where the Chan Master sits is very precarious. The Master replied, "What precariousness do I, this old monk, possess?"
The Minister of State was even more skeptical. He said, "I am a disciple who holds the position of a regional governor; what danger could there possibly be?
The Master replied, "When fuel and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not cease; is this not dangerous? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. The Minister remarked, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say that. The Master [replied], "It is easy for a child to speak such words; it is difficult for an old man to carry them out."
He said, "Though a three-year-old child may speak of it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. The official then paid his respects and departed.
Throughout his various postings, he frequently sought out the ancestral path (Buddhism). Whenever he composed writings, they invariably concerned edification, all of which praised the Buddha-vehicle.
He commissioned artisans to paint scenes of the Western Pure Land, prostrated himself before them, and made a vow, praising it with this verse: *Jile* (Sukhāvatī) — The Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In the pure land of the world, there are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings. May those like my own body—aging and ill—be reborn together with me in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha.
The Duke was at Donglin Temple, sitting by the water. He composed a poem that said: "Formerly, I was a guest within the Eastern Fence;
Now, I am a member of the Western Society. Holding a willow branch, I sit by the water, Reflecting idly on past events as if they were my former life."

The Layman Lord Gong, Wen Yanbo of Lu County, whose courtesy name was Kuānfū, held the metropolitan degree and served as Governor of Luoyang. He once attended a ritual fast and went to Long’an Temple to gaze upon and pay homage to the sacred images.
Suddenly, he saw that the statue had broken and fallen to the ground. He showed no sign of reverence, merely looking at it as he departed. A monk nearby asked, "Why do you not pay your respects?
The official replied, "Since the statue is already broken, with what shall I pay my respects? The monk said, "The former masters have said:

'It is like the earth of an official road; a person digs it up to fashion a statue. The wise know it is still road-earth, while ordinary people say the statue has come to life. Later, when the official..."

As he was about to depart, he returned and filled the road with images. These images are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; the road likewise has no newness or antiquity. Upon hearing this, the official attained a realization.

Thereupon, he sought the Way with great vigor, recollecting the Buddha with intense devotion and vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land. Burning incense at dawn and sitting in meditation at night, he would frequently make this vow:
"May I always be diligent and zealously cultivate all virtues. May I fulfill my aspiration for the essence of the school and extensively deliver all beings."

Whenever he encountered sentient beings, he would always encourage them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, vowing to gather ten thousand people to share the same conditions for rebirth in the Pure Land.
The Layman Ruru praised him with this verse: "I know your courage is as vast as heaven; You vow to form the karmic ties of ten thousand in the West.
Not seeking a livelihood for yourself alone, The whole community shall board the boat at the ferry-head together. When the Master was approaching his death...
He passed away while peacefully reciting the Buddha’s name.

The lay practitioner (upāsaka) Wang Gu, a Court Gentleman (Shilang), whose courtesy name was Minzhong, was a native of Dongdu. By nature he was benevolent and compassionate, and he propagated the Buddhist teachings extensively. For seven generations, his ancestors had observed the precepts.

He practiced the rite of killing to release living beings. As a venerable elder who frequented the monastic centers like a fish in the deep waters, he once visited various masters to discuss the Way, including Huanglong, Cuiyan, Haitang, and Yangqi, with whom he attained a profound realization of their fundamental tenets.

Furthermore, admiring the excellence of the Pure Land dharma-gate, he composed the *Zhizhi jingtu jueyi ji* (A Collection for Resolving Doubts Concerning the Direct Guidance to the Pure Land) in three fascicles.
He also compiled various sutras and treatises, providing a comprehensive exposition of the essential methods for rebirth in the Pure Land.

He was diligent in the practice of Buddha-recollection, never letting his rosary leave his hand. Once, a monk traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and saw that the Minister and Grand Officer Ge Fan were both there together.
The Minister remarked, "Sentient beings within Amitābha’s heart are constantly being gathered and transformed."
The Pure Land resides within the minds of sentient beings; in every thought-moment one is reborn there, taking form within a lotus womb without ever departing from this very place.

Though the spirit traverses many lands, it never leaves the body and mind. By contemplating the immeasurable light of the original nature—which is fundamentally free of thought—one gives birth to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) of the Mind-Only school, which is truly non-arising.
Since the time of the various worthies of Mount Lu, I have continued this path to assist [the tradition].
As for those from Yangzhou, only you, Master Gong, and Yang Cigong were renowned;
both were reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

You, Master Gong, styled Xuzhong, was a graduate of the National Academy (Guoxue) and a lay practitioner of Longshu. Having composed several hundred thousand words of commentaries and transmissions on the Six Classics, one day—

Duanzhi said, "These are all merely habitual karmic tendencies; they are not the ultimate Dharma. I shall seek my return to the Western Land. He studied under Huanglong and Jingshan, attaining a profound realization.
He had long cultivated the practices of the Pure Land. At the age of sixty, wearing simple robes and eating vegetarian food, he traveled a thousand li with blistered feet.

He used these teachings to instruct others. When living in seclusion, he maintained the precepts with great strictness; he remained in tranquil stillness whenever seated and wore his cap and sash even while lying down.
His countenance was radiant and luminous. He said that he would perform a thousand prostrations daily before retiring to sleep at midnight. He composed a text on the Pure Land to exhort the world.

Three days before his passing, he took leave of all his relatives and acquaintances, saying that they would not see one another again. When the appointed day arrived, after finishing his recitation of scriptures, he passed away as usual.
He constantly paid homage and recited [the Buddha’s name]. Suddenly, he called out in a stern voice, “Amitābha Buddha! and proclaimed, “The Buddha comes to welcome me.
He stood upright and passed away like a tree planted in the ground. A local person dreamed that two youths in green robes led the Master westward.
From then on, every household made offerings to him.
The layman said, "True nature is like a mirror; all that has life is like a reflection. These are reflections manifested within true nature.
Reflections come and go, yet the mirror remains ever as it is. Sentient beings undergo birth and death, yet true nature is *tathatā* (suchness).
Once birth and death are eliminated, true nature manifests—what is called 'the wild landscape, no longer interrupted by mountains,' where heaven..."
The light extends directly, connecting with the water.
The layman said: "Mencius said that for the benevolent person, it is simply a matter of being fully cultivated. Therefore, the gentleman does not depart from benevolence for even a single day;
he must abide in it even in moments of haste, and he must abide in it even in times of distress. To be able to do so is what is required."
Thus, there is nowhere one goes that one does not practice benevolence (*ren*). It is the same for those who cultivate the Pure Land (*śuddhāvāsabhūmi*):

in all activities—whether rising or sitting, eating or drinking, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still—one never forgets the Pure Land. Then, although this body may dwell within the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), the mind is already in the Pure Land.
Zhuan’An said: "The form of the setting sun resembles a suspended drum; sit cross-legged and upright, facing west."
"Even though the body has not yet reached the lotus pond, the mind is first sent back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is precisely what that means.
The lay practitioner Chenguàn, known as Lǎowēng Shìzhì, whose courtesy name was Yíngzhōng, was a native of Nánjiàn.
He achieved high honors in the civil service examinations in his youth and served his office with upright integrity; he was later posthumously titled Zhōngxù. He constantly...
He was demoted to serve as the governor of Taizhou. There, he sought out the essential tenets of Tiantai, with which he found great resonance.

Later, when he visited Master Lingyuan Qing, he clung to his own learning and experience in his quest for intellectual understanding. Qing said to him, "If you take your own interpretations as the core principle, when will you ever find harmony?

At this, the master attained awakening and sent a verse to his teacher, saying: "In the quietude of the study hall, myriad anxieties cease; The sun is warm and the breeze gentle, the flora and fauna are secluded. Who would recognize the two thousand [years]..."

Regarding matters at the end of the year: nowadays, it all rests upon the eyes. Master Gong composed the *Record of the Pure Land of Yanqing in Siming*, wherein he fully set forth the causes and effects of the Western Paradise and the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.
He often spoke to others of the Pure Land of Mind-Only, briefly stating:
"The skillful means of Śākyamuni are most profound; Amitābha’s preaching of the Dharma is uninterrupted. Yet the Elder Vimukta did not go to [the land of] Peace."
In the Land of Bliss, the Great Being Samantabhadra personally beheld Amitābha within the realm of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

While the essential point lies in "going without going," what hindrance is there in "returning after having gone" within the sphere of skillful means (*upāya*)? When the faculties are matured and the resonance is profound, it is necessary that the task be accomplished.
Prime Minister Qian Xiangzu was the Layman Zhizhan.
His courtesy name was Gongxiang, and he was a native of Qiantang. He sought the Way from Chan Master Quan of Baoning and further studied under Chan Master Yuan of Ciyuan at Huguo Temple.
The Master said: "If you wish to investigate this matter, you must reach the point where both mind and dharmas are forgotten. Regarding "dharmas":
"Grasping has not yet been forgotten; though one accords with principle, it is still not awakening. The Duke said, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of conceptual thought.

How can this be? The Master replied, "It is fundamentally without sores; do not wound it. The Duke attained a profound realization and returned from his post as Left Prime Minister to daily cultivate the practice of purity.
One day, manifesting a slight illness, he wrote a verse: "The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land."
The lapis lazuli ground is free from even the slightest speck of dust; my mind is pure and transcends that. Today, from afar, I know a single flower has blossomed.
Three days later, when a monk came to inquire after his health, the Master said, "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death.

I shall not be reborn in the heavens, nor as a human being; I seek only birth upon the Pure Land. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Later, someone dreamed...
A voice from the sky said: "Prime Minister Qian has already been reborn in the lotus palace of the Western Paradise as the Bodhisattva Ciji.
As for the layman Jiang Gongwang, a Gentleman of the Palace for Remonstrance, his courtesy name is Minbiao;

he is a native of Diaotai. His wisdom and insight are lofty and clear, and he maintains a pure cultivation through a vegetarian diet. While serving as a remonstrance official, he spoke with direct honesty."
He had no secrets; his writings became famous in his time. He was intensely devoted to the Chan school (Zongmen) and attained realization while studying under spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

In his later years, he dedicated himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. Furthermore, he carved a stone inscription titled "An Essay on the Expedient Means of Buddha-Recitation" to awaken the world.

He once wrote in his private academy: "For those of sharp faculties, every thought does not arise, and every mind has nothing to grasp. The six sense organs are profoundly still, and the various consciousnesses..."
All phenomena dissolve away; every dharma is entirely true, and every gate is free from dependence. In a mere flash, one achieves the contemplation of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).

For beginners and those of later learning, if they concentrate their minds with single-minded mindfulness, even while the Tathāgata has them attend to household affairs and perform various tasks, these will not hinder one another.
If one can fully withdraw the six sense faculties and maintain a succession of pure mindfulness, within no more than ten days, one will achieve success.

Samādhi. Therefore, those of superior faculties and great capacity transcend directly in a single thought-moment. As for those of ordinary disposition, they must skillfully observe the expedient means.
You had a son who died young; he appeared in a dream and said: "My lord practices the Way, and his meritorious achievements are already complete.

In the Netherworld, there is a golden plaque inscribed with the words: 'Jiang Gongwang of Yanzhou. Though you occupy a position of official censure, your will yearns for suffering and emptiness; you have personally attended to [the practice of]..."

He devoted himself to ascetic practice (*dhyāna* and *śīla*). His mind was free from attachment; whether in motion or stillness, he did not contravene the Buddha-dharma. Whether speaking or remaining silent, his timing always accorded with the spirit of the school.

Renowned for being liberated from the world of Jambudvīpa, his body returned to the Pure Land. Later, while serving as the Governor of Guangde Commandery, he suddenly became ill-free of ailment and, facing west, passed away while sitting upright.
Yihezi said: "To employ conditions as they arise while forgetting the contrivance is to attain the essence;

to blend and harmonize with the state of affairs while darkly coinciding with the wheel of the mechanism is the家风 (family style) of the Miao-yang lineage—like the moon falling into the pond leaving no shadow, or clouds arising on the mountain wearing its garment.
As for the school of Fayen, the tips of their arrows meet, their phrases and meanings coincide with the mechanism, layer upon layer like blossoms."
The treasury of teachings interpenetrates; each and every net of jewels is perfectly lustrous. Thus, from the wind-swept branches and moonlit shores, the true mind is revealed;

amidst the misty clouds and forest groves, the wondrous Dharma is proclaimed. Therefore, Chan Master Yongming Yanshou produced the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source Mirror), unifying Chan and Pure Land into a single school.
Furthermore, Chan Master Wuzhuo Xi, admiring the tradition of Mount Wutai, demonstrated that there is [no contradiction] in the practice of nianfo.
There are two points. Furthermore, if one considers the ancient masters such as Bai Xia Shan, Qian Zhian, and others, they were none of them unenlightened regarding this matter;
yet they remained so earnestly devoted to the Pure Land. From this we know that those who practice Chan do so within a maze of a thousand paths and ten thousand tracks.
Having found a direct path, it is very convenient for reaching home. Yet, once one has reached home, poverty remains poverty by its own nature, and wealth remains wealth by its own magnitude.
If there is no method of restraint and moderation, then the impurities of the habits of ignorance will not be refined away;
the roots and seeds of the emotional faculties will remain sticky and unclean, utterly lacking the fine lock and sturdy bolt that reach far into the depths.
Pán. This is why we hold this single phrase of Buddha-recitation so dear. With every sound, one awakens the master;
one desires nothing more than for emotional thoughts to wither away and for both mind and environment to become utterly still. Only then is one a "white ox in the open field.

As the ancient masters said, "One cultivates the Way only after seeing the Way"—this is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, since the practice of Buddha-recitation is a most profound Dharma-gate, when one recites until the mind...
When one portion of the defilements is removed, one portion of the light of wisdom manifests, and one thus perceives a single Buddha appearing in the world.
When immeasurable mental defilements are removed, immeasurable lights of wisdom manifest, illuminating and revealing immeasurable Buddhas;
