therein, mindfulness becomes inexhaustible and the realization of the Dharma likewise becomes inexhaustible—all because the Buddha is the dhāraṇī that sustains all phenomena.
Therefore, those with true resolve must by no means be reckless in treating Zhaozhou’s single turning word as a pass for exemption.
It is a pity that they mistakenly recognize Zhaozhou’s function, failing to perceive those who breathe from the same nostril as the ancients.
The Venerable Master Huiyuan of Donglin on Mount Lu, a patriarch of antiquity and present, and the Great Master Yuanwu (the founder of the Lotus School), was a native of Yanmen.
His secular surname was Jia. He had extensively mastered the Six Classics and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. Having heard of Dharma Master Dao’an...
While lecturing on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained a sudden and great awakening. He and his younger brother Huichi then cast aside their hairpins and shaved their heads.
Huiyuan constantly took it upon himself to propagate the Great Dharma. Daoan sighed and said, "He who shall cause the Way to flow throughout the Middle Kingdom must be Huiyuan.

When the Master arrived at Xunyang, he loved the seclusion and vastness of Mount Lu, feeling it was a place where one could quiet the mind. Raising his staff and striking the ground, he said, "If there is a spring here, I shall dwell. Suddenly—
A spring gushed forth, and the mountain deity appeared in a dream. One night, amidst thunder and rain, timber arrived of its own accord.
The Prefect, struck by this marvel, memorialized the throne to establish Donglin Monastery and named its main hall "Shenyun" (Divine Transport).

Hearing that a miraculous image of Mañjuśrī had been found by Tao Jiuzhou but had been submerged in the river for many years, the Master went to the riverbank and prayed with utmost devotion. The image indeed floated out; he welcomed it back and enshrined it in the hall.
Huiyuan considered that among all essential gateways for entering the Way, the practice of Buddha-recitation was supreme.

He established the White Lotus Society with one hundred and forty eminent monks and great scholars to cultivate the Pure Land practices. Six times each day, he performed prostrations and recitations to the Three Sages of the Western Paradise.

For thirty years, he did not enter secular society; he used the stream as a boundary when seeing off guests, and if anyone crossed it, tigers would howl. Consequently, it was named Tiger Creek (Huxi).

The Master was diligent in the practice of Pure Land. He entered meditative absorption at the Prajñā Terrace for eighteen days, during which he beheld the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others from the Lotus Pond Assembly.
There, flowing waters radiated light as they proclaimed the wondrous Dharma. A Buddha said to him, "Seven days hence, you shall be reborn in my land.
Upon emerging from meditation, he told his disciples, "Since I first resided here, I have three times beheld these sacred manifestations; now I have seen them once again."

It was certain that he would be reborn in the Pure Land. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and entered into stillness. The Provincial Governor and his disciples enshrined his entire body for burial on the Western Ridge.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Zhengjue (Right Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Ningji (Tranquil Stillness).

The Master composed the "Preface to the Poems on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation," which states: "What is the samādhi of Buddha-recitation? It is the term for focused thought and tranquil contemplation. When thought is focused, the will..."

First is non-deflection. When one contemplates stillness, the vital energy (*qi*) becomes empty and the spirit (*shen*) becomes lucid. When the vital energy is empty, wisdom shines with tranquil clarity;
when the spirit is lucid, there is no obscurity it does not penetrate. These two are the profound tally of nature, which, by uniting as one, brings forth their function.

Therefore, by being serene and reverent within the inner chamber, one moves in resonance with things and attains spiritual penetration; by governing the mind with rectitude, one acts and enters the subtle.

This is still merely using cultivation to concentrate the spirit and accumulating practice to transform one's nature; yet even this can achieve such results—how much more so for those who dwell like a corpse and sit in forgetfulness!
His profound contemplation reaches the ultimate; his wisdom encompasses the universe. Yet he walks the Great Way in the darkness. Let me speak of its beginning:
when the Bodhisattva first ascends to the stage of the Way, he has barely glimpsed the gate of the profound. His essence is quiescent and non-active, yet there is nothing he does not do.

When his spiritual transformations manifest, they cause long and short to alter their constant measures, and the large and the small to contradict one another. The three luminaries turn their radiance to shift [the world].

It illuminates heaven and earth, then rolls back and enters the breast. Furthermore, while the names of the various *samādhis* are exceedingly numerous, none is more sublime in merit or easier to advance toward than the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*).

Why is this? Because the honored title of the Tathāgata exhausts the profound mystery and reaches the ultimate stillness; his divine body unites with all transformations and responds without fixed form.

Therefore, those who enter this concentration become oblivious and forget their cognition; they take that which is the object of focus to perfect their discernment, and as this discernment becomes clear, [the truth is realized].
Thus, as internal illumination reflects one another, the myriad phenomena arise. Though they do not reach the range of the ears or eyes, hearing and seeing proceed.
Thereupon, beholding the body of the profound, still, and empty mirror, one awakens to the fact that the numinous marks are serene and unified, clear and bright by nature.
Examining the mysterious resonance that strikes the heart’s listening, defilements and burdens are constantly dispelled, and obstructed emotions melt into clarity. This is not... [Heaven].

How supreme and wondrous this is! Who could possibly equal it? Viewed from this perspective, the impact of a single encounter can trigger the deep-seated obscurations of long-standing habituation and suddenly dispel the profound delusions of the ignorant and mundane.

Even if one were to judge it by the objective conditions of an ordinary person’s collective consensus, its superiority would be self-evident. Therefore, the virtuous who revere sincerity all contemplate this singular [experience].
Reflecting upon the *Xiè* (the *Xièyuán jīng*), I am moved by the fleeting shadows of every passing moment and fearful that my future provisions have not yet been accumulated.

Thereupon, I purify my mind in the Dharma Hall and straighten my robes toward the pure direction. Forgetting sleep at the division of night, I am diligent from dawn until dusk, hoping that through the power of steadfast application I may fulfill the aspiration of the Three Vehicles.
May I ferry others across the ford and, like those of the Nine Schools, proceed together toward liberation; may I look upward to assist them and lead them to transcendence.

The rise of Mao drew in the weak and humble from below and provided his guidance from behind. By examining the brushstrokes of his various compositions, one sees that they are by no means merely literary verses.
The Master of Nanyue, Huisi, was a native of Wujin.
His surname was Li. He possessed a *uṣṇīṣa* upon his head. One night, he dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life;

he immediately took leave of his kin to enter the Way. Upon receiving full ordination, he practiced *zuo-chan* (seated meditation) and ate but one meal a day. He heard of the Chan master Huiwen of Northern Qi...
The Master’s Way and Dharma were widely practiced; [Nanyue] thus went to serve him. He was granted the secret instructions for the contemplation of the mind.
After twenty-one days, he leaned his body against a wall and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He recovered his past wisdom and attained the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra. He spoke in verse:

"Suddenly awakening to the source of the mind, the precious treasury is opened. Hidden or manifest, spiritual penetration reveals the true aspect. Walking alone or sitting alone, it is ever majestic. A hundred..."
Billions of manifested bodies are beyond measure; even if they were to fill and congest the entirety of empty space, when one looks, not so much as a speck of dust can be seen.
This laughable thing is beyond all comparison. From his mouth he spits forth bright pearls, their light shimmering and dazzling.

What is commonly seen and spoken of is inconceivable. A single word defines it; its name is established below. When the Master arrived at Nanyue Hengyang, he encountered a place where the forest and springs were most excellent.
It was different. He told the assembly, "I resided here in a previous life; now I shall restore it as a temple. He had them excavate the site, and the foundations were still there.

His spiritual influence flourished even more greatly. When he made a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land, he experienced a dream-vision of Amitābha preaching the Dharma, and the water in his pitcher filled itself.
Miraculous auspicious signs appeared in succession. Emperor Chen paid his respects and titled him the Great Chan Master. Master Zhigong sent someone to deliver this message:
"Why do you not go down the mountain to transform and save sentient beings? Why do you merely gaze at the clouds and the Milky Way? The Master replied: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time..."
"I have swallowed them all in a single gulp; where else could there be sentient beings left to transform? Such was the function of his spiritual capacity.

When he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he gathered his disciples and said: "You must not spare your own bodies or lives; you should constantly practice the Lotus Samādhi, the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, and the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, as well as the Vaipulya repentance rites.
Impermanence is swift; each of you should exert yourselves. Sit upright and chant the name of the Buddha so that he may come to welcome you."
He passed away with his palms joined; a rare fragrance filled the room, and his countenance remained as if alive.
Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, who practiced dhyāna, was styled De’an.
His surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yingchuan. At the time of his birth, auspicious light illuminated the neighboring houses; he had double pupils in his eyes and bushy eyebrows.

His skin was of eight colors and never retained any impurity. From his youth, whenever he saw an image [of the Buddha], he would invariably prostrate; whenever he encountered a monk, he would invariably bow. At eighteen, he left the household life.
By nature, he delighted in practicing dhyāna and mastered the profound texts of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Later, he went to pay homage to the Great Dhyāna Master Si of Mount Nanyue. Si said:
"Formerly on Vulture Peak, you and I together heard the Lotus Sūtra; now you have come here once again. He then showed him the four practices of peaceful bliss at the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda.
The Master entered meditative contemplation for twenty-one days. When he reached the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter of the sūtra, he said: "This is true diligence."
"This is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. His body and mind were suddenly enlightened; he saw the single assembly on Vulture Peak as solemnly present as ever, undispersed.
He reported what he had realized to Huishi, who said: "It is not you who could not realize it, nor am I one who could not recognize it.
This is the preliminary skillful means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, the initial *dhāraṇī* of revolving. You may transmit the lamp; do not become the last one to sever it."
A person of the Buddha-seed, he thereupon propagated the Dharma in Jinling, subduing renowned masters. Later, he entered Tiantai, where he subdued demons and advanced his practice.
Monarchs and ministers of two successive reigns respectfully received his magnificent transformation; Emperor Yang held him in high esteem and titled him "The Wise One" (Zhizhe).

He laid the foundation for a vast legacy, fully establishing the doctrinal and contemplative systems of his own school. Devoted to the Western Paradise, he exhorted others to cultivate the practices of the Pure Land. All that he authored...
[This work] was compiled by his disciple Guanding, who could record ten thousand words daily. It is collectively titled the *Tiantai Jiao* (The Teachings of Tiantai). The Master said:
"Since the principles of the various Buddhas' teachings have been clarified, there is no means other than contemplative practice (*guanxing*) to restore one's nature.

Thus, based on the principle of the three truths within a single mind (*zhen-su-zhong*), he demonstrated the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation. In each instance of contemplating the mind, every thought-moment is ungraspable. First...

"Emptiness comes first, the provisional follows, and the middle is last; observing the one mind while remaining free from the two extremes is like the moon beyond the clouds—this is the practice-pattern (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
Furthermore, it is said: 'In destroying all delusions, nothing surpasses emptiness; in establishing all phenomena, nothing surpasses the provisional;
in ultimately realizing all natures, nothing is greater than the middle. Therefore, within the one is the middle of all.'"

There is nothing that is not central, whether it be the provisional or the empty; the same applies to the empty and the provisional. This is precisely the phenomenal aspect of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As for the practitioner:
at the time of recollecting the Buddha, the mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the cause, and the white tuft of hair and the circular halo serve as the condition; the mindfulness thus aroused—

Regarding the very dharmas that arise: when the mind is stirred by the contemplation of the Buddha with earnest mindfulness, this is merely a provisional name; its essence is emptiness. To penetrate and discern this mind is to realize the Tathāgatagarbha.
Departing from extremes to reveal the Middle Way, both sense faculties and sense objects are entirely the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
In a single thought-moment, there is universal response; within these very extremes lies the Middle. There is neither Buddha nor thought—this is the perfect cultivation of the Mahāyāna.
This is the Dharma-gate of the three contemplations on the Buddha-nature. It may be described as being without marks, neither empty nor non-empty;
this is the true mark of the Tathāgata. Subsequently, among those who widely propagated the Tiantai teachings, the Venerable of Siming, the Great Master Fazhi, was acclaimed as the foremost.
Venerable Sir, the Dharma Master named Zhili composed the *Miaozong chuanjiao guan* (The Sublime Commentary on the Transmission of the Teachings and Contemplation).
He constantly burned four fingers as an offering to the Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise. Furthermore, he intended to cremate his own body to return to the Pure Land.

When Yang Yi, the Duke Wen, sent him a letter earnestly exhorting him to remain in this world, several years later, on the first day of the year, he established the *Guangming chan* (Luminous Repentance) with the vow to attain rebirth within seven days. By the fifth day...
On that day, he summoned the assembly to preach the Dharma. Suddenly, he recited the Buddha’s name several hundred times and then passed away while seated.
Zhao Qingxian Gong Bian composed the inscription for his stupa.
There is a method for observing the practice of the assembly: although the observation may be profound and subtle, it is fundamentally intended for those at the initial stage of the path.

If one can advance in their efforts, why worry about not succeeding? Even if one has not yet entered the ranks of the noble ones, the causal conditions are nonetheless powerful; upon being born in that land, one will be permitted to participate in the great assembly.
The environments and inhabitants seen are subtle and marvelous, beyond thought; one swiftly ascends the stages of the sages and delivers sentient beings on a vast scale.
This is forever distinct from mundane goodness or the practices of the Lesser Vehicle. Those who attain rebirth here are like those in this land who have long cultivated the perfect path:

in all their assemblies, the signs they perceive are extraordinary, and they easily awaken to the Dharma upon hearing it. By comparing this case with others, one sees that the merit lies in the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary). However—
Because one’s meritorious observance of the precepts is not pure and lacks the vow for rebirth [in a Pure Land], one remains in this defiled land.

To hear the Dharma and enter the truth, one must fear that the *Saha* world does not always provide the opportunity to meet a Buddha. Even if one encounters virtuous friends, if the physical and mental faculties are not superior, it is difficult to give rise to the bodhicitta.

Moreover, as the sensory objects are coarse and powerful, this place is truly a perilous one. Therefore, although one externally applies ritual repentances and internally exerts oneself in contemplation of the principle, [the mind may still waver].
He assisted in the dual practice and added a vow of solemn restraint, vowing that he would surely realize non-arising (anutpāda) in a precious land.
When the wise one’s conditions for transformation were exhausted, he went before the Great Stone Buddha at Xinchang and manifested illness.
After reciting the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he spoke again: “The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; its lotus ponds and jeweled trees are easy to reach.”

There was no one there. The appearance of the fire chariot manifested; yet even those who repent at a single thought can still attain rebirth, let alone those who have cultivated the power of the holy path through the熏修 (xūnxīu—perfuming and cultivation) of precepts and meditative concentration.
"My teachers and friends are all following Avalokiteśvara to come and welcome me," he said, having finished speaking.
He chanted the names of the Triple Gem and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture, as if entering samādhi.
Yuan Cizhao, the Master and Patriarch of Dianshan Bailianzi, styled himself "All Affairs Ceased" (Wan Shi Xiu).
He was the son of the Mao family of Kunshan; his mother was of the Chai clan. He was born after his mother dreamed that a Buddha entered her door.

He was named Folei because his parents had passed away early and he had entered the monastic life at Yanxiang Temple in his native province. There he practiced the dhyāna methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
One day, hearing the cry of a crow, he composed this verse: "For more than twenty years I have sought on paper; Seeking and seeking, I grew ever more despondent.
Suddenly, hearing the cry of a compassionate crow, I finally believe my former efforts were misplaced. Thereupon, he resolved to propagate [the Dharma] extensively.

Duyuan admired the legacy of the Lotus Society at Mount Lu and exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name. On behalf of all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm, he performed prostrations and repentance, praying for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Later, he went to Lake Dian and established the White Lotus Repentance Hall, where he diligently cultivated Pure Land practices.

He composed the *Diagram for Selecting Buddhas through the Four Lands and Three Contemplations of Perfect Fusion*, providing an essential guide for the Lotus School regarding both adverse and favorable circumstances.

Throughout his life, he never stirred a single thought. Traveling in all directions to exhort and transform others, he spontaneously composed verses which he titled the *Xixing ji* (Anthology of Wandering West).

He also authored the *Mituo jiyao* (Essentials of Amitābha), the *Zhengdao ge* (Song of Realizing the Way), and the *Fengyue ji* (Anthology of Wind and Moon), all of which have circulated in the world. Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree summoning him to the Deyou Hall.
He expounded the Dharma of the Pure Land, specifically bestowing upon him the title "Compassionate Illumination Patriarch, Master of Pure Deeds. He had once made a vow:
"May all people on this great earth universally awaken to the wondrous Way; taking the four characters as the core of my name, I shall guide others to single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha."
He returned to the Pure Land, and his moral influence was greatly revitalized. Later, at Duocheng, he addressed the assembly, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation are now exhausted;

it is time for me to depart. Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed into nirvana. His body was cremated, yielding countless śarīra relics, which were enshrined in a stupa at Songjiang.
[The Buddha] conferred the posthumous title "Most Victorious" upon his stupa.

The Master said: "A person of superior capacity and wisdom who awakens to this profound principle should cultivate a mind of universal equality as vast as space, free from the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Knowing there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes saṃsāra? Furthermore, there is no body or mind that receives such birth."

Death. This is called the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance through the Departure from Characteristics (*lixiang nianfo sanmei*). In this state, Amitābha appears in every thought-moment, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss manifests everywhere.

For one who contemplates in this way, it is a remembrance that is non-remembrance; remembrance is thus True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is a birth that is non-birth; birth is thus the Reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

There is not a single dharma that is inherently existent, nor is there a single dharma that is newly produced. Self and other mutually encompass one another; phenomena and principle are without [duality].
Obstructions are absent; every dust mote is complete, and every land is fully manifest. The Master said:
"A person who recites the Buddha's name has three doubts at the time of death that prevent them from being born in the Pure Land. First, they doubt:
'I have committed extremely heavy karmic deeds since birth, while my practice has been shallow for only a few days; I fear I shall not be born there. Second, they doubt: 'I owe debts to others.'"
First, there may be unfulfilled worldly desires, as well as unabated greed, anger, and delusion; fearing that one will not attain rebirth. Second, there may be doubt, thinking:

"Although I am mindful of Amitābha, I fear that when my life ends, the Buddha will not come to welcome me. Third, there may be doubt, thinking: "Although I am mindful of Amitābha, I fear that at the time of death, the Buddha will not come to receive me.

Due to these three doubts, obstacles are formed; one loses right mindfulness and fails to attain rebirth. Therefore, those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name must most earnestly and faithfully believe the Buddhist scriptures.
Understand this intent; simply do not give rise to doubt. Regarding the "Four Gates at the Hour of Death," the Master said:
Although ordinary beings possess the conditions for faith and the practice of nianfo, because their karmic obstructions from past lives are heavy, they are destined to fall into hell.
Relying on the power of the Buddha, one may exchange light for heavy between the bedding and pillows.
If there is an ignorant person who does not understand this matter, they will instead say, "I am now reciting the Buddha's name, yet I still suffer from illness," and thus slander Amitābha.

Because of this single moment of evil thought, they will go straight to hell; this is the first barrier. Second, although one possesses the conditions for upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha's name, [the following occurs...]
To speak of the Pure Land with one’s mouth while the mind remains attached to this Sahā world; to fail to seek supramundane roots of goodness; to fear death and crave life;

to invoke spirits and summon ghosts—because of such a deviant mind, one lacks the protection of the Buddhas. Consequently, driven by compassion for those drifting and falling into the three miserable realms, this is the second barrier.
Third, it may be due to taking medicine that requires the use of wine or pungent flavors, or being pressured by relatives to reciprocate...
Third: This person lacks decisive faith and has lost their roots of goodness. At the moment of death, they are summoned before the King and left to his judgment;
this is the third barrier. Fourth: At the time of death, they remain bound by their wealth and possessions and harbor deep attachment to their kin.
Losing right mindfulness, they fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), continuing to guard their household as if they were still alive. This is... [the fourth barrier].
These constitute the four barriers. Therefore, those who cultivate the Pure Land should eliminate superficial thoughts and delusive imaginings, and at every moment of thought, focus on Amitābha.
Letting go of everything with the whole body, if one can simply maintain this single-mindedness, one will be able to shatter those four barriers;
then the Pure Land will not be far away.
The Chan Master Yeo-u of Seontam Beopgyeong resided at Unmun Stream.
He constructed the Amitābha Hall and exhorted both monastics and laypeople to practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) with diligent devotion for thirty years.
He was a close friend of Chan Master Jeok-jang; through investigating the *nien-fo* kōan, he attained realization. He once composed a verse which begins: "Within the void, a thousand..."
A mountain net. In a dream, he saw a lotus pond made of the seven treasures; his path to the Western Land was firm, and not a single trace of doubt remained.

As he was about to pass away, a divine being appeared in a dream and told him: "Your fellow student, Zhezhang, has attained the Samādhi of Samantabhadra’s Vows and has already been born in the Pure Land;
he is currently waiting for you. The Master then bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright in meditation facing [the west].
The assembly said, "The Pure Land has appeared before us; we shall now depart. He wrote a verse and passed away. The verse says:
"Originally there is no home to which one can return; Who knows the path amidst the clouds? The light of the stream reflects the setting moon of the western mountains;
This is precisely the moment the dream of the immortal pond is severed."
Master Shanzhu Fudu Youtan of Mount Lu was a son of the Jiang family of Danyang.
His family had served the Buddha for generations. He left home to become a monk at the age of twenty. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Huai of Longhua Baoshan, who held him in high esteem.

Later, he traveled to various regions to seek instruction until he attained realization. He composed the *Jingyao de Nianfo* (Essential Exhortations on Mindfulness of the Buddha) as a preface to the Lotus [Sutra].
The *Zongbaojian* (Mirror of the Essence of the School) in ten fascicles was deeply praised by Zen Master Dongyan Wansong Xingxiu of Tiantong.
